Prior IFSP outcome 2 addressed requesting help during daily routines. Prior IFSP outcome 4 addressed participation in shared play. Current assessment combined interview, record review, standardized measures, bilingual language sampling, play observation, and dynamic teaching. Examiner used English and Spanish directly. Interpreter Nora Villaseñor supported the extended family interview and clarified regional vocabulary. Interpreter responses were excluded from pt scoring. CG reports pregnancy complicated by gestational hypertension and reduced fetal growth. Delivery occurred at Willowmere Regional Birth Hospital following induction. No seizures, major head injury, or known progressive neurological condition reported. CG reports mild seasonal congestion. Medication details were not available for review. Feeding includes varied soft and crunchy foods; no coughing, choking, or recurrent chest illness reported. Pt sometimes avoids mixed textures. OT Maeve Quintera monitors sensory participation and utensil use.

Early milestones were uneven. CG recalls independent walking at approx 17 months and consistent meaningful words at approx 22 months. Word combinations emerged near 34 months. These are retrospective estimates. PT Darius Fenwick previously supported balance and stair use; CG reports discharge after functional goals improved. No loss of acquired words or motor skills reported.

FAMILY / LANGUAGE HISTORY

Pt lives w/ mother Marisol Valdés Rentería, father Julián Serrano Baeza, and brother Tomás Serrano Valdés, age 7 years. Grandmother Inés Rentería Solano provides after-school care. During play, pt gave a doll food, placed it in bed, and pretended to call a family member. Symbolic play sequences were present but brief. Examiner expansion produced longer sequences w/ min cues. Pt accepted adult turns and protested appropriately when a preferred item was withheld.

| PLS-5 Spanish — Expressive Communication | 74 | 4th percentile | 69–82 | 2;9 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Total Language | 75 | 5th percentile | 70–83 | 2;11 |

Confidence intervals use the 90% level. No scaled scores were generated by these measures. CG reviewed the difference between a standard score and an age equivalent.

On Auditory Comprehension, strengths included identification of familiar objects, recognition of common actions, and understanding simple routine directions. Pt identified familiar pictured nouns in 8/10 supplemental trials. Performance declined when directions included a location word plus an attribute or required attention to grammatical information.

Pt followed related two-step directions in 3/6 trials independently and 5/6 w/ mod cues. Pt understood “in” and “on” more consistently than “behind” or “between”. Questions involving an absent object or a predicted event were difficult in both languages.

On Expressive Communication, pt named common objects, used several action words, and combined words for requests and comments. Pt had difficulty describing object function, explaining a simple event, and giving a complete response to an open question. Responses often omitted the subject, auxiliary, or a needed location word.

English and Spanish weaknesses overlapped. Familiar Spanish vocabulary improved access to some items but did not resolve difficulty organizing a message. This pattern supports a language concern beyond reduced English exposure. Results require ongoing review as school experience and treatment increase.

LANGUAGE SAMPLE / DYNAMIC ASSESSMENT

A bilingual play sample included pretend food, vehicles, a picture book, and a help-seeking routine. Spontaneous productions included “quiero más”, “baby sleep”, “no cabe”, “car go ahí”, and “me help”. These examples show communicative intent, emerging combinations, and mixed-language resources.

Pt also said "Brisa come" while looking at a dog picture. During a family photo discussion, pt said "mamá Marisol Valdés Rentería aquí." These productions were transcribed without converting the names into clinical preservation spans.

Examiner used Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) conventions for descriptive coding. An omitted obligatory English word was marked [EW]. Spanish structures were judged within Spanish grammar. Examiner did not apply English omission rules to valid Spanish subject omission.

The sample contained frequent requests and labels, fewer comments, and limited explanations. Pt answered familiar “what” questions in 7/10 opportunities. Responses to “where” questions were accurate in 4/10 opportunities independently and 7/10 after visual choices and mod cues.

For dynamic teaching, examiner modeled a short subject-action-object pattern, paired it w/ pictures, and then reduced support. Pt expanded a message in 6/8 teaching trials w/ mod cues. After a brief delay, pt independently used the practiced pattern in 3/8 opportunities. Learning was evident, but generalization remained limited.

CG observed that expansions were more successful when adults followed pt's interest. Repeated direct questions increased short answers and occasional withdrawal. Examiner coached CG to pause, comment, and offer a useful model. Pt then initiated several new play turns without direct prompting.

SPEECH SOUND / ORAL MECHANISM FINDINGS

Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation 3 (GFTA-3) — Sounds-in-Words provided a structured English elicitation sample. Standard scores were withheld b/c this administration served descriptive bilingual analysis and included supplemental Spanish elicitation. No normative inference was made from the English-only sample.

Oral structures appeared adequate for speech during this brief examination. Facial movement was symmetrical. Lip closure, tongue lateral movement, and jaw opening were observed during imitation and play. Pt needed mod cues for unfamiliar movement directions. No diagnostic nonspeech strength testing was completed.

Speech showed fronting of velar targets, variable final-consonant omission, and cluster reduction. Target /k/ was sometimes realized as [t]; target /g/ was sometimes realized as [d]. English target “key” elicited “tea”. Target “goat” elicited “doe”. Spanish target “casa” elicited “tasa”.

Pt produced /k/ in isolation in 5/10 trials w/ max cues and in a simple syllable in 2/10 trials w/ max cues. Spanish /ɾ/ and /r/ were variable; these findings were interpreted cautiously given age, dialect, and task demands.

Connected-speech intelligibility was estimated at approx 55% for the unfamiliar examiner when context was available. CG estimated approx 80% understanding at home. These are listener estimates, not standardized scores. Longer utterances were harder to understand than single words.

No consistent vowel distortion, disrupted stress, or visible articulatory groping occurred. The available sample does not establish childhood apraxia of speech. Continue monitoring consistency and sequencing as utterance length increases. Voice quality was functional; no persistent dysfluency observed.

IMPRESSIONS

Ana Lucía Serrano Valdés presents w/ receptive-expressive language weaknesses and a speech sound disorder that affect participation across home and school routines. Difficulties appeared in both languages and persisted despite familiar vocabulary, supportive presentation, and opportunities to respond conceptually.

Clinical impression supports F80.2 and F80.0. Bilingual exposure does not explain the full pattern. Relative strengths include social interest, symbolic play, shared enjoyment, functional requesting, and response to visual support. Prognosis for functional improvement is favorable w/ consistent treatment and CG participation.

Pt requires support to understand expanded directions, organize short messages, repair breakdowns, and produce selected consonant contrasts. Communication frustration may contribute to taking materials or leaving an activity. Classroom supports should address access to language before staff infer a behavior problem.

This assessment does not determine eligibility for other services or establish a broader developmental diagnosis. School eligibility decisions require the educational team's review. Hearing history remains relevant, although the reviewed audiology report supports adequate current speech access.

RECOMMENDATIONS / PLAN

1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy twice weekly, approx thirty minutes per visit, with periodic CG coaching. Use Spanish and English according to each activity, listener, and functional need. Coordinate home and classroom targets.

2. Use Hanen interaction strategies, including following pt's lead, waiting, and expanding messages. Consider It Takes Two to Talk parent education where available. Give CG brief practice examples tied to meals, dressing, books, and pretend play.

3. Use selected Cycles activities for phonological patterns after baseline sampling. Include meaningful contrasts and speech practice. Consider PROMPT only when assessment identifies a specific motor support need and the treating clinician has appropriate training. Kaufman methods are not selected at present; reconsider only if later findings support that approach.

4. Offer picture supports for choices, help, breaks, and repair. A formal PECS program is optional and would require individualized assessment. Pt may benefit from simple visual supports without a full protocol.

5. For Goal 1, pt will follow related two-step directions containing one location concept in 8/10 opportunities w/ min cues across therapy and a familiar routine.

6. For Goal 2, pt will produce a functional message containing a person, action, and object or location in 8/10 opportunities w/ min cues. Accept an appropriate response in either language.

7. For Goal 3, pt will repair a misunderstood message by repeating, adding information, pointing, or using a picture in 4/5 opportunities w/ min cues.

8. For Goal 4, pt will produce selected velar contrasts in practiced words with 70% accuracy w/ mod cues. Establish targets separately for each language and check transfer.

9. Share results with Ms. Elena Figueroa and assistant Jonah Mirell. Recommend visual directions, extra response time, and modeled peer-entry phrases. Practice with willing classmates during supported play; avoid requiring public repetition after an error.

10. Coordinate with OT Maeve Quintera for shared routines and regulation supports. Contact Dr. Owen Bellamy if listening changes recur. Review progress on November 19, 2026 and revise targets using functional samples.

CG stated understanding through teach-back and selected snack requests and toy cleanup for initial home practice. Written bilingual strategies were provided. Release status must be checked before sharing this fictional report outside the evaluation team.

BACKGROUND AND REFERRAL

The referral concerns limited phrase use, difficulty understanding unfamiliar directions, and reduced speech clarity during play. Ms. Marisol Varela requested an assessment that considered both Spanish and English. She reported that unfamiliar adults often miss the meaning of Elian's messages. The family wants practical strategies for meals, dressing, shared reading, and communication with other children.

The referring office is Oficina de Servicios del Desarrollo Infantil de los Condados de Briarleaf y Juniper. Its short name is CDSA Briarleaf-Juniper. The service coordinator, Nadia Beltrán, works through Agencia Comunitaria de Coordinación de Servicios y Enlace Familiar del Este de Carolina del Norte. The agency uses the short name Enlace Familiar del Este. These names identify separate organizations with different responsibilities.

The current individualized family service plan began on April 21, 2026. The referral record identifies IFSP Outcome 1 as improving everyday requests and IFSP Outcome 2 as improving participation in family routines. The family reported steady progress with gestures but slower progress with spoken combinations. No loss of previously acquired skills was reported.

Ms. Marisol Varela gave consent for assessment and exchange of relevant findings with the service coordinator and pediatrician. The clinician reviewed referral records, interviewed the parent, observed play, and completed structured assessment activities.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

Elian Tomás Varela was born at Pine Lantern Health Women’s Hospital, Meadowbank Campus following spontaneous preterm labor. Gestational age was 35 weeks 4 days. Recorded birth weight was 2,410 g. Apgar scores were 7 at the first measurement and 9 at the subsequent measurement. The available discharge summary described brief respiratory support and difficulty maintaining feeding endurance.

The child spent twelve days in the neonatal intensive care unit at Pine Lantern Health Women’s Hospital, Meadowbank Campus. The discharge record documented a passed newborn hearing screen. The parent reported no seizures, major surgery, or prolonged hospitalization after discharge. Early motor development was described as gradual, with independent walking at 16 months.

Dr. Priya Desai follows growth and development at Pine Lantern Health Pediatric Clinic, Alder Creek Campus. The parent reported several middle-ear infections during the previous winter. The most recent documented infection occurred on February 6, 2026. An audiology visit on June 18, 2026 at Pine Lantern Health ENT and Audiology, Juniper Campus documented responses within the expected range in sound-field testing.

Audiologist Marcus Ibarra recommended an ear-specific follow-up because sound-field responses cannot establish separate hearing levels for each ear. That appointment is scheduled for August 12, 2026 at 8:30 a.m.. No medication was administered during this evaluation. The parent reported typical sleep, a varied diet, and no current choking concerns.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Elian lives with his parents and his older sister, Inés Varela, who is 6 years old. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Cárdenas, provides care on two afternoons each week. A family friend, Lucinda Mora, sometimes provides evening care. The household includes a dog named Nube, who frequently appears in the child’s play and spontaneous messages.

Spanish is the main language used by Ms. Marisol Varela and grandmother Rosa Cárdenas. Mr. Andrés Varela uses both languages. Sister Inés usually speaks English during pretend play and Spanish during meals. The parent estimated current exposure as 65% Spanish and 35% English. These estimates describe exposure, not proficiency.

The family has used both languages since infancy. The parent reported that comprehension appears stronger in familiar Spanish routines, while several preferred toy labels occur in English. Mixed-language combinations are accepted at home. The family does not want intervention to reduce Spanish use or require one language per caregiver.

Ms. Marisol Varela works at Juniper Loom Packaging. Mr. Andrés Varela works at Alder Creek Orchard Supply. Their schedules affect appointment availability. Transportation assistance is sometimes arranged by Briarleaf County Department of Social Services, through caseworker Tessa Rowan.

EARLY LEARNING AND COMMUNITY SERVICES

Elian attends Little Lantern Grove Childcare on weekday mornings. Lead teacher Ms. Brielle Santos reported that he joins movement songs, watches peers, and brings objects to adults for help. Classroom assistant Mr. Owen Pell reported more successful participation when instructions include gestures and a clear demonstration.

The child frequently plays beside classmates Mila Fenwick and Noah Calder. During a recent classroom observation, Mila offered a toy truck, and Eli responded with a smile and a pointing gesture. Staff reported that frustration increases when another child takes an object before he can communicate a request.

The family receives nutrition support from Briarleaf County WIC Program. A family resource referral is active with Smart Start of Briarleaf and Juniper. Home-based family support is available through Lantern Valley Early Head Start. These agencies do not currently provide direct speech-language treatment.

Transition planning includes contact with Alder Creek County Schools. The service coordinator will help the family request a preschool evaluation before the child’s third birthday. A transition meeting is scheduled for August 20, 2026. Eligibility decisions remain the responsibility of the receiving school team.

ASSESSMENT CONDITIONS AND METHODS

Camila R. Serrano completed the evaluation in English and Spanish without an interpreter. The parent remained present and helped identify familiar vocabulary. The child entered comfortably, explored materials, and tolerated transitions when activities alternated between table tasks and floor play. Two movement breaks supported participation.

The assessment included Preschool Language Scales–Fifth Edition, abbreviated PLS-5, Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation–Third Edition, and Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test–Fifth Edition. English standardized administration occurred before additional Spanish probes. Spanish responses and supported trials were documented separately and were not substituted into English scoring.

Selected items from Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale supported a descriptive review of communication milestones. The clinician also reviewed a prior Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development–Fourth Edition report completed at 26 months. That report served as historical context rather than a current developmental estimate.

English norm-referenced scores compare performance with each instrument’s reference sample. They do not estimate total bilingual ability. Interpretation therefore combined parent reports, observations across languages, developmental history, language sampling, and response to teaching.

Attention varied with task demands. No fatigue or distress required termination. The clinician considered the observed communication patterns representative of the child’s current participation, with the usual limitation that one visit cannot capture every home or classroom skill.

STANDARDIZED AND DESCRIPTIVE RESULTS

Measure	Subtest or domain	Score type	Result	Percentile	Confidence interval or developmental range
PLS-5	Auditory Comprehension	Standard score	78	7th percentile	73–85
PLS-5	Expressive Communication	Standard score	74	4th percentile	68–81
PLS-5	Total Language	Standard score	75	5th percentile	70–82
Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation–Third Edition	Sounds-in-Words	Standard score	79	8th percentile	73–86
Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test–Fifth Edition	Receptive Vocabulary	Standard score	77	6th percentile	71–84
Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development–Fourth Edition	Receptive Communication	Historical scaled score	6	Not reported	Not reported

Confidence intervals shown above use the 90% level. Developmental ranges describe sampled milestones and are not precise measures of developmental age. English vocabulary performance may reflect language exposure as well as underlying language skill. Scores must remain connected to these limitations when shared with another provider.

RECEPTIVE AND EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE FINDINGS

Elian understood familiar object labels, routine action words, and several body-part labels across languages. He followed familiar one-step directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Performance decreased to 3/8 for unfamiliar directions containing two actions. With visual cues and a demonstration, he completed 6/8 supported trials.

The child identified common pictures more consistently when labels occurred in either familiar language. He showed emerging understanding of simple location concepts but relied on the adult’s pointing for less familiar relationships. Responses to questions were strongest when the relevant object remained visible. Questions about a recent event produced fewer clear answers.

Spontaneous speech included single words, sound effects, and occasional combinations. Examples included “más agua,” “my car,” “mamá ven,” and “no shoe.” These combinations communicated requests, protests, possession, and social contact. Mixing languages did not itself indicate impairment.

During teaching, Eli learned a new action label after repeated models and used it again during play. However, he needed mod cues to combine the label with another meaningful word. Similar support was needed in both languages. The parent described the same difficulty during familiar home routines.

A conversational sample contained 42 analyzable utterances. Mean length of utterance in words was 1.7, interpreted descriptively across the mixed-language sample. The clinician marked [EW] on utterances containing an extra word and reviewed those examples individually. No conclusion about bilingual grammar depended on that code alone.

SPEECH SOUND AND INTELLIGIBILITY FINDINGS

The speech sample showed variable production of consonants in longer words and frequent simplification of consonant clusters. The child sometimes produced /k/ as [t] and /g/ as [d]; these productions are represented here as /k/, [t], /g/, and [d]. Production of /s/ varied by word position and speaking rate.

The clinician heard [w] in some English words containing /r/. Spanish /ɾ/ was inconsistent, and Spanish /r/ was not established in the sample. These later-developing sounds were considered within age and language expectations. Their absence alone does not justify a disorder diagnosis.

Examples included “tat” for “cat” and “poon” for “spoon.” When talking about the dog, he said “Nube go.” That named production was recorded separately from the phonetic examples. The clinician avoided treating an unfamiliar English label as evidence of a speech sound error.

An unfamiliar listener understood approximately 55% of spontaneous messages when the topic was known. Intelligibility improved to approximately 75% when gestures and objects supplied context. These are clinical estimates from this visit, not standardized scores. The parent reported better understanding at home.

Stimulability probes showed correct /k/ production in 4/10 trials with max cues, improving to 7/10 with a placement model and slowed practice. These findings support further assessment during treatment before selecting a fixed speech sound protocol.

PLAY, SOCIAL COMMUNICATION, AND FEEDING

Elian used eye gaze, pointing, giving, and shared smiles to connect with adults. He initiated joint attention during preferred play and checked the parent’s reaction when a toy made an unexpected sound. Pretend play included feeding a doll, parking vehicles, and placing animals inside a toy house.

Turn-taking was successful in 4 of 5 supported opportunities. The child needed mod cues to request another turn using speech rather than reaching. Communication breakdowns usually led to repeated gestures, louder speech, or bringing the object closer. He accepted an adult model and sometimes tried again.

The oral mechanism screening showed functional facial symmetry and movement for the observed speech and eating tasks. The clinician did not complete a detailed feeding evaluation. The child drank water and ate a familiar snack without observed coughing, wet vocal quality, or distress.

The parent reported occasional refusal of unfamiliar textures but no growth concern. Current information does not support a feeding referral. The family should contact the pediatrician if swallowing symptoms or reduced intake develop. Ear-specific hearing follow-up remains relevant because fluctuating access to sound can affect communication learning.

CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, documented with F80.2. The conclusion rests on difficulty learning and combining language across both languages, limited comprehension beyond familiar routines, caregiver concerns, and the need for sustained support during teaching. English test scores contribute context but do not independently establish the diagnosis.

Elian has useful communication strengths, including social interest, gesture use, pretend play, and a positive response to models. These strengths should guide intervention. Speech sound development also warrants treatment monitoring because reduced clarity limits participation. The current sample does not support a definitive motor speech diagnosis.

The clinician recommends bilingual intervention and continued Spanish use at home. The family’s language choices support relationships and access to daily routines. Progress should be measured through functional communication across settings, rather than through English performance alone.

RECOMMENDATIONS AND SERVICE PLAN

1. Begin speech-language treatment focused on comprehension, meaningful word combinations, and repair of communication breakdowns. Use focused stimulation, Enhanced Milieu Teaching, and caregiver coaching within preferred routines. Select vocabulary with the family and classroom staff.

2. Introduce two-word models that match the child’s intended message. Examples include “más pan,” “abre caja,” “help me,” and “car go.” Accept speech, gestures, and mixed-language responses. Expand the message without requiring repeated correction.

3. Use Hanen-informed interaction strategies, including waiting, following the child’s lead, and balancing adult turns with child turns. This recommendation describes strategies; it does not represent enrollment in a certified parent program.

4. Support comprehension through visual cues, short directions, and meaningful demonstrations. Gradually reduce assistance from mod cues to min cues as performance stabilizes. Confirm understanding through the child’s action rather than repeated questioning.

5. Address speech clarity through play-based practice of functional words. Consider Cycles only after collecting a broader bilingual speech sample. PROMPT and PECS are not current treatment recommendations because this assessment did not establish a need for those approaches.

6. Complete the scheduled audiology follow-up. Share the findings with the pediatrician and treating clinician. The service coordinator should confirm that transportation and appointment information are available to the family.

PROPOSED SERVICE SCHEDULE

Service	Provider or agency	Frequency and duration	Preferred time	Start or review date
Individual speech-language treatment	Camila R. Serrano, Two Rivers Pediatric Communication	Weekly, forty-five minutes	10:00 a.m.	July 28, 2026
Caregiver coaching	Treating clinician and parent	Within each treatment visit	10:30 a.m.	July 28, 2026
Classroom consultation	Little Lantern Grove Childcare	Monthly, twenty minutes	11:15 a.m.	August 6, 2026
Transition coordination	CDSA Briarleaf-Juniper and Enlace Familiar del Este	As needed through transition	By arrangement	August 20, 2026
Progress review	Treating clinician and service coordinator	After the initial treatment block	9:30 a.m.	September 8, 2026

FUNCTIONAL OUTCOMES AND FOLLOW-UP

For IFSP Outcome 1, Elian will use a meaningful word combination or coordinated speech and gesture to request help in 4 of 5 routine opportunities with min cues. The family will record examples during meals and dressing.

For IFSP Outcome 2, the child will follow a familiar direction containing two related actions in 80% of opportunities with min cues. Treatment will begin with real objects and daily activities. The team will track Spanish and English opportunities separately while considering overall functional progress.

The clinician will review progress with Nadia Beltrán before preschool transition. Recommendations may change after additional hearing information, classroom observations, and treatment response. The parent received an English report and a verbal explanation in Spanish. Ms. Marisol Varela accurately restated the main recommendations and identified meals as the preferred starting routine.

Dear Mariela de la Cruz and Gabriel Santos-Reyes,

Thank you for bringing Nicolás to meet with me. This letter explains what we learned, what the results mean, and how we can help. Your child showed curiosity, humor, and a strong wish to connect. Those strengths will support his progress.

The referral from Dr. Avery Bellamy arrived on August 19, 2026. It described concerns about language development and requested a speech-language assessment. Our office reviewed the referral, your questionnaire, classroom notes, and an earlier developmental service summary.

The birth history described an uncomplicated delivery and no extended hospital stay. You reported no feeding tube, breathing support, seizures, or major surgery. These details came from your questionnaire and interview; I did not independently review the delivery record.

Early feeding was comfortable overall. You recalled some difficulty moving from smooth foods to mixed textures. He now eats several familiar family foods and drinks from an open cup. You reported no current coughing, choking, or pain with meals.

There were several ear infections during early childhood. The audiology report from Lena Okafor at Cedar Moon Children's Hospital, dated August 28, 2026, documented hearing adequate for speech access during that visit. Please continue routine hearing follow-up with his medical team.

Dr. Avery Bellamy remains the primary care physician. You reported no daily prescription medicines and no known medication allergies. Sleep is usually steady, although settling takes longer after busy days. No new medical concern appeared during this assessment.

You recalled independent walking at approximately 14 months and recognizable words near 20 months. Word combinations became more common around 30 months. These are parent estimates. They help describe development but do not establish a diagnosis alone.

Nico lives with both parents and his sister, Lucía Santos-Reyes, who is 7 years old. His grandmother, Mercedes del Río, visits regularly. A family caregiver, doña Lupe, provides care on some afternoons.

The family dog, Bongo, often appears in his play stories. During our visit, he said, “Bongo go outside.” Because that message concerned a familiar pet, you understood his meaning immediately. I needed the surrounding play to understand it.

Spanish is the main language used during family meals and visits. English is common at daycare and during community activities. Gabriel Santos-Reyes uses both languages at home. Mariela de la Cruz usually speaks Spanish during bedtime stories.

His sister, Lucía, moves comfortably between the languages during play. His grandmother, Mercedes del Río, prefers Spanish. You described these language choices as natural family routines. You do not use a fixed schedule for either language.

Gabriel Santos-Reyes works at Meadowglass Packaging Cooperative. A changing work schedule affects who handles pickup and evening routines. The neighbor who sometimes assists with transportation, Mr. Tom, does not provide language instruction or therapy.

You reported no known family history of childhood hearing loss. A relative reportedly received speech support, but you did not have records or a clear description. We treated that information as background rather than evidence of a particular inherited condition.

Learning two languages does not explain all the difficulties described here. We considered language exposure, opportunities to practice, and communication in both languages. Your goal of keeping Spanish is appropriate. Family language gives him access to relationships, stories, and everyday learning.

During the session, Nicolás explored toy animals, a pretend kitchen, picture books, and blocks. He checked my face, shared discoveries, and brought objects to request help. He accepted transitions best when I showed the next activity first.

He initially stayed close to his mother, Mariela de la Cruz. After a short warm-up, he played with me while she remained nearby. Brief movement breaks helped him return to table activities. His participation was sufficient for the tasks described below.

I administered the English Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) according to its directions for the scored items. Separate Spanish activities included conversation, play, directions, and learning trials. Translated or coached responses did not contribute to standardized scores.

The PLS-5 compares performance with its reference group. Its scores describe his performance on English tasks during this visit. They do not measure his full knowledge across languages. The table therefore belongs beside the family interview and bilingual observations.

| PLS-5 Expressive Communication | 72 | 3rd percentile | 66–81 | 2;9 |
| PLS-5 Total Language | 73 | 4th percentile | 68–81 | 2;10 |

The confidence intervals use a 90% confidence level. Age equivalents summarize particular test performance. They do not mean that he functions like a younger child in every area. We will use daily communication skills to guide treatment.

On Auditory Comprehension, he understood familiar actions and identified common objects. Directions became harder when they included location words, several details, or a less familiar sentence form. He sometimes acted on the last word he heard.

During separate play tasks, he followed familiar single-step directions in 8/10 opportunities, or 80%, with min cues. He followed related two-step directions in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. These observations were outside standardized scoring.

On Expressive Communication, he named familiar items and combined words for requests. He had difficulty explaining an event, adding needed details, and forming some questions. His message length varied with familiarity, language, and the support available.

In English play, he produced “want more car” and “baby sleeping”. In Spanish play, he produced “más agua” and “perro corre”. These messages showed useful meaning, although longer explanations often needed adult help.

When asked to describe a picture, he first said “boy fall”. After a model and mod cues, he added “boy fall down”. In a separate Spanish activity, he also needed support to explain who acted and what happened.

Learning trials showed a useful response to teaching. After demonstrations, he used a new location word in 4/6 opportunities with mod cues. Later, he used it in 2/6 opportunities with min cues. Continued practice across activities will matter.

Speech clarity varied with message length. I heard substitutions involving /k/ and /g/ in some English words. During informal imitation, the target “car” became “tar”. I also heard [w] for /r/ in an English sample.

Spanish speech included variable production of /ɾ/. These observations require further sampling before a separate speech diagnosis. We must consider each language's sound system and expected development. Accent or differences between languages should not be treated as errors.

His lips, tongue, and jaw appeared functional for the speech tasks observed. Voice sounded comfortable, and I did not hear persistent stuttering during the sample. A brief clinic sample cannot describe every speaking situation.

The language sample included [EW] when coding an extra word. Sample codes organize observations; they are not diagnoses. I considered communication success, sentence patterns, gestures, and responses to support together.

My impression is a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, ICD-10 F80.2. This impression rests on difficulties understanding and expressing messages across languages, developmental history, family concerns, and classroom examples. The English standardized scores provide supporting information within their limits.

His strengths include social interest, shared attention, pretend play, persistence, and improvement after models. He already uses several ways to communicate. Treatment should build spoken language while allowing gestures, pictures, and other supports that help him participate.

I recommend the following plan:

1. Begin speech-language treatment through PLPSLT twice weekly, subject to the approved service plan. Individual treatment would use CPT 92507. Start with useful requests, help-seeking, directions, and short explanations in both languages.

2. Teach caregivers practical strategies through Hanen-informed coaching. Follow his interests, pause for a response, and expand his message slightly. If he says “more juice”, an adult can model “I want more juice” without requiring repetition.

3. Use brief practice during meals, books, and play. Offer choices and allow time to answer. Acknowledge gestures and partial words. Model the message he needs, then continue the activity so communication remains useful and enjoyable.

4. Develop IFSP Outcome 3 from the earlier plan dated May 16, 2025 into current family priorities. The Juniper Bend Children's Developmental Services Agency record provides background. Confirm the present service pathway with coordinator Tessa Morgan.

5. For treatment Goal 1, target complete requests in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. For Goal 2, target related two-step directions in 4/5 opportunities with min cues. Measure performance across familiar activities and both languages.

6. Coordinate classroom supports with Miss Ana and la maestra Carmen. Use pictures, short directions, and a pause before repeating. Arrange supported play with Sofía or Eli, while keeping participation comfortable for every child.

7. Request an educational evaluation through Willow Lantern Elementary School if you want school services considered. Share this report and classroom concerns. The school team will determine eligibility and the appropriate educational plan through its own process.

8. Review progress on December 14, 2026. Bring examples of successful messages and difficult situations. We will adjust goals using therapy data, family observations, and teacher reports. Contact us sooner if communication changes sharply or new hearing concerns arise.

Please keep speaking the languages that feel natural to your family. You do not need to translate every sentence or correct every attempt. Warm, repeated exchanges during ordinary activities give him many chances to understand, respond, and learn.

Thank you for sharing your observations and hopes for Nicolás. Your knowledge helped make this assessment useful. I look forward to helping your family build communication that works at home, in care, and with friends.

Warmly,

Elena Marisol Vega-Pérez, MS, CCC-SLP  
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist  
Pine Lantern Pediatric Speech and Language Therapy, PLLC  
(919) 555-0146  
elena.vega@pinelantern.example

text:
Document Type: Pediatric Speech-Language Evaluation
Record Status: Fictional synthetic EMR export for offline de-identification testing
Client: Elena Marisol Vega
Preferred Name: Lena
Date of Birth: 08/13/2022
Age at Evaluation: 4;2
Medical Record Number: NC-SLP-482716
Medicaid Member Number: 583104927Q
Referral Number: REF-260918-731
Authorization Number: AUTH-SL-609284
Evaluation Date: October 15, 2026
Report Date: October 19, 2026
Visit Time: 9:10 a.m. to 10:45 a.m.
Location: Cedar Lantern Pediatric Communication
Office Address: 418 Willowglass Lane, Suite 204, Alderhaven, North Carolina 27684
County: Bellwater County
Parent: Mariana Vega
Parent: Daniel Vega
Home Address: 72 Finchmeadow Court, Alderhaven, North Carolina 27684
Contact Telephone: 919-555-0146
Contact Email: mariana.vega@example.com
Clinic Website: https://cedarlantern.example.org
Referring Physician: Dr. Priya Nalin
Evaluating Clinician: Isabel Cárdenas, MS, CCC-SLP
Clinician Role: Bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist
Interpreter: None; clinician provided direct English and Spanish assessment
Billing: CPT 92523
Referral Diagnosis: ICD-10 F80.9
Assessment Diagnoses: ICD-10 F80.2; ICD-10 F80.0
School District: Bellwater County Learning District
School: Juniper Lantern Elementary School
Classroom: Ms. Lopez's room

REASON FOR REFERRAL

Elena was referred because her family and preschool team reported limited sentence development and difficulty being understood. Her mother, Mariana Vega, described frequent frustration when familiar adults could not interpret requests. Her father, Daniel Vega, reported that she sometimes abandoned messages after repeating them. The referral requested evaluation of receptive language, expressive language, speech production, and functional communication across English and Spanish.

The family wanted practical information about the child's communication needs in both languages. They specifically requested guidance that would preserve Spanish participation at home while supporting English participation at school. Their priorities included asking for help, describing events, following classroom directions, and repairing misunderstood messages. This evaluation combined standardized English testing with bilingual observation, caregiver interview, classroom information, and structured teaching tasks. All histories and findings in this document describe a fictional case.

BACKGROUND AND RECORD REVIEW

Records reviewed included a pediatric referral dated September 18, 2026, a school communication form dated September 30, 2026, and an early intervention summary dated June 11, 2025. The referral from Dr. Priya Nalin documented concerns about sentence length and speech clarity. The school form described variable participation during group instruction, particularly when directions contained unfamiliar vocabulary or several actions.

Earlier services were coordinated through Bellwater Children’s Developmental Services Agency. The prior IFSP listed outcome 2, which addressed communicating needs during daily routines, and outcome 4, which addressed joining family play. Services ended after transition planning. The family reported no current outpatient speech-language treatment. School staff were gathering information for an educational evaluation; this clinical assessment does not determine school eligibility.

The mother provided the developmental history in Spanish and English. The father supplied additional information by a written questionnaire. Both accounts described stronger communication during familiar routines than during unfamiliar activities. Neither parent reported loss of previously acquired words or social engagement. The clinician treated caregiver reports as contextual information and compared them with direct observations.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

The child was born at 38 weeks, 4 days gestation at Meadow Harbor Women’s and Children’s Hospital in Alderhaven, North Carolina. Reported birth weight was 6 lb 11 oz. Apgar scores were 8 at the first assessment and 9 at the second assessment. The mother reported an uncomplicated delivery and discharge with the family. No neonatal intensive care admission, assisted ventilation, or feeding tube was reported.

Medical history included intermittent middle ear infections during toddlerhood. The family reported no ear surgery, seizures, significant head injury, or known neurological diagnosis. An audiology report from Maya Sen at Meadow Harbor Children’s Hospital, dated August 27, 2026, described hearing sufficient for speech access in the tested conditions. Continued monitoring was recommended if ear symptoms returned. Hearing was not independently measured during this appointment.

Early motor development was described as generally unremarkable. First independent steps occurred at approximately 13 months. Meaningful first words were reported near 19 months, with consistent word combinations emerging around 32 months. The parents could not provide exact dates for these milestones. These ages represent caregiver estimates rather than contemporaneous developmental records.

The child eats a varied diet and drinks from an open cup. No coughing, choking, recurrent respiratory illness, or prolonged mealtimes was reported. Sleep was described as consistent, with occasional difficulty settling after active evenings. No medication was administered during the evaluation. The mother reported no current pain, acute illness, or visual concern that appeared to affect participation.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Elena lives with her parents and her brother, Sol Vega, who is 7 years old. Her maternal grandmother, Rosa Benítez, provides care after school. An aunt, Hope Benítez, visits regularly and reads with the children. A family babysitter, Will Mercado, occasionally provides evening care. The household dog, Mango, was mentioned repeatedly during the interview and language sample.

Spanish is the main language used by the mother and grandmother. The father uses both English and Spanish, depending on the activity and communication partner. The brother usually initiates play in English and responds to Spanish directions. English exposure increased when the child began daycare at 2;8. The family described daily, meaningful opportunities to hear and use both languages, with different vocabulary associated with each setting.

The mother works at Alderhaven Orchard Supply, where she uses Spanish with coworkers and English during some customer interactions. The father works at Finchstone Equipment Services. These routines influence which adult completes school pickup and which language is used during evening activities. The family did not identify one language as consistently stronger across every communication task.

Caregivers reported that the child understands familiar Spanish routines well but struggles with new explanations in either language. She often combines an English noun with a Spanish verb or article. Such language mixing was treated as an expected bilingual behavior, not an error by itself. Concerns focused on limited sentence organization, weak message detail, and persistent difficulty learning new forms across both languages.

EDUCATIONAL AND DAYCARE HISTORY

The child attends a preschool program within Juniper Lantern Elementary School, part of Bellwater County Learning District. Her lead teacher is Ms. Ana Lopez. Classroom assistant Tessa Rowan supports transitions and small group activities. The family and school commonly refer to the classroom as Ms. Lopez's room. The classroom schedule includes shared reading, centers, outdoor play, and lunch.

Before preschool, she attended Little Lantern Daycare in Briar Hollow, North Carolina. Her former teacher, Ms. Nadia Cruz, reported that gestures and familiar routines helped her communicate. The daycare report noted that she enjoyed pretend cooking and vehicle play but rarely explained a problem without adult support. No formal language scores were available from that setting.

Current classroom information described interest in peers and a tendency to watch before joining activities. Classmates Milo Hart and Esme Reed frequently invite her into pretend play. During group discussions, she may answer with a related noun rather than a complete explanation. Staff reported that visual demonstrations improve participation. Difficulties increase when the class is noisy or when directions require remembering several unfamiliar details.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES AND LIMITATIONS

The evaluation included the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, abbreviated PLS-5, and the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition, abbreviated GFTA-3. English standardized administration was completed before bilingual teaching activities. The clinician also obtained conversational samples, observed play, examined oral structures, and compared responses across languages. Spanish tasks were informal and were not assigned standardized scores.

English test scores describe performance under the administered conditions. The normative samples do not fully represent this child's language experience. Scores therefore cannot independently establish a disorder or measure total bilingual knowledge. The clinician did not translate standardized items during scoring, combine English and Spanish item totals, or treat informal Spanish responses as norm-referenced results.

Confidence intervals reflect measurement uncertainty within each test's scoring framework. They do not correct for differences between the normative population and the child's language exposure. Age equivalents are descriptive estimates and should not be used as developmental ages or service thresholds. Diagnostic interpretation relied on converging evidence from both languages, learning tasks, family history, and functional participation.

BEHAVIORAL OBSERVATIONS

The child entered the room with her mother and initially stayed nearby. She began exploring play materials after a brief demonstration. She shared attention, showed objects, and checked the clinician's reaction during humorous routines. Her activity level remained manageable, and she accepted changes between tasks when the next activity was shown. A short movement break supported return to structured work.

She used pointing, facial expression, single words, and short phrases to communicate. When misunderstood, she sometimes repeated the same message more loudly. With a model, she could add a gesture or another word. During a familiar play sequence, she said "Mango run" while moving a toy dog. The named production was retained as a contextual example of communication.

Participation was strongest with concrete materials and predictable exchanges. Open-ended questions often produced silence, a related word, or a gesture. Performance improved when the clinician reduced language demands and allowed additional response time. The observed difficulties were not fully explained by reluctance to interact, although unfamiliar testing demands likely reduced some responses.

STANDARDIZED SCORE SUMMARY

| Measure | Administration date | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5: Auditory Comprehension | 10/15/2026 | 81 | 10th percentile | 75–89, 90% confidence | 3;3 |
| PLS-5: Expressive Communication | 10/15/2026 | 74 | 4th percentile | 68–82, 90% confidence | 2;10 |
| PLS-5: Total Language | 10/15/2026 | 76 | 5th percentile | 70–84, 90% confidence | 3;0 |
| GFTA-3: Sounds-in-Words | 10/15/2026 | 72 | 3rd percentile | 67–80, 90% confidence | 2;6–2;9 |

No scaled scores were calculated. The listed confidence levels and ranges accompany the corresponding scores. All results require the bilingual interpretation described above.

RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE FINDINGS

On Auditory Comprehension, the child demonstrated understanding of familiar objects, common actions, simple spatial relationships, and routine directions. She identified pictured actions more consistently than she answered questions about reasons or consequences. Familiar vocabulary supported successful responses. Unfamiliar relational terms and longer sentences increased errors, even when the pictured objects were known.

Informal Spanish activities showed a similar pattern. She followed concrete directions involving familiar toys but needed repetition or demonstration when an instruction included several relationships. In a bilingual direction task, she completed 6/10 items independently and 8/10 after a visual demonstration. These figures describe this session only and are not standardized scores.

The clinician checked whether incorrect responses reflected unfamiliar English words. Some responses improved when a comparable Spanish instruction was provided. Other difficulties remained in both languages, particularly when she needed to integrate an action, location, and sequence. This pattern supports a concern about language processing beyond limited English exposure alone.

During book sharing, she located named characters and objects but inconsistently explained what happened before or after an event. She benefited from pictures, shorter questions, and contextual reminders. Classroom supports should therefore include visible sequences and checks of understanding through action or explanation. A simple affirmative response did not reliably show that she understood a direction.

EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE FINDINGS

On Expressive Communication, the child named familiar objects and used short combinations to request or comment. She had difficulty describing events, adding grammatical detail, and producing complete answers to open-ended questions. Her responses often conveyed the main topic while omitting relationships between people, actions, and objects. Similar limitations appeared during informal Spanish conversation.

Across play samples, she used productions such as "baby eat", "want more car", and "no está aquí". Language mixing included "quiero blue one". Mixing itself was not counted as evidence of disorder. The clinician examined whether each message carried sufficient information and whether the child could expand it within a familiar routine.

When asked about her brother, she said "Sol my truck". The clinician interpreted the message with contextual support rather than assuming a specific grammatical meaning. When discussing a classroom event, she said "Milo fall". These examples showed purposeful communication but limited detail about ownership, timing, or what happened next.

She described a short picture sequence using isolated actions and needed adult support to connect events. With modeling, she expanded "girl wet" to "girl got wet". On a structured description task, she provided an action and a relevant participant in 3 of 8 opportunities independently and 6 of 8 with mod cues. Expansion remained inconsistent when the pictures changed.

SPEECH PRODUCTION AND ORAL EXAMINATION

Oral examination showed adequate apparent symmetry and movement for the observed speech tasks. The child opened and closed her jaw, rounded and spread her lips, and moved her tongue during imitation. No obvious structural difference was observed. This examination was brief and did not constitute a feeding or dental assessment. Voice quality and fluency were unremarkable during the sample.

On Sounds-in-Words, errors included variable omission of final consonants, reduction of consonant clusters, and substitutions affecting several English consonants. In connected speech, unfamiliar listeners needed contextual support. The clinician estimated approximately 65% intelligibility during structured play. This estimate reflects one listener and one setting, not a standardized intelligibility measure.

Examples included /t/ for /k/ in "key", [w for /ɹ/ in "red", and reduced clusters in "spoon". Spanish samples also showed substitutions involving /k/ and reduced production of some word endings. Difficulty with Spanish /ɾ/ was considered alongside age expectations and language experience rather than treated as an isolated diagnostic marker.

The clinician separated likely cross-language influences from patterns that reduced clarity across languages. Speech targets should prioritize frequent, functional contrasts and intelligibility. With direct modeling and mod cues, the child produced /k/ accurately in 4/10 syllable trials. Accuracy did not consistently transfer to words during this visit.

SOCIAL COMMUNICATION AND PLAY

The child showed interest in shared activities and used communication for requesting, protesting, commenting, and gaining attention. She coordinated gaze with gestures and took turns during familiar games. Pretend play included feeding a doll, repairing a vehicle, and preparing food. These behaviors supported participation and provided useful contexts for language teaching.

Communication repair was a relative weakness. She repeated an unclear production before trying another strategy. When coached, she could point, show an object, or add an action word. During play about school, she said "Lopez book" and used a gesture to show reading. The message became understandable when the listener connected it with the classroom context.

No diagnosis related to social communication was established from this visit. Observed participation difficulties appeared closely linked to language demands and reduced speech clarity. Continued monitoring across settings is appropriate because clinic play does not capture every classroom demand. Teacher observations should document the task, available supports, and the child's response.

DYNAMIC ASSESSMENT AND LEARNING RESPONSE

A structured teaching sequence introduced unfamiliar action vocabulary and sentence expansions through demonstration, repeated play, and recasting. The clinician used both languages while keeping the intended meaning consistent. Before teaching, the child used the target action in 1/5 opportunities. After teaching, she used it in 4/5 immediate opportunities with min cues.

Retention and transfer were less consistent. After another activity, she used the action independently in 2/5 opportunities. A visual reminder improved performance. These findings indicate that supported learning was possible, while independent access remained fragile. The results favor repeated practice across meaningful routines rather than reliance on a single teaching episode.

The mother practiced waiting, acknowledging the child's message, and adding a short model. The child responded positively to these strategies. Caregiver coaching drew on Hanen principles without implying enrollment in a specific course. Speech practice used selected elements of Cycles planning. No formal PROMPT protocol was administered, and PECS was not assessed as a complete program.

CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

The combined findings support mixed receptive-expressive language difficulties and a speech sound disorder affecting functional communication. Difficulties appeared in both languages, persisted during familiar activities, and affected classroom and home participation. Bilingual exposure does not explain the full observed pattern. The English standardized scores provide supporting descriptive information but are not the sole basis for these impressions.

Strengths include social interest, pretend play, responsiveness to visual models, and caregiver engagement. The child can communicate clear intentions and benefits from brief, meaningful teaching. Needs include understanding longer messages, organizing sentences, describing events, improving speech clarity, and repairing misunderstood communication. Intervention should connect these skills to activities the child already values.

The clinical diagnoses are ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. Educational eligibility remains the responsibility of the school team. Prognosis for functional improvement is favorable with consistent support, although the rate of progress cannot be predicted from this evaluation. Hearing changes, attendance, practice opportunities, and classroom demands may influence outcomes.

RECOMMENDATIONS

Begin speech-language intervention with a bilingual clinician when available. An initial schedule of weekly direct treatment with caregiver participation is reasonable. Review the schedule against functional progress and family access. Use English and Spanish according to communication partners and routines. The family should continue meaningful Spanish interaction rather than reducing the home language.

Teach comprehension through concrete activities, visible sequences, and gradual increases in sentence complexity. Ask the child to show or explain what she will do. Avoid relying only on repetition or yes-or-no confirmation. Provide processing time before adding another direction. Practice unfamiliar vocabulary in several relevant contexts, including books, play, and classroom routines.

Build expressive language through responsive modeling, expansions, and opportunities to describe actions. Models should be short enough to imitate and useful enough to reuse. Accept gestures and meaningful language mixing while supporting clearer messages. Teach repair strategies such as showing, pointing, adding a word, and asking for help. Coordinate speech practice with words that matter to the child.

Share this report with the school team only through the family's authorized process. Classroom supports should include visual directions, previewed vocabulary, supported peer play, and opportunities to answer without time pressure. Ms. Lopez and Tessa Rowan can track which supports improve participation. Coordinate with Dr. Priya Nalin if hearing concerns recur.

INITIAL FUNCTIONAL GOALS

Goal 1: During play or classroom routines, follow directions containing an action and a spatial relationship in 8/10 opportunities with min cues across repeated observations.

Goal 2: Produce a message containing a participant, action, and relevant detail in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues, using English, Spanish, or a meaningful combination.

Goal 3: When a listener signals misunderstanding, use a taught repair strategy in 4/5 opportunities with min cues across familiar activities.

Goal 4: Produce selected functional words containing /k/ with 80% accuracy during structured practice with mod cues, then reassess carryover into spontaneous communication.

FOLLOW-UP AND FAMILY RESPONSE

Review functional progress on January 14, 2027. Reassess goals using caregiver reports, classroom observations, and comparable language samples. Repeated standardized testing is not required at every review. Document the language, task, and supports used so that changes can be interpreted accurately.

The mother, Mariana Vega, summarized the recommendations and identified meals and shared reading as initial practice routines. No outside communication occurred during this fictional encounter. The clinician, Isabel Cárdenas, finalized this report on October 19, 2026, at 3:25 p.m..
