Summary

Nico participated in an evaluation of language comprehension, spoken expression, speech sounds, and functional communication across Spanish and English. His mother provided the developmental history and helped identify familiar vocabulary. Information also came from a fictional daycare questionnaire and direct observation. The clinician used structured tasks, play, conversation, and caregiver-supported activities. Results suggest difficulty understanding longer directions, organizing spoken messages, and producing several speech sounds. These difficulties affected communication in both languages, although performance changed with familiarity, language choice, visual support, and task demands.

Nico showed clear strengths in social interest, pretend play, gesture, shared enjoyment, and persistence when adults understood his intent. He used communication for requesting, protesting, commenting, and seeking help. He often combined pointing with a short spoken message. He communicated more effectively when an adult slowed the interaction and provided a model. The findings support bilingual speech-language intervention and coordinated classroom support. English test scores provide limited descriptive information because the child's language experience differs from the test's comparison group. Recommendations therefore draw on the combined evidence rather than a single score.

Background and reason for referral

Dr. Arden referred Nico after his mother described frequent communication breakdowns at home and daycare. She reported that familiar adults usually understand the child's immediate needs but often need gestures to understand explanations. He becomes frustrated when asked to repeat a message without additional help. The family wants him to explain what happened during play, ask for assistance before becoming upset, and participate more comfortably in classroom conversation. The referral did not identify a concern about loss of previously acquired skills.

Nico attends Little Learners Daycare in Briar Glen. His lead teacher, Ms. Tessa Rowan, reported that he joins familiar classroom routines and follows peers during transitions. He needs additional support when directions include several actions or unfamiliar location words. Classroom assistant Mr. Owen Marsh described successful communication during construction play, especially when materials remain visible. The child has difficulty telling adults about events that occurred outside their view. Staff requested practical strategies that fit existing classroom activities.

The family previously attended an orientation for the Little Learners Program, a play-based therapy program offered through the clinician's company. The child has not yet completed a treatment block. Service coordinator Marta Fenwick from the Bellhaven County Partnership for Children helped the family identify evaluation options. The family also receives nutrition support through Bellhaven County WIC. These services were reported by the caregiver; this evaluation did not independently inspect agency records.

Birth and medical history

Camila Valera reported an uncomplicated pregnancy until a brief period of elevated blood pressure near delivery. Nico was born at 38 weeks, 4 days of gestation at Juniper Vale Community Hospital in Juniper Vale, North Carolina. His reported birth weight was 7 pounds, 2 ounces. Reported Apgar scores were 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. He remained with his mother after delivery and did not require a neonatal intensive care admission.

The caregiver reported that Nico passed his newborn hearing screening. She recalled two episodes of middle-ear infection during toddlerhood, with no ear tubes or hospital admission. A hearing screen completed by audiologist Priya Lennox on May 28, 2026 was reported as passing in both ears. The written screening summary was available for review. The child has no reported seizure history, craniofacial condition, or major injury. His mother reported no daily medication and no known medication allergy.

Early feeding included breast milk and formula, followed by a gradual transition to family foods. The caregiver recalled independent sitting at approximately 7 months, walking at approximately 14 months, and first recognizable words at approximately 18 months. Word combinations appeared around 30 months. These ages reflect caregiver recall rather than contemporaneous records. Current feeding concerns were not reported. The child eats mixed textures and drinks from an open cup with occasional spills. Feeding and swallowing were not formally assessed during this visit.

Sleep varies with the family's work schedule. The caregiver described a usual bedtime near 8:30 p.m. and waking near 6:45 a.m.. The child occasionally wakes when household members return from work. No persistent snoring or breathing pauses were reported. His mother said that communication becomes harder when he is tired or hungry. During the evaluation, the clinician offered water, a snack break, and movement opportunities. The child remained available for interaction after each break and showed no visible distress related to physical discomfort.

Family, caregiving, and language history

Nico lives with his parents and his sister, Hope Valera, who is 7 years old. His maternal aunt, Luz Serrano, provides care on some workdays. His maternal grandmother, Inés Serrano, visits regularly and speaks Spanish with the children. The family has a dog named Mango. The caregiver described a supportive household with frequent shared meals, music, picture books, and pretend cooking. Family members sometimes anticipate the child's needs before he finishes a message, particularly when the household is busy.

Mom works nights at Lantern Ridge Linen Services as a commercial laundry technician. Her shift usually begins at 10:00 p.m. and ends at 6:00 a.m.. Dad works at Cedarbend Equipment Repair as a small-engine mechanic, with a usual start at 7:30 a.m.. Aunt Luz often handles daycare drop-off. These schedules affect appointment availability and the amount of time each adult spends in daily language routines. The family requested suggestions that can be shared across caregivers without a complex worksheet.

Spanish has been present since birth. English exposure increased when Nico entered daycare at 2;8. His mother estimated current waking exposure as approximately 60% Spanish and 40% English. These estimates describe typical opportunities, not measured language use. Spanish is common during family conversation, meals, and visits with relatives. English is common during daycare activities and some sibling play. The child sometimes changes languages within an interaction, especially when a familiar word is easier to retrieve in the other language.

Andrés Valera reported that the child understands familiar Spanish routines more easily than unfamiliar English directions. Camila Valera described short messages and omitted information in both languages. Sister Hope often offers a word when the child pauses, which helps the interaction continue but can obscure his independent skill. The clinician encouraged family members to maintain their comfortable languages. The evaluation treated bilingual exposure as part of the child's development and examined whether communication concerns persisted across languages and settings.

Evaluation procedures and behavioral observations

The evaluation included the Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5), the Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3), informal bilingual probes, an oral-mechanism observation, and a play-based language sample. The clinician completed the English standardized tasks before providing teaching support or Spanish clarification. Later bilingual activities explored understanding and learning beyond the standardized format. Results from those modified activities were recorded separately. No translated item was treated as a standardized response, and the clinician did not calculate a combined bilingual standardized score.

Nico entered the room holding his mother's hand and watched the clinician arrange the toys. He began playing after his mother joined a short pretend-food routine. He maintained shared attention, offered materials, and checked the adult's reaction during humorous play. He requested preferred items through gesture and speech. When a task became difficult, he sometimes looked toward his mother or pushed the materials away. The clinician interpreted these behaviors within the interaction rather than assuming that every incomplete response represented a skill deficit.

Attention was strongest during movement, vehicles, and pretend cooking. The child needed min cues to return to a familiar play sequence and mod cues to complete less preferred table tasks. A break ran from 10:02 a.m. to 10:12 a.m.. Following the break, participation improved when tasks alternated between listening and active play. The clinician used short directions, adequate wait time, and visible choices during informal activities. These supports were not added to the standardized scoring procedures.

The child tolerated an informal examination of visible oral structures and movements. Lip closure, jaw movement, and tongue movement appeared adequate for the observed speech tasks. The clinician did not observe drooling, persistent open-mouth posture, or obvious asymmetry. Voice quality and loudness were functional during play. Fluency showed occasional revisions and repeated starts without visible tension. These observations provide a limited snapshot. They do not replace a comprehensive motor-speech, voice, feeding, or fluency assessment when a specific concern emerges.

Test results

The following scores summarize performance under the English standardized administration. They describe comparison with the tests' published reference groups and require caution for this bilingual child. Confidence intervals reflect measurement uncertainty within the test framework; they do not resolve differences in language exposure. Age equivalents are included because the referral requested them, but they should not be read as the child's overall developmental age. Functional observations and bilingual learning probes carry substantial weight in the clinical interpretation.

| Measure | Raw score | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| PLS-5 Auditory Comprehension | 36 | 77 | 6th | 72-85 | 2;11 |
| PLS-5 Expressive Communication | 33 | 75 | 5th | 70-83 | 2;8 |
| PLS-5 Total Language | 69 | 74 | 4th | 70-81 | 2;9 |
| GFTA-3 Sounds-in-Words | 48 | 72 | 3rd | 67-79 | 2;6–2;8 |

On Auditory Comprehension, Nico identified familiar objects and actions more consistently than relational concepts. He followed concrete directions when the relevant materials were visible. He had difficulty with negation, longer sentences, and directions requiring attention to more than one detail. During informal Spanish probes, familiar vocabulary improved access, but difficulty with the direction structure remained. He followed 6/10 two-part directions independently and 9/10 after a demonstration with mod cues. These probe results were not included in standardized scoring.

On Expressive Communication, the child used familiar nouns, verbs, and short combinations. He had difficulty giving a complete explanation, marking some grammatical relationships, and answering questions about events that were not visible. During supported play, he produced phrases such as "I want more car" and "se cayó aquí". He sometimes omitted the person or object needed for the listener to understand the message. When asked about a picture sequence, he named visible elements but needed a model to connect the actions.

A bilingual picture-description probe showed similar message-planning needs across languages. Nico described a complete actor-action relationship in 3 of 8 opportunities independently. After a brief teaching sequence, he did so in 6 of 8 opportunities with min cues. He retained the model when the materials changed slightly, suggesting useful learning capacity. He still needed support to add location or cause. The clinician considered the improvement clinically useful but did not treat this small probe as a standardized measure or a precise prediction of treatment response.

On Sounds-in-Words, the child showed substitutions and omissions that reduced clarity. Observed patterns included fronting of /k/ and /g/, stopping of /s/, and reduction of some consonant clusters. In spontaneous English, "tar" occurred for "car", and "poon" occurred for "spoon". In Spanish, the clinician observed variable production of /ɾ/ and reduced consonants in longer words. These patterns require language-specific analysis. A difference between English and Spanish sound systems was not counted as an error by itself.

Stimulability testing showed accurate /k/ in 5/10 syllable attempts with max cues, improving to 8/10 with a consistent placement model. The child produced /s/ in isolation during 4/6 opportunities with mod cues. He did not consistently carry these productions into conversation. The clinician heard [w] in several English words containing an adult /r/ target. That observation alone does not establish a treatment priority. Initial goals should emphasize patterns that most affect understanding and respond to useful practice.

Language sample and functional communication

The clinician collected a play sample using SALT-style transcription conventions. A child production such as "him go there [EW]" received the code [EW] for an observed word-level error in the English context. Language switching was described separately and was not automatically coded as an error. During pet play, the child said, "Mango run." During a family routine, he said, "Hope help me." These messages showed purposeful communication even when the surrounding grammar or information was incomplete.

The sample included requests, comments, questions, and brief pretend dialogue. Estimated intelligibility to the unfamiliar clinician was 62% when the topic was visible and 44% when the message referred to an unseen event. These estimates came from this session and should not be generalized to every listener. The child repaired a misunderstood message independently in 2/7 opportunities. With a choice, gesture model, or request for one missing detail, he repaired the message in 6/7 opportunities with mod cues.

Daycare staff reported that Will Benton often understands the child's construction-play requests, while Rosa Keene sometimes leaves the activity when the message remains unclear. Staff described one interaction in which the child said, "Will take truck," while pointing toward a shelf. The intended message was unclear to the adult. The clinician recommended checking intent through visible choices before correcting wording. The report treats these classroom examples as staff observations rather than directly observed evaluation events.

Impressions

The combined findings are consistent with a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder. The clinical formulation supports consideration of ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. Evidence includes caregiver concerns across languages, classroom difficulty with directions and explanations, observed speech patterns, and persistent need for language support during bilingual probes. English standardized results support concern but do not independently establish the diagnosis. Continued observation during intervention will help refine the formulation and identify the most useful targets.

Nico's strengths include social engagement, symbolic play, willingness to imitate within meaningful activities, and improved performance after brief teaching. His communication needs affect participation when listeners cannot see the topic or when instructions contain several relationships. Bilingual exposure does not explain the full pattern observed here. The family should continue using Spanish and English in natural routines. Prognosis for functional improvement is favorable with consistent, accessible support, although this evaluation cannot predict the rate or final extent of progress.

Recommendations and initial treatment plan

1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy through the Little Learners Program twice weekly for thirty minutes per session over an initial twelve-week period. Provide treatment in both languages according to the activity, caregiver participation, and child's response. Review attendance, participation, and functional change before extending the plan. The proposed appointment window is 3:30 p.m. to 4:00 p.m., subject to the family's work and transportation arrangements.

2. Use play-based language intervention with focused models, expansions, and repeated opportunities to communicate. Selected caregiver coaching strategies from Hanen may support responsive interaction. Use principles from Cycles when addressing speech patterns, with targets selected from the child's actual productions. The clinician did not identify a current need for a full PECS protocol or specialized PROMPT treatment. These approaches should be reconsidered only if later assessment identifies a specific benefit.

3. Address Goal 1 by helping the child follow two related actions during familiar play. Aim for 8/10 opportunities with min cues across more than one activity. Teach the meaning of the direction before increasing its length. Record the language used, the support provided, and whether the materials were visible. Reduce support gradually rather than changing several task demands at once.

4. Address Goal 2 by helping the child produce a clear message containing an actor, action, and relevant object or location. Aim for 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Accept an effective response in either language during mixed-language play. Model a slightly longer message after acknowledging the child's meaning. Avoid requiring repeated imitation when the child has already communicated successfully.

5. Address Goal 3 by teaching a repair strategy when the listener does not understand. The child may point, show, repeat one key word, or add missing information. Aim for successful repair in 80% of supported opportunities with min cues. Adults should explain which part they understood and request only the missing detail. This approach gives the child a practical route back into the interaction.

6. Address Goal 4 by improving selected speech patterns in meaningful words. Begin with /k/ and /g/ if ongoing probes confirm readiness. Aim for 70% accuracy in practiced words with mod cues, then check unfamiliar words and conversational use. Keep practice brief and successful. Separate sound practice from moments when the child urgently needs help or is already frustrated.

7. Coordinate classroom support with Ms. Rowan and Mr. Marsh after the parents authorize information sharing. Pair directions with a visible demonstration, pause before repeating, and check understanding through action. Provide opportunities to speak during preferred play with several classmates. Give the child time to finish before another child supplies the answer. Record examples of successful communication as well as breakdowns.

8. Share a short home routine with both parents and aunt Luz Serrano. During meals, play, or dressing, follow the child's interest and model one useful message. Practice for a few minutes when the child is comfortable. The family preferred a routine near 6:30 p.m. on days when both parents are available. Each caregiver should use the language that feels natural and easy to sustain.

Follow-up and care coordination

Schedule a treatment review for September 8, 2026. Compare progress through repeated functional probes, caregiver examples, and classroom observations. Repeat standardized testing only when timing and clinical need support useful interpretation. If hearing concerns recur, request follow-up with Priya Lennox. Discuss educational evaluation options with the family and the service coordinator, using current concerns and parent priorities. No outside referral or record transmission occurred during this synthetic visit.

The clinician reviewed the findings with Camila Valera at 11:00 a.m.. She identified clearer requests, fewer frustrated exchanges, and better daycare participation as the immediate priorities. She demonstrated an expansion and a repair prompt during play. The clinician provided a plain-language summary and proposed goals for family review. The next clinical step is to confirm scheduling and begin baseline probes in familiar activities.

Signed: Elena Marisol Varela, MS, CCC-SLP  
Willowbridge Pediatric Communication Services

SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Record type: Fictional clinical document for offline de-identification testing. All people, organizations, contact details, identifiers, and clinical events are invented.

Child: Mateo Andrés Salcedo
Preferred name: Teo
Date of birth: 01/03/2021
Age at evaluation: 4;2

Home address: 284 Lantern Finch Lane, Bellmarsh, North Carolina 27984

Employer: Lantern Grove Pediatric Communication
Office: 63 Willowglass Court, Bellmarsh, North Carolina 27984
Office telephone: 252-555-0182

Billing references: CPT 92523; modifier GN

Background and history

Mateo was referred because his family and classroom staff reported difficulty understanding his speech and helping him explain events. His mother, Lucía Salcedo, described frequent frustration when listeners requested repetition. His father, Daniel Salcedo, reported that familiar routines were easier than unexpected questions. The evaluation examined communication across Spanish and English, with attention to language exposure, functional participation, and response to teaching.

Consent was documented on 02/24/2025. The parent completed a Spanish questionnaire dated 3 de marzo de 2025. Records included an earlier developmental appointment listed as el martes 4 de junio de 2024. Interviews occurred in each adult’s preferred language. The clinician conducted both evaluation visits directly in Spanish and English; an interpreter was not needed. Findings reflect a fictional assessment scenario and are not actual patient data.

Mateo lives with both parents and his sister, Inés Salcedo, age 7 years. His maternal grandmother, Rosa Nájera, provides care after preschool. A babysitter, Alma Vélez, provides occasional evening care. The family dog, Mango, often appears in conversation and pretend play. During the interview, the child pointed toward a photograph and said, “Mango come,” while gesturing toward the door.

The mother works at Briar Lantern Packaging, and the father works at Pinewheel Equipment Works. Their schedules affect who attends appointments. Spanish is the main language during meals, play, and extended-family visits. English occurs through preschool, community activities, and some television programs. The parents estimated weekly exposure as approximately 65% Spanish and 35% English, with substantial variation between weekdays and weekends.

Birth and medical history were provided by the mother and compared with the available referral summary. Mateo was born at Willowglass Regional Hospital following a pregnancy without reported complications. Gestational age was 39 weeks, 2 days, and birth weight was 3.28 kg. Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The mother reported no neonatal intensive care admission, feeding tube, or prolonged oxygen support.

The parent reported independent walking at 14 months and first meaningful words at approximately 18 months. Consistent word combinations appeared near 30 months. There was no reported loss of previously acquired skills. The family described recurrent ear infections between 18 months and 30 months. An audiology report dated 11/18/2024 documented hearing adequate for speech access under the test conditions, with follow-up recommended if concerns returned.

Dr. Varela follows the child at Finch Hollow Children’s Clinic. The parent reported no current daily medication, seizure history, or swallowing concerns. Sleep sometimes becomes irregular after late family gatherings. A dental visit on 1/22/25 identified no concern requiring changes to this assessment. The clinician observed comfortable breathing, adequate saliva control, and functional chewing during a brief snack. These observations did not constitute a feeding evaluation.

Early intervention records came from Bellmarsh Children’s Developmental Services Agency. Service coordinator J. Ortiz documented intake at age 26 months. The historical plan listed IFSP outcome 3 for requesting help during daily routines and IFSP outcome 5 for combining words during play. The child later transitioned to preschool services. The current evaluation did not treat those historical outcomes as an active IFSP.

Mateo attends Juniper Lantern Preschool in Bellmarsh, within Mossfern County. His teacher, Ms. Nora Beltrán, reported that he follows familiar classroom routines and enjoys construction toys. Classroom assistant Evan Pike noted difficulty explaining conflicts. Classmates Lila Moreno and Theo Mercer often interpret gestures for him. The child also attends occasional afternoon care at Little Fern Nest.

Assessment and results

Testing occurred in a quiet room with movement breaks and parent participation. Teo separated comfortably after a brief shared activity. He used eye contact, pointing, showing, and facial expressions to communicate interest. Attention improved when tasks included objects and predictable turns. He needed min cues to return after breaks and mod cues during unfamiliar picture-based tasks. No score was adjusted because of these supports.

The assessment included Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition, Spanish, abbreviated PLS-5 Spanish, a bilingual language sample, a speech sample, oral mechanism observations, and dynamic teaching tasks. The clinician also administered selected items from Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition, abbreviated GFTA-3. Because the English articulation measure did not fully represent this child’s language experience, its results were used descriptively without a standard score.

The following table summarizes the language measure. Confidence intervals use the measure’s reported 90% level. Age equivalents describe performance on this instrument and do not represent the child’s overall developmental age. The clinician considered these results alongside interviews, observation, language sampling, and response to instruction.

| Measure or subtest | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th | 73-83 | 2;6–3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | 74 | 4th | 69–80 | 2;4-2;8 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Total Language | 75 | 5th | 70-81 | 2;5–2;10 |

On Auditory Comprehension, Mateo identified familiar objects, understood simple action words, and followed contextual directions. He had more difficulty with location terms, descriptions containing several attributes, and questions about events outside the immediate setting. Accuracy increased when the clinician repeated directions slowly and allowed pointing. Similar difficulty appeared in Spanish and English after vocabulary familiarity was checked.

On Expressive Communication, he named common objects and combined words to request, comment, and protest. Longer explanations often omitted information needed by an unfamiliar listener. During pretend cooking, he produced "quiero más sopa" and "baby eat now". These productions showed purposeful communication across languages. They were not scored as errors simply because they contained different grammatical structures or reflected bilingual language use.

The bilingual sample contained 50 analyzable utterances across play and conversation. The clinician used Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts, abbreviated SALT, to organize descriptive observations. The [EW] code identified a word-level error where appropriate; code-switching alone did not receive that code. Mean utterance length was 2.8 words. The child answered event questions in 3 of 5 opportunities when pictures remained visible.

Dynamic assessment examined learning after brief models and guided practice. Before teaching, Mateo completed unfamiliar two-part directions in 2/10 opportunities. After demonstration and practice, he completed 8/10 with min cues. On a separate retell task, he included an action and result in 2 of 5 trials with max cues, improving to 4 of 5 with mod cues.

The speech sample showed frequent fronting of English /k/ and /g/, with comparable substitutions in familiar Spanish words. The child produced "tasa" for the target "casa" and "tat" for "cat". Some consonants were omitted in longer words. Productions varied with word length and speaking rate. The clinician distinguished these patterns from differences expected across the two languages.

English /ɹ/ sometimes became [w], while Spanish /ɾ/ was inconsistent. These findings received less diagnostic weight than errors affecting earlier sounds and whole-word structure. The clinician obtained accurate /k/ in isolation with max cues, then in simple syllables with mod cues. Oral movements appeared symmetrical. The sample did not provide sufficient evidence to identify a motor speech disorder.

The mother understood approximately 80% of spontaneous speech during the visit. The unfamiliar clinician understood approximately 55% without contextual support. These estimates came from the observed sample and should not be generalized to every setting. When a message failed, the child usually repeated the same form before adding a gesture. He successfully repaired 4/10 breakdowns after an adult offered a specific clarification prompt.

Impressions and recommendations

The combined findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder in this fictional case. Suggested diagnostic references are ICD-10 F80.2 and F80.0. Difficulties affected both languages and limited classroom explanations, independent requesting, and communication with unfamiliar listeners. Bilingual exposure does not explain the full pattern. Strengths included social interest, pretend play, persistent communication attempts, and clear benefit from structured teaching.

Scores require cautious interpretation because no standardized measure captures every bilingual child’s experience. The clinician did not compare separate language scores as if they measured identical exposure. Language sampling and dynamic assessment strengthened the interpretation, while variable attention and limited observation across settings remain constraints. Recommendations should be reviewed with the family and school team after an initial treatment period.

Begin individual speech-language therapy twice weekly, using Spanish and English according to each activity and communication partner. Use focused stimulation, expansions, visual supports, and selected principles from Hanen. Consider a Cycles approach for speech patterns if follow-up probes show stable targets. PROMPT and PECS are not included in the initial plan. Their use would require a documented clinical reason and appropriate clinician training.

The proposed schedule begins on 03/24/2025. Appointment availability remains provisional until the family and sites confirm it.

Treatment goal 1 addresses following two-part directions with familiar vocabulary in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Goal 2 addresses combining an agent, action, and object in 4 of 5 supported play opportunities with mod cues. Goal 3 addresses producing /k/ and /g/ in selected functional words with 80% accuracy and mod cues.

At home, caregivers should offer brief models in the language they use most comfortably. Expand the child’s message without requiring repeated correction. Practice targets such as "help me", "abre la caja", and "my turn" during meaningful routines. When the child says, “Teo want,” an adult can model a complete request using the object name. Keep practice brief and stop when frustration rises.

At school, provide visual choices, extra response time, and direct prompts for communication repair. Ms. Beltrán should avoid relying on classmates to interpret every message. Ask the child to show, point, or add one useful word before requesting a full repetition. Coordinate classroom targets with the treating clinician. Review progress on 06/16/2025 using repeated probes, caregiver reports, and a comparable language sample.

Referral agency	Centro de Coordinación Comunitaria para el Desarrollo Infantil y el Apoyo Integral a Familias Bilingües de Carolina del Norte (CCCDIAIFB)
Referral date	3 de marzo de 2025

BACKGROUND AND REASON FOR REFERRAL

Emilio Rafael Varela attended with his mother, Marina Varela, and his father, Andrés Soto. His parents requested an assessment because unfamiliar listeners often miss his message, and he sometimes stops speaking when asked to repeat. They also reported difficulty answering questions about recent events and following directions during busy routines. The referral asked whether these concerns reflect bilingual development, a communication disorder, or both.

The assessment included caregiver interviews, record review, structured testing, play observation, connected speech sampling, and teaching trials. The clinician used English and Spanish throughout the visit. No interpreter participated. The family selected English for this written report and requested Spanish explanations during feedback. The report describes communication across both languages and identifies supports that can begin in familiar routines.

Contacts and information sources are listed below. Each source contributed different observations. Caregiver reports describe home participation. Classroom information describes communication with staff and peers. Medical records provide background but do not establish the current communication diagnosis.

Contact	Role	Contact information	Contribution
Marina Varela	Mother	(919) 555-0146	Home language and developmental history
Andrés Soto	Father	andres.soto@example.org	Play routines and communication priorities
Ms. Rosa Peña	Classroom teacher	(984) 555-0172	Classroom participation summary
Nora Salcedo	Service coordinator, CCCDIAIFB	(919) 555-0128	Referral and transition records
Dr. Daniel Castañeda	Primary care physician	(984) 555-0163	Medical summary
Isabel Moreno	Evaluating speech-language pathologist	imoreno@example.org	Assessment and family feedback

Clinic information URL: https://willowlantern.example.org/bilingual-services

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

The parents reported an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery at Silver Heron Regional Hospital in Bellhaven. Gestational age was 39 weeks, 2 days. Birth weight was 7 pounds, 4 ounces. Recorded Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The newborn remained with his mother after delivery and went home without additional respiratory support. The reviewed discharge summary did not describe feeding concerns or a prolonged hospital stay.

The family reported early sitting, walking, and play development without a major concern. First meaningful words emerged at approximately 18 months, and consistent word combinations emerged near 30 months. Parents recalled gradual progress rather than loss of previously used words. They described a history of middle ear infections, with the most recent episode documented on 02-11-2025. No ear tubes or other surgeries were reported.

A hearing assessment completed on 7/9/25 at Silver Heron Regional Hospital documented responses within the expected range for the procedures completed. Audiologist Elena Duarte recommended monitoring if ear infections recur. The child takes no daily medication according to the caregiver interview. Seasonal congestion was reported. Parents denied current swallowing difficulty, coughing with meals, or concerns about chewing ordinary family foods.

Sleep is generally consistent, although the child sometimes wakes after an unusually busy day. Vision screening results were reported as satisfactory by the parents; the original screening record was unavailable. The clinician therefore treated this information as caregiver report. Oral structure and movement appeared adequate during informal observation. A dental gap affected appearance but did not explain the observed language difficulties or the full speech error pattern.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

The child lives with both parents and his sister, Camila Soto, who is 7 years old. His maternal grandmother, Teresa Varela, provides care after preschool. An aunt, Lidia Varela, occasionally helps with transportation. The family’s dog, Nube, frequently joins floor play. During the interview, the child pointed toward a photograph and said, “Nube corre.” This utterance showed a spontaneous comment connected to a familiar relationship.

Spanish is the main language used by the mother and grandmother. The father uses Spanish during meals and English during some games. The sister usually speaks English during pretend play and switches to Spanish when helping with household routines. The parents estimated exposure at 65% Spanish and 35% English. These estimates describe current routines, rather than measured proficiency or a fixed language preference.

The mother works at Juniper Thread Packing Cooperative in Larkmere. Her work schedule sometimes changes who completes preschool pickup. The family uses CCCDIAIFB for service coordination and attends family activities at Brisa Family Resource Center. They also join story sessions at Meadow Lantern Community Library. Volunteer Adela Campos leads the bilingual picture-book group. These settings offer opportunities for communication outside the immediate household.

Parents reported that a cousin, Tomás Rivas, received speech services during childhood. They did not know his diagnosis or treatment details. No additional family communication history was confirmed. The family values Spanish for relationships with relatives and wants the child to participate comfortably in English at school. Maintaining both languages is an explicit family priority and will guide treatment planning and home practice.

EDUCATIONAL AND SERVICE HISTORY

The child attends Little Willow Early Learning Center and will enter a preschool classroom at Lantern Creek Primary School. His current teacher, Ms. Peña, reported that he participates best during movement songs, construction play, and small groups. Classroom assistant M.R. noted that visual examples help him begin tasks. Staff described difficulty explaining conflicts, asking for clarification, and completing unfamiliar spoken directions.

Preferred play partners include Lucía Ferrer and Benji Park. The child often follows their play ideas but contributes fewer spoken details when the group becomes noisy. Staff have observed him pointing or handing over an object after an unsuccessful verbal request. They reported no consistent aggression or withdrawal. Communication breakdowns appear more frequent when the activity requires quick responses or when several children speak together.

Earlier service records describe caregiver coaching under IFSP outcome 2. A transition meeting occurred on el martes 4 de junio de 2024. The family recalled useful routines but could not identify a named treatment program from that period. No current private speech-language treatment was reported. School eligibility decisions remain the responsibility of the receiving educational team and require consideration of classroom performance.

ASSESSMENT CONDITIONS AND PROCEDURES

The visit began at 9:10 a.m. and ended at 11:05 a.m.. The child separated comfortably for play, with parents available nearby. He needed movement breaks and occasional encouragement after difficult items. Attention improved when materials were visible and the examiner used a predictable sequence. Fatigue affected the final structured activity, so the clinician completed additional observations during a quieter play routine.

English standardized procedures were completed without translating scored items. Spanish activities followed separately and were interpreted descriptively. English normative scores provide a limited view because the comparison groups do not fully represent this child’s language experience. The clinician considered the scores alongside performance in both languages, caregiver reports, classroom information, and response to teaching. No translated task received an English-derived normative score.

TEST RESULTS

Measure	Subtest or composite	Raw score	Standard score	Percentile	Confidence interval	Age equivalent
Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5)	Auditory Comprehension	38	78	7th percentile	73-86	3;0
PLS-5	Expressive Communication	35	74	4th percentile	69-82	2;9
PLS-5	Total Language Score	73	75	5th percentile	70-83	2;10
Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3)	Sounds-in-Words	49	72	3rd percentile	68-80	Not reported

The listed intervals are 90% confidence intervals. Age equivalents summarize performance on specific test items; they do not describe the child’s overall developmental age. Differences between individual scores were not treated as evidence of a meaningful receptive-expressive split. The English results indicate difficulty under those testing conditions. The bilingual observations below provide the broader evidence used for clinical interpretation.

RECEPTIVE AND EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE

During familiar play, the child identified common objects and actions in both languages. He followed related directions more consistently when the objects remained visible. He completed 8/10 familiar single-step directions independently and 3 of 5 related two-step directions with min cues. Performance decreased when instructions included an unfamiliar location word or required remembering an item that was no longer visible.

Spanish comprehension was stronger for household vocabulary, while English comprehension was stronger for classroom routines. Across both languages, the child had difficulty explaining relationships, answering questions about a short event sequence, and identifying what a character might do next. Repetition alone did not consistently resolve these difficulties. Pictures, demonstration, and shorter sentences improved access to the task and reduced frustration.

Spontaneous language included requests, protests, labels, comments, and brief pretend-play dialogue. The child produced “I want big truck” and “el bebé está dormido” during supported play. He sometimes omitted small grammatical words in English and had difficulty producing consistent verb forms in Spanish. The clinician considered these patterns within each language and did not count ordinary language mixing as an error.

A picture sequence prompted “boy fall” followed by a gesture toward the ground. With mod cues, the child added “he fall because wet”. The response showed emerging cause-and-effect language but limited independent detail. Naming performance improved when the examiner accepted either language. However, difficulty retrieving action words and organizing a complete message remained evident across both languages.

The clinician used Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) conventions for a brief descriptive sample. Clear lexical errors received [EW], and unintelligible segments received [X]. The sample was too short and context-dependent for a normative comparison. It nevertheless showed frequent reliance on gesture when the child needed to repair a message or describe an event without visible objects.

SPEECH SOUND FINDINGS

Speech errors reduced clarity in both languages. Observed patterns included inconsistent production of /k/ and /g/, reduction of some consonant clusters, and variable marking of final consonants. The child used [t] for /k/ in “cat” during naming. He also produced “poon” for “spoon”. Some English differences reflected language influence and were not automatically classified as disordered.

In Spanish, the child produced several multisyllabic words with omitted sounds or syllables. His production of /ɾ/ varied by word and speaking rate. The clinician did not diagnose an isolated rhotic problem from these observations. The broader concern was reduced consistency and clarity across familiar words. Connected speech was less understandable than single-word naming, especially when he spoke quickly or provided little context.

The clinician understood approximately 70% of English connected speech and 75% of Spanish connected speech during supported play. These are contextual estimates, not standardized scores. The mother understood more of the sample and supplied several meanings that the clinician could not confirm independently. Voice and fluency appeared functional during the visit. The observed sample did not support a separate voice or fluency diagnosis.

DYNAMIC ASSESSMENT AND PARTICIPATION

Teaching trials used focused stimulation, recasts, and visual supports. After a model, the child produced the target phrase “help me open” in 6/8 opportunities with min cues. He later used “ayúdame a abrir” during a different activity. Carryover was less consistent when the materials changed, suggesting that he benefited from teaching but still needed support to generalize a new form.

For speech practice, the clinician introduced /k/ through brief listening and imitation activities. Accuracy improved from 2/10 independent attempts to 7/10 attempts with mod cues. The child accepted feedback and remained engaged when practice alternated with play. This response supports a trial of structured intervention. It does not establish a motor speech diagnosis or predict a fixed treatment duration.

The child shared enjoyment, sought adult attention, and used gesture effectively. He became quiet after repeated communication failures but returned to play when the examiner acknowledged his message. Parents identified successful repair as their highest priority. They want him to ask for help, describe a problem, and continue an interaction without relying on an adult to guess the intended message.

IMPRESSIONS

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder, represented by F80.2 and F80.0. Difficulty appeared across languages and affected everyday participation. The conclusion rests on converging observations, rather than English test scores alone. Strengths include social interest, symbolic play, use of gesture, family engagement, and a positive response to direct teaching with meaningful materials.

Bilingual exposure does not adequately explain the full pattern observed. However, language experience affects vocabulary distribution and some speech productions. Treatment must distinguish those differences from errors that limit communication across languages. The current assessment does not establish a broader developmental diagnosis. Additional evaluation should follow specific concerns identified by the medical or educational team.

RECOMMENDATIONS AND SERVICE PLAN

Begin bilingual speech-language therapy with coordinated caregiver coaching. Use Spanish and English according to the activity and communication partner. Support message repair, direction following, sentence organization, and speech clarity. Initial intervention should use milieu teaching, focused stimulation, and recasts. Consider a Cycles approach after establishing a stable baseline for speech patterns and selecting targets relevant to both languages.

Goal	Functional target	Initial criterion
Goal 1	Request help or repair a misunderstood message	4/5 opportunities with min cues
Goal 2	Follow related two-step directions during play	8/10 opportunities with min cues
Goal 3	Describe a brief event with an action and relevant detail	4/5 opportunities with mod cues
Goal 4	Produce selected speech targets in practiced words	80% accuracy with mod cues

Service	Frequency and duration	Proposed schedule	Location
Individual speech-language therapy	Weekly, forty-five minutes	Wednesday at 3:30 p.m.	Willow Lantern Pediatric Communication, PLLC
Caregiver coaching	Within each therapy visit	Final ten minutes	Clinic or secure video visit
Classroom consultation	Monthly, twenty minutes	Thursday at 12:15 p.m.	Little Willow Early Learning Center
Progress review	After an initial treatment block	11/19/2025	Clinic and caregiver conference

At home, adults should pause, acknowledge the intended message, and model a short useful sentence. Offer choices without requiring repeated imitation. Continue shared reading in Spanish and English. During classroom transitions, staff should pair concise directions with pictures and check understanding through action. Coordinate target selection across settings. Review progress using repeated functional samples, caregiver reports, and classroom participation.

Parents received bilingual feedback and a written explanation of the proposed plan. They agreed with the communication priorities and requested coordination with the preschool team. Scheduling and coverage remain pending. The service coordinator will confirm available options before treatment begins.

FICTIONAL PEDIATRIC SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION REPORT

Client: María José Cárdenas Villalba
Preferred name: Majo
Date of birth: March 18, 2022
Chronological age: 4;2
Evaluation date: May 20, 2026
Report date: May 27, 2026
Appointment: 9:15 a.m.–11:05 a.m.
Record number: SL-260520-047
Medicaid member number: 483726915Q
Authorization number: NC-SLP-2605-118
Evaluator: Isabel Marín Vega, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist
Practice: Little Lantern Bilingual Therapy
Practice address: 184 Lantern Finch Lane, Alder Creek, North Carolina 27864
Telephone: 919-555-0146
Email: imarin@littlelantern.example
Website: https://littlelantern.example
Referral source: Dr. Elena Soria Patel
Service coordinator: Cora Ellis Reed

## 1. Referral and Purpose

### 1.1 Presenting concerns

María José was referred for a bilingual evaluation because her family and classroom staff reported difficulty understanding directions, combining words, and producing clear speech. Her mother, Ana Lucía Cárdenas Molina, requested practical guidance for communication during meals, dressing, and preschool activities. Her father, Diego Villalba Torres, reported that unfamiliar listeners frequently ask for repetition.

The evaluation examined communication across Spanish and English. Its purpose was to describe functional strengths, identify support needs, and guide treatment planning. Spanish exposure and English exposure were considered throughout interpretation.

### 1.2 Sources of information

Information came from caregiver interviews, referral records, classroom notes, direct observation, structured testing, and bilingual play samples. The evaluator reviewed records supplied by the family and Alder Creek CDSA Office. Intake assistant Nora Bellamy confirmed the appointment and demographic information.

Caregiver statements are identified as reported history. Performance descriptions reflect this evaluation session. Differences between settings were considered clinically meaningful.

## 2. Birth and Medical History

### 2.1 Pregnancy and neonatal course

The mother reported an uncomplicated pregnancy until premature rupture of membranes. María José Cárdenas Villalba was born at 34 weeks, 5 days gestation at Carolina Lantern Health Alder Creek Campus Hospital. Birth weight was 2,180 grams. Recorded Apgar scores were 7 and 9.

The child received care in the NICU at Carolina Lantern Health Alder Creek Campus Hospital for feeding support and temperature regulation. Discharge occurred on April 2, 2022. The available summary described brief supplemental oxygen and no documented seizure activity. The family reported no subsequent hospitalization.

### 2.2 Current health and hearing

Dr. Elena Soria Patel provides primary care at Carolina Lantern Health Alder Creek Campus Pediatric Clinic. The family reported recurrent middle-ear infections and seasonal congestion. Otolaryngologist Dr. Jonah Mercer Lin evaluated the child on February 12, 2026.

Audiologist Tessa Ríos Grant completed testing at Carolina Lantern Health Briar Hollow Campus Audiology on April 9, 2026. The supplied report described hearing adequate for conversational speech under test conditions. Continued surveillance was recommended because of the infection history. Caregivers reported no current daily medication.

## 3. Family and Language History

### 3.1 Household and caregivers

María José lives with both parents and her brother, Sol Villalba Cárdenas, aged 7;1, in Alder Creek, Juniper County. Maternal aunt Luz Cárdenas Molina provides afternoon care. The family dog, Nube, often participates in home play.

The mother works at Pinewheel Packaging Cooperative. The father works at Juniper Glassworks Company. Their schedules affect which caregiver attends appointments. Both parents requested consistent written guidance that can be shared with the aunt.

### 3.2 Language exposure

Spanish is the main home language. English is used most often in preschool and community activities. Caregivers estimated current exposure as approximately 65% Spanish and 35% English. These estimates describe exposure, not proficiency.

The family reported first meaningful words at 19 months and emerging word combinations at 33 months. Majo uses more familiar routines in Spanish but sometimes selects English words learned at school. The parents described limited sentence length in both languages. Neither parent reported a loss of previously acquired communication skills.

## 4. Educational and Agency Background

### 4.1 Classroom participation

The child attends Alder Creek Preschool Learning Center and receives afternoon care at Willow Window Childcare. Teacher Ms. Camila Benton reported strong interest in songs, pretend cooking, and picture books. Classroom assistant Mr. Owen Price described difficulty following directions during cleanup and transitions.

María José frequently plays beside classmates Hope Bell and Eli Ortega. She sometimes hands them materials without explaining her intended activity. Staff reported that communication breakdowns may lead to withdrawal or crying, especially when several children speak together.

### 4.2 Agency involvement

Alder Creek CDSA Office previously coordinated early intervention. Service coordinator Cora Ellis Reed now assists the family with record transfer and preschool referrals. The family also receives support from Juniper County WIC Program and Juniper County Smart Start Partnership.

Alder Creek Early Head Start supplied earlier developmental notes. Juniper County DSS assisted with benefit paperwork; the supplied documents identified no protective-services involvement. The prior IFSP, dated January 15, 2025, listed Outcome 2 for functional requesting and Outcome 3 for participation in shared play. Those records provide historical context.

## 5. Evaluation Procedures and Behavioral Observations

### 5.1 Assessment conditions

Isabel Marín Vega conducted the evaluation in Spanish and English without an interpreter. The mother remained present. Activities included caregiver interview, structured language tasks, speech sampling, oral examination, pretend play, picture description, and supported teaching trials.

The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition (PLS-5) and Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) informed the assessment. English standardized tasks were administered under their stated conditions. Separate Spanish activities examined similar communication skills. Spanish responses were not inserted into English standard-score calculations.

### 5.2 Participation and validity

María José entered quietly, explored the toy kitchen, and gradually initiated interaction. She benefited from movement breaks and predictable transitions. Attention was strongest during meaningful play and weaker during extended picture tasks.

English normative comparisons have limited applicability because her language experience differs from the reference population. Scores therefore describe performance under specific conditions. They do not independently establish a disorder. Interpretation also relied on Spanish performance, caregiver examples, classroom concerns, and response to teaching.

Fatigue increased near the session’s end. The evaluator repeated selected informal tasks after a break, while preserving the standardized administration record.

## 6. Standardized Test Results

### 6.1 Score summary

All values below represent fictional results for this report. Confidence intervals use the 90% level.

| Measure | Subtest or composite | Standard score | Percentile rank | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| PLS-5 | Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-85 | 3;0 |
| PLS-5 | Expressive Communication | 81 | 10th percentile | 76-88 | 3;2 |
| PLS-5 | Total Language | 78 | 7th percentile | 74-84 | 3;1 |
| GFTA-3 | Sounds-in-Words | 74 | 4th percentile | 69-82 | 2;6–2;8 |

### 6.2 Interpretation limits

The PLS-5 results showed difficulty with increasingly complex English language tasks. The GFTA-3 results identified reduced accuracy for several consonants in elicited English words. These findings agree with reported functional concerns, but the normative values require caution.

Age equivalents describe the test’s raw-score mapping. They do not represent the child’s overall developmental age or appropriate classroom placement. The range 2;6–2;8 must not be treated as a complete description of communication ability.

The confidence interval 73-85 reflects measurement uncertainty around one obtained score. It does not predict the effect of treatment. Bilingual performance patterns and everyday participation provide more useful guidance for intervention priorities than a single number.

## 7. Receptive and Expressive Language Findings

### 7.1 Understanding language

In Spanish play, María José followed familiar single-step directions in 8/10 opportunities. Performance decreased to 4/10 for related two-step directions without gestures. In English, she completed 6/10 familiar single-step directions and 3/10 related two-step directions.

She identified common objects, familiar actions, and basic body parts. Spatial terms and pronoun contrasts were less consistent in both languages. She benefited from demonstration, shorter sentences, and repetition. With mod cues, she completed 7/10 supported two-step directions.

These informal findings reflect task performance rather than standardized scores. Familiar vocabulary and contextual information substantially improved understanding.

### 7.2 Expressive communication

The child used gestures, single words, and short combinations. Spanish examples included “quiero agua,” “mamá ayuda,” and “bebé duerme.” English examples included “more bubbles” and “baby sleeping.” She sometimes said “yo want agua,” which showed access to vocabulary across languages.

During pretend play, she said “Luz help” and later “Nube come.” These requests contained recognizable names and clear communicative intent.

Responses to open questions were usually brief. She often omitted information needed by an unfamiliar listener. After a model and min cues, she expanded a request in 6/10 opportunities. Novel descriptions remained difficult despite support.

## 8. Speech Production and Oral Mechanism

### 8.1 Speech patterns

Speech sampling showed frequent fronting of /k/ and /g/, reduction of English consonant clusters, and variable omission of final consonants. Examples included “tat” for “cat” and “poon” for “spoon.” Production of Spanish /ɾ/ and /r/ was variable and was interpreted in developmental context.

A substitution of [w] for English /l/ occurred in several words. Cross-language differences were considered before classifying errors. Some English productions reflected language experience, while recurring patterns across languages reduced clarity.

The evaluator understood approximately 62% of connected speech with contextual support. The mother estimated familiar-listener understanding at 80%. These percentages describe different listening conditions and should not be directly equated.

### 8.2 Stimulability and oral findings

With mod cues, the child produced /k/ in isolation in 7/10 trials. Accuracy decreased to 3/10 in simple words. Lip movement, tongue movement, and visible oral structures appeared adequate for sampled tasks.

Voice quality and fluency showed no consistent concern during this session. No feeding assessment was completed. The observed speech patterns did not establish a motor-speech diagnosis.

## 9. Play, Pragmatics, and Dynamic Assessment

### 9.1 Social communication

María José shared enjoyment, checked the adult’s face, and invited participation through gestures. She took pretend-play roles and responded to another person’s actions. Communication breakdowns occurred when her message required a longer explanation.

She repaired misunderstood requests by repeating the same words or pointing. Independent verbal repair occurred in 2/8 opportunities. With mod cues, she added useful information in 6/8 opportunities.

### 9.2 Learning response

Brief teaching trials used modeling, visual choices, and repeated practice within play. The child learned a new request frame and retained it after an activity change. This response supports intervention through predictable routines.

Language samples used SALT conventions where applicable. An extraneous-word event received [EW]. No single sample code or isolated interaction was used to infer a broader developmental condition.

## 10. Clinical Impressions

### 10.1 Integrated findings

The assessment supports receptive and expressive language needs that affect participation across home and preschool settings. Difficulties appeared in both languages, although English exposure influenced task performance. The child’s bilingual development does not itself explain the full pattern of reported and observed concerns.

Speech sound errors also reduce clarity. Priorities include patterns that affect many words and occur across languages. Spanish sound development and English sound development require separate consideration.

Strengths include social interest, symbolic play, clear communicative intent, caregiver involvement, and a positive response to supported teaching. These strengths provide useful entry points for treatment.

### 10.2 Diagnostic and billing information

The working clinical impressions are mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, F80.2, and speech sound disorder, F80.0. Diagnostic confidence should be reviewed as additional bilingual samples and classroom observations become available.

The evaluation service is represented by CPT 92523. Proposed individual treatment is represented by CPT 92507, with modifier GN when required by the applicable claim process. These codes do not determine service eligibility, authorization, or educational placement.

## 11. Recommendations and Proposed Goals

### 11.1 Treatment plan

1. Begin bilingual speech-language treatment twice weekly, with sessions lasting approximately thirty minutes. Combine direct practice with caregiver coaching.
2. Use Spanish and English according to the child’s communication partners and daily needs. Support continued Spanish use at home.
3. Apply Enhanced Milieu Teaching and selected Hanen strategies for functional language. Consider the Cycles approach for recurring phonological patterns.
4. Coordinate classroom supports with Ms. Camila Benton and Mr. Owen Price, following documented family consent.
5. Continue hearing follow-up through the existing audiology provider if infections recur or listening changes emerge.

### 11.2 Initial treatment goals

Proposed Goal 1: Follow related two-step directions during familiar routines in 8/10 opportunities with min cues.

Proposed Goal 2: Use a functional combination containing an action and relevant information in 8/10 opportunities with min cues.

Proposed Goal 3: Produce /k/ in selected functional words with 80% accuracy using mod cues, then reduce support.

Proposed Goal 4: Repair an unclear message by adding a word, gesture, or visual reference in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues.

### 11.3 Home practice

Caregivers should pause during familiar routines, acknowledge all clear communication, and model a short expansion. Practice should remain brief and playful. Useful targets include “open box,” “quiero más,” and “help me.” Avoid requiring repeated correction before meeting an understood need.

## 12. Follow-Up and Family Discussion

### 12.1 Review arrangements

The evaluator discussed findings with Ana Lucía Cárdenas Molina and provided a written summary for Diego Villalba Torres. The family agreed that easier requesting, clearer speech, and successful classroom transitions were the most useful initial priorities.

With family consent, Cora Ellis Reed will assist with referral coordination. A treatment review is proposed for August 19, 2026. The review should compare supported and independent performance across both languages. It should also include caregiver observations and classroom examples.

### 12.2 Closing statement

This report describes one evaluation and the records available at that time. Treatment targets should change as the child’s communication develops. Additional concerns about hearing, feeding, or broader development should be shared with the primary care provider.

Prepared and electronically signed on May 27, 2026 by Isabel Marín Vega, MS, CCC-SLP.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

The mother reported an uncomplicated pregnancy and delivery at Lantern Valley Community Hospital in Willowbend. Gestational age was 39 weeks 2 days. Birth weight was 3,240 g. Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The child received routine newborn care and went home with her family. The parents reported no neonatal respiratory support, feeding tube, or prolonged hospital stay.

FAMILY AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

The child lives with both parents and her brother, Diego del Río Salcedo, age 5;6. Her grandmother, doña Lupe, provides afternoon care. Their dog, Canela, often joins family play. The mother works for Lantern Orchard Packaging Cooperative. The father works for Willowbend Bicycle Repair Collective. These schedules influence which caregiver attends visits.

Caregivers estimated Spanish exposure at 70% and English exposure at 30%. These estimates describe daily opportunities, not measured proficiency. Spanish predominates at home. English and Spanish are both used at Little Lantern Meadow Daycare. Miss Ana leads the toddler classroom, and la maestra Carmen supports bilingual activities. Classroom peers include Inés Rojas and Mateo Reed-Báez. The brother attends Willowbend Garden Primary School.

The family wants continued support for both languages. They reported no loss of previously used words. The child understands familiar Spanish routines and some English daycare directions. Switching languages sometimes helps her respond. Neither bilingual exposure nor mixed-language productions were treated as evidence of disorder.

TEST RESULTS

PLS-5 Spanish was administered by the bilingual clinician using its prescribed bilingual procedures. Scores are fictional results for this synthetic report. Behavioral observations and caregiver information informed interpretation. Age equivalents describe test performance and do not represent a child’s overall developmental age.

Confidence intervals reflect a 90% confidence level. The child’s strongest responses involved familiar objects, routine actions, and shared play. She had more difficulty following unfamiliar directions and producing varied word combinations. An informal bilingual sample showed meaningful communication through pointing, gaze, vocalization, and words. Speech observations were descriptive because the sample was small.

IMPRESSIONS

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder in this fictional case. Expressive difficulties were more apparent than receptive difficulties. The child showed social interest, shared enjoyment, and readiness to learn through familiar routines. Reduced intelligibility sometimes limited communication, but the available sample did not support a separate motor speech diagnosis. Continued observation is indicated.

The child repeated a vocalization when an adult did not understand, but she did not consistently change her message. She repaired communication in 2 of 5 opportunities with max cues, usually by pointing after an adult demonstrated the option. During pretend play, she said "Canela no" and then moved the dog away from the plate. The action clarified her intention. Her grandmother reported similar attempts at home. This outcome remains in progress. Treatment will emphasize showing and pointing as valid repairs while spoken vocabulary develops. Adults will document whether a repair succeeded with familiar and unfamiliar partners.	October 12, 2026
Outcome 8: Participate in daycare transitions using understandable messages and visual supports.	The clinician will coordinate with Miss Ana and la maestra Carmen through the family’s approved communication process. Classroom strategies will include a visual routine, consistent transition language, and an accessible request for assistance. Target messages include "help please", "vamos", and "all done". Staff will prepare the child before changing activities and acknowledge her communication attempts. The review criterion is participation in 4 of 5 observed transitions with min cues. Staff notes will describe the activity, the child’s message, and the support provided without comparing her directly with classmates.	Classroom progress was reported by staff and was not directly observed during this clinic visit. Staff described easier transitions when the child carries a familiar object and sees the next activity. She reportedly used a gesture or word in 3 of 5 recent transitions with mod cues. During clinic cleanup, she said "all done" after a model and placed toys in a container. This observation supports the usefulness of a predictable routine but does not verify daycare performance. The clinician will request a brief classroom sample at the next review, subject to family agreement and site procedures.	October 12, 2026
Outcome 9: Join simple play with another child and communicate a turn.	Adults will arrange brief activities with duplicate materials and a clear shared purpose. Useful activities include rolling a ball, building a short tower, and feeding toy animals. Models include "my turn", "tu turno", and "toma". The clinician will teach adults to support entry into play without speaking for the child throughout the interaction. Peer participation will remain voluntary. The review criterion is a communicative turn with another child in 3 of 5 supported opportunities with mod cues. Caregivers will note whether the child initiates, responds, or watches before joining.	The child showed interest when her brother entered the room near the end of the visit. She offered a block and said "Diego aquí". She completed communicative turns in 2 of 5 supported opportunities with mod cues. Her mother reported that she often watches other children before approaching. Classroom staff described occasional toy exchanges with Inés Rojas and parallel play near Mateo Reed-Báez. These reports suggest an emerging base for shared activity. Treatment will support simple exchanges and reduce pressure to perform longer conversations that exceed the child’s current communication skills.	October 12, 2026
Outcome 10: Participate in book sharing through pointing, sounds, and meaningful words.	Caregivers will choose short books with familiar actions and clear pictures. Adults will comment, pause, and respond to the child’s focus instead of asking a question about every page. Targets may include "mira", "big dog", and "se cayó". The clinician will model ways to repeat useful language while accepting gestures and sound effects. Books may be shared in either language. A library volunteer, Mr. Tom, may support familiar story routines when the family attends community activities. The review criterion is participation in 4 of 5 book-sharing exchanges with min cues.	The child pointed to pictures, turned pages, and imitated an animal sound. She participated in 3 of 5 exchanges with mod cues. Her attention improved when the adult followed her selected page. The mother reported that the child returns to the same books and anticipates familiar actions. The clinician recommends repeating those books while adding small variations in comments. A language sample from book sharing included "dog eat" and an omitted English article coded [EW] in the transcription. This isolated code describes the sample and does not establish a grammatical disorder across both languages.	October 12, 2026
Outcome 11: Express choices, refusal, and requests for comfort during care routines.	Adults will offer meaningful choices and honor a clear refusal when the situation allows. They will model "no quiero", "otro", "stop", and "mamá ven". Visual choices will support participation during dressing, snacks, and quiet activities. The clinician will coach adults to distinguish refusal from a request for help or a break. The review criterion is an understandable choice, refusal, or comfort request in 8/10 natural opportunities with min cues. Communication support will continue during distress, with fewer words and an accessible response option.	The child communicated preferences clearly through reaching and moving objects away. Spoken or pictured messages occurred in 5/10 opportunities with mod cues. During dressing play, she said "no shoe" and selected a different shoe. Her father reported that communication becomes harder when she is tired. The clinician recommends keeping familiar pictures available and accepting a gesture before offering a spoken model. Progress is present, but the child needs more reliable access to messages across caregivers. Adults will record whether the message was understood and honored, because successful communication depends on the partner’s response as well as the child’s production.	October 12, 2026
Outcome 12: Use communication strategies consistently across family caregivers.	The clinician will coach each available caregiver during a routine they already manage. Shared strategies will include waiting, modeling a short message, expanding a word, and responding to gesture. The family will maintain a brief vocabulary list with Spanish and English examples. The list will describe meaning rather than require identical words from every adult. The review criterion is caregiver use of agreed strategies in 4 of 5 observed opportunities with min cues. Coordination with Willowbend Family Nutrition Program will address appointment access when requested. Clinical information will remain limited to the purpose of coordination.	The mother demonstrated waiting and expansion in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. The father demonstrated these strategies in 3 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Doña Lupe did not attend, so her strategy use was not observed. The parents reported that she uses songs and familiar household routines. The clinician will offer coaching in her preferred language at a later visit. This outcome shows progress with the attending caregivers and remains open for generalization. The service coordinator will help schedule a time that fits work and caregiving responsibilities without adding unnecessary family burden.	October 12, 2026
Outcome 13: Review communication gains and adjust services using functional evidence.	Recommend weekly bilingual speech-language intervention with caregiver participation and periodic classroom consultation. Sessions should address the outcomes above through play and daily routines. The clinician will collect brief samples, track support levels, and compare performance across communication partners. A review is scheduled for January 11, 2027. Earlier reassessment is appropriate if caregivers report loss of skills, new hearing concerns, or a major change in participation. The next standardized evaluation should use an appropriate bilingual method. Repeated administration of PLS-5 Spanish should follow its guidance rather than serve as a weekly progress measure.	Overall progress is emerging across requesting, shared play, and word combinations. Understanding of familiar routines remains a relative strength. The team will prioritize successful communication in both languages and maintain access to gestures and pictures. Immediate next actions are caregiver coaching, classroom coordination, and a broader speech sample. The clinician will document spontaneous responses separately from responses with min cues, mod cues, or max cues. The family agreed with the priorities described in this fictional review.
