BILINGUAL PEDIATRIC SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION

Client: Maria Jose Salcedo Varela
Preferred name: Majo
Date of birth: August 9, 2022
Age at evaluation: 4;2
Evaluation date: October 9, 2026
Report date: October 11, 2026
Appointment: 9:15 a.m. to 11:00 a.m.
Record number: SL-2609418
Medicaid member number: 684209731Q
Authorization number: NC-SLP-482761
Procedure: CPT 92523
Service modifier: GN

Parents: Elena Marisol Varela Soto and Jesus Ramon Salcedo Pena
Address: 1846 Cedar Lantern Lane, Hollybend, North Carolina 27500
Telephone: 919-555-0146
Parent email: elena.varela@example.com

Evaluating clinician: Daniela Isabel Montejo Cruz, MS, CCC-SLP
Employer: Little Lantern Bilingual Therapy
Office: 720 Meadowglass Drive, Hollybend, North Carolina 27500
Office telephone: 919-555-0182
Clinician email: d.montejo@example.com
Website: https://littlelantern.example.com

This synthetic clinical record contains fictional identifying information, history, observations, and results.

BACKGROUND AND REASON FOR REFERRAL

Maria Jose Salcedo Varela attended an outpatient evaluation because her family and preschool staff reported difficulty understanding her speech. They also described short sentences, inconsistent answers to questions, and frustration during group activities. Her parents requested an assessment that considered both Spanish and English. Their main concern was whether her communication difficulties exceeded the differences expected during bilingual development.

The referral came from Dr. Adrian Tomas Beltran, her pediatrician at Meadowglass Children's Hospital. The family supplied a referral dated September 18, 2026. A prior service summary from Willowmere Children's Developmental Services Agency identified early concerns about expressive language. Service coordinator Nora Elise Benton confirmed that services ended after the transition to preschool.

Majo attends Cedar Lantern Early Learning School in Hollybend, Willowmere County. Lead teacher Ms. Rachel Dana Mercer reported that the child joins pretend play but often watches before speaking. Classroom assistant Mr. Luis Esteban Navarro noted that visual demonstrations help her follow classroom routines. Both staff members described steady attendance and interest in books, animals, and kitchen play.

Her parents want her to explain what happened, ask for help, and participate without an adult guessing her message. They do not want the family to reduce Spanish use. The assessment therefore included caregiver interviews, record review, structured testing, play observation, and supported teaching tasks across both languages.

BIRTH AND MEDICAL HISTORY

According to her mother, Elena Marisol Varela Soto, the pregnancy included monitored hypertension and concerns about fetal growth. Delivery occurred at 36 weeks, 5 days at River Lantern Regional Hospital in Ashgrove, North Carolina. Birth weight was 2.48 kg. Reported Apgar scores were 7 and 9. Obstetrician Dr. Miriam Celeste Aranda attended the delivery.

Maria Jose entered the NICU at River Lantern Regional Hospital for feeding support, temperature monitoring, and brief respiratory observation. Neonatologist Dr. Peter Julian Hensley supervised care. Her mother reported discharge on August 17, 2022, with oral feeding established and no home oxygen. The available discharge summary supported the reported admission and discharge dates.

The family described slow feeding during infancy and occasional coughing when drinking quickly. These concerns resolved with pacing and a slower bottle nipple. There is no current report of coughing during meals, food refusal, or prolonged chewing. The child eats familiar family foods and drinks from an open cup. No feeding assessment was requested during this visit.

Dr. Adrian Tomas Beltran follows growth and general development. The family reported recurrent middle ear infections during toddlerhood. Otolaryngologist Dr. Sofia Pilar Trevino evaluated the child at Meadowglass Children's Hospital on February 12, 2025. No surgery was reported. Audiologist Grace Linette Farrow documented hearing adequate for speech access on September 24, 2026. The report recommended continued monitoring if infections return.

The child reportedly sat independently at 8 months and walked at 16 months. Her parents recalled recognizable words at approximately 20 months and spontaneous word combinations near 30 months. These milestones came from caregiver recall rather than contemporaneous records. There is no reported loss of communication skills, seizure history, head injury, or current prescription medication.

During the evaluation, breathing appeared comfortable, and alertness remained stable. Oral structures appeared symmetrical during informal observation. Lip closure and tongue movement supported eating and the speech tasks attempted. This observation does not replace a medical examination. Fatigue affected participation near the end of the visit, but a movement break restored engagement.

FAMILY, CAREGIVER, AND LANGUAGE HISTORY

Majo lives with both parents and her brother, Jose Antonio Salcedo Varela, called Pepe, age 7;1. Her sister, Ana Lucia Salcedo Varela, age 18 months, also lives in the home. Her father, Jesus Ramon Salcedo Pena, uses the nickname Chuy. The family uses these names interchangeably during ordinary conversation.

Her maternal grandmother, Guadalupe Teresa Soto Rivas, called Lupita, provides afternoon care. Her uncle, Mateo Andres Varela Soto, called Teo, visits regularly. Babysitter Irene Sol Campos provides occasional evening care. The family dog, Canela, often becomes the topic of the child's play and stories.

The parents described current and former workplaces using English labels and Spanish word order. Her mother works at the store Cedar Basket Market, described as la tienda Cedar Basket Market. She previously worked at the restaurant Blue Lantern Kitchen, described as el restaurante Blue Lantern Kitchen. She also accepts shifts with the cleaning service Morning Fern Cleaning, described as el servicio de limpieza Morning Fern Cleaning.

Her father works at the factory Pinebridge Packaging Plant, described as la fabrica Pinebridge Packaging Plant. His seasonal employment includes the farm Silver Acorn Farm, described as la granja Silver Acorn Farm. He previously worked for the construction company Cedar Span Construction, described as la compania de construccion Cedar Span Construction. Changing work schedules affect transportation and appointment availability.

Spanish is the main language during meals, family visits, and evening routines. English is common at preschool and during sibling play. The caregivers estimated current exposure at 65% Spanish and 35% English. These estimates describe opportunity for exposure, rather than proficiency. The clinician did not treat language preference as evidence of impairment.

The mother described stronger understanding in Spanish and more frequent English labels for classroom materials. The father reported that the child sometimes begins in Spanish and finishes in English. This pattern also occurred during the assessment. Her grandmother understands many messages because she knows the routines, but unfamiliar listeners often need repetition.

The family reported a history of late talking in the paternal uncle. No relative has a documented language diagnosis in the records reviewed. The child previously attended Acorn Window Family Daycare, where caregiver Rosa Ines Calderon used Spanish throughout the day. Her current classroom provides English instruction with Spanish support during transitions.

BEHAVIOR AND PARTICIPATION

Maria Jose Salcedo Varela entered the room with her mother and inspected the toy shelves before approaching the clinician. She responded to a greeting with a wave and a quiet verbal response. She separated comfortably when her mother moved to a nearby chair. Shared attention, pointing, and coordinated eye gaze occurred during preferred activities.

The child sustained play with a kitchen set, animal figures, and a picture book. She offered toys to the clinician and checked the adult's reaction during pretend accidents. She requested missing materials through gestures and short phrases. When the listener misunderstood, she sometimes repeated the same message louder instead of adding information.

The parent reported that friend Juan Emilio Rojas Mena, called Juanito, usually understands her play ideas. Classmate Alma Isabel Torres Vega often helps explain her requests to classroom staff. Another group member, Diego Samuel Luna Perez, reportedly leaves activities when communication breaks down. These descriptions came from the parent and were not independently observed.

Attention improved when the clinician offered clear transitions and allowed the child to choose materials. Performance declined with lengthy spoken directions and unfamiliar vocabulary. Brief demonstrations supported participation without changing the intended task. The clinician documented additional support whenever it affected interpretation. No interpreter participated because the evaluating clinician conducted the assessment directly in both languages.

ASSESSMENT PROCEDURES AND RESULTS

The clinician administered selected procedures from PLS-5 Spanish and GFTA-3, then completed bilingual play sampling and supported learning tasks. The language results reflect the procedures used during this fictional assessment. English articulation scores require caution because the reference sample does not fully represent this child's language experience.

The table separates standard scores, percentiles, confidence intervals, and age equivalents. Age equivalents describe performance within a test framework. They do not establish a developmental age or determine placement. Clinical interpretation also considers functional communication, language exposure, caregiver reports, and response to teaching.

| Test or subtest | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-83 | 3;0–3;4 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | 74 | 4th percentile | 69-79 | 2;6–3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | 75 | 5th percentile | 70-80 | 2;9–3;2 |
| GFTA-3: Sounds-in-Words | 72 | 3rd percentile | 68-77 | 2;8–3;1 |

The confidence intervals shown use a 90% confidence level. No scaled scores were generated. The clinician used the articulation findings mainly to describe speech patterns and identify potential treatment targets. The numerical result did not serve as the sole basis for a speech diagnosis.

During Auditory Comprehension, the child identified familiar objects and understood routine action words. She followed related directions in 8/10 opportunities with gestures available. Performance fell to 3/8 when directions required an unfamiliar spatial relationship without visual support. She benefited from min cues for familiar routines and mod cues for less familiar directions.

During Expressive Communication, she named familiar pictures and combined words for requests. She had difficulty explaining an object's function and describing events outside the immediate activity. She answered action questions in 4 of 6 opportunities. Responses to explanation questions were usually gestures, isolated words, or repetitions of the adult's question.

Supported learning tasks showed useful responsiveness. After brief teaching, she identified a new action in 4/5 opportunities and used the corresponding word in 3/5. She required mod cues initially and min cues during the final practice. This improvement supports continued teaching in both languages, while persistent difficulties across settings remain clinically relevant.

SPEECH AND LANGUAGE SAMPLE

The clinician collected conversational samples during play and book sharing. Majo used requests, comments, protests, and answers in both languages. She produced "yo quiere agua", "baby sleeping", and "se cayo". These examples illustrate communication attempts; individual grammatical differences require interpretation within her bilingual development.

Mean utterance length was 2.7 words in the sampled interactions. The clinician marked word errors with the SALT code [EW] and omitted words with [OM]. These codes described the sample rather than establishing a diagnosis. Repetitions increased when the adult asked for clarification without providing a specific repair prompt.

Speech included fronting of /k/ toward [t] and inconsistent production of /g/. Some English consonant clusters were reduced. Spanish /ɾ/ was variable and was not selected as an immediate treatment target. The clinician considered developmental expectations and language differences before identifying errors for intervention.

The target "casa" was produced as "tasa" during picture naming. The target "spoon" was produced as "poon". With a model and mod cues, the child produced /k/ accurately in 6/10 syllable attempts. Accuracy fell to 2/10 during unsupported word attempts.

Estimated intelligibility was 58% for the unfamiliar clinician in connected speech. The mother estimated 85% understanding during familiar home routines. The child said, "Canela come," while moving an animal figure. She also said, "Juanito my friend." These phrases showed that personally meaningful topics increased spontaneous communication.

CLINICAL IMPRESSIONS

Findings support a mixed receptive and expressive language difficulty with a co-occurring speech sound difficulty. The concerns appeared across languages and affected everyday participation. Reduced exposure to English alone does not explain the full pattern reported and observed. The child's strengths include social interest, pretend play, gesture use, and improvement with focused teaching.

Provisional diagnostic codes are ICD-10 F80.2 and ICD-10 F80.0. The clinician will review these impressions as additional classroom information and treatment data become available. The assessment did not evaluate literacy, cognition, or motor development in depth. No conclusion about those areas is supported by this report.

Prognosis for improved functional communication is favorable with regular intervention and caregiver practice. Scheduling changes and inconsistent access to transportation may affect attendance. Family engagement, bilingual support, and the child's willingness to imitate provide useful treatment resources.

The parents received an explanation in English and Spanish. Elena Marisol Varela Soto summarized the main findings accurately. Jesus Ramon Salcedo Pena requested practical activities that fit meal preparation and travel routines. Both parents agreed that successful communication should guide treatment priorities.

RECOMMENDATIONS AND PLAN

1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy with direct practice and caregiver coaching. Use familiar play routines to expand requests, comments, and explanations. Accept meaningful responses in either language. Add models that match the language used during each activity.

2. Address comprehension through short directions, visual supports, and gradual removal of assistance. For proposed goal 1, the child will follow related directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Record the language, materials, and support used so progress can be interpreted accurately.

3. Expand spontaneous phrase use and communication repair. For proposed goal 2, the child will add information after a misunderstanding in 4 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Adults can offer a choice, identify the missing information, and allow time for a response.

4. Select speech targets that improve intelligibility in both languages. For proposed goal 3, the child will produce /k/ in selected words with 80% accuracy and mod cues. Begin with meaningful targets such as "casa" and "cup". Review progress before adding less functional targets.

5. Consider Cycles for persistent patterned speech errors and Hanen strategies for caregiver interaction. PROMPT is not included in the initial plan. PECS is also not included; the team can reconsider communication supports if participation needs change.

6. Coordinate with Ms. Rachel Dana Mercer and Mr. Luis Esteban Navarro after the family completes the appropriate release. Provide classroom strategies that support understanding, peer interaction, and repair. Avoid requiring repeated public corrections during group activities.

7. Continue Spanish during family routines. Use shared books, pretend play, and conversations about familiar events. Give a clear model, pause, and respond to the child's meaning. Caregivers should avoid turning every interaction into a naming task.

8. Contact Willowmere Early Learning Partnership for transportation resources if needed. Service coordinator Nora Elise Benton supplied contact information during the transition review. The prior IFSP outcome 2 addressed requesting help during daily routines and can inform current priorities.

9. Review progress on January 8, 2027. Obtain updated hearing information if infections or listening concerns return. Repeat selected assessment procedures only when they answer a specific clinical question.

Report completed by Daniela Isabel Montejo Cruz, MS, CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, Little Lantern Bilingual Therapy, North Carolina.

INDIVIDUALIZED FAMILY SERVICE PLAN

Service coordinator: Julian Ortiz, documented in contact notes as J. Ortiz

Clinician employer: Cedar Lantern Pediatric Communication Services
Clinician telephone: 252-555-0168
Clinician email: elena.duarte@example.com

The meeting occurred in the family home. Both parents, the service coordinator, and the speech-language pathologist attended. Grandmother joined the discussion by telephone. The family declined a separate interpreter because the clinician could discuss the plan directly in Spanish and English. Parents had time to ask questions and revise the proposed outcomes.

The coordinator explained family participation, consent, record access, and available service settings. Parents selected home and daycare visits because communication problems occur in both settings. They requested advance notice before another professional observes a visit.

DEVELOPMENTAL AND HEALTH SUMMARY

Parents reported an uncomplicated pregnancy and birth at Willow Harbor Community Hospital. Gestational age was 39 weeks, 2 days. Reported birth weight was 3,280 g. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. These details came from the family intake form; the hospital record was not available for this meeting.

Primary care physician Dr. Owen Bellamy follows routine health needs. Parents reported no daily medication, feeding tube, surgery, or known food allergy. Hearing screening documentation dated August 12, 2026 indicated responses within the screening criteria. Audiologist Priya Nand recommended follow-up if listening concerns increase.

The child walks independently, climbs onto a low chair, brings familiar objects to adults, and enjoys pretend feeding. Parents described communication frustration during meals, toy exchanges, and departures. They reported that unfamiliar adults often need help understanding requests.

The bilingual evaluation occurred on August 19, 2026. It included caregiver interview, play observation, and structured testing. English test scores provide limited information because the child's experience includes both languages. The clinician considered communication across languages and routines when recommending services.

ASSESSMENT SUMMARY

| Measure | Score | Confidence interval | Percentile | Age equivalent | Assessment date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| PLS-5: Auditory Comprehension | Standard score 78 | 90% interval 73-85 | 7th percentile | 1;8 | August 19, 2026 |
| PLS-5: Expressive Communication | Standard score 74 | 90% interval 69-82 | 4th percentile | 1;5 | August 19, 2026 |
| PLS-5: Total Language | Standard score 75 | 90% interval 71-83 | 5th percentile | 1;6 | August 19, 2026 |

These age equivalents describe test performance and do not represent the child's overall developmental age. No scaled scores were generated. The clinician did not combine Spanish and English responses into an altered standard score.

During supported play, Maria Jose followed familiar directions in 6/10 opportunities. With gestures, performance increased to 8/10. Independent requests occurred in 3 of 10 opportunities. Requests increased to 7 of 10 when adults offered choices and waited.

Observed consonants included /m/, /b/, and /p/. A familiar word beginning with /r/ was produced with [w]. The sample was too small for a stable speech sound diagnosis. Language-sample notation included the SALT code [EW] for an extra word.

FAMILY CONCERNS, PRIORITIES, AND RESOURCES

The mother stated, "She knows what she wants, but we guess too much. I want her to ask before she gets upset."

The father stated, "At dinner she points, and we bring the wrong thing. Then she cries. We want meals to feel easier."

Grandmother stated, "I want to understand her without asking her brother every time. I want to keep speaking Spanish with her."

Parents identified meals, daycare pickup, and shared play as their first priorities. They want practical strategies that fit ordinary activities. They prefer short demonstrations followed by their own practice. They do not want a long worksheet after each visit.

The family has stable housing, transportation, and regular telephone access. Both parents can attend some visits together. Grandmother can join morning visits. The babysitter can receive a brief strategy summary with parental consent. The family has picture books, blocks, toy animals, and familiar containers that can support practice.

Parents described their child as curious, affectionate, and persistent. They want adults to notice successful gestures and words. They also want adults to respect a refusal and provide help before frustration increases.

DAILY ROUTINES

The family usually begins the day at 6:45 a.m.. Breakfast occurs near 7:15 a.m.. The mother offers familiar foods while the father prepares the daycare bag. Requests are easiest when objects remain visible. Requests become harder when adults move quickly or ask several questions.

Arrival at Little Learners Daycare is usually at 8:10 a.m.. Classroom teacher Ms. Dana Whitcomb greets the child with a picture schedule. Assistant teacher J. Mercer supports handwashing and snack. Staff report that pointing is more frequent than spoken requesting.

Classmates Avery Moss and Lena Brook often play nearby. Classmate Theo Finch sometimes takes a preferred truck. Adults currently step in quickly. The family wants staff to model an easy request before resolving a manageable toy conflict.

Pickup occurs near 4:20 p.m.. The child often needs quiet contact before discussing the day. At home, sibling Nico enjoys building towers. Cousins Sofia Valdez and Emilio Valdez visit on weekends. Babysitter Paloma uses songs during cleanup.

The family dog, Chispa, joins floor play. During observation, the child said "Chispa ven" while pointing toward the door. Adults agreed to practice during calm play and keep the dog away from food activities.

OTHER AGENCIES AND COMMUNITY CONTACTS

The family receives nutrition support from Pine Hollow WIC Office. Contact person Mara Keene helped identify a convenient appointment time. The family also uses book activities through Briar Glen Smart Start Partnership.

No current involvement with Pine Hollow Department of Social Services was reported. The coordinator recorded this as family report, without requesting unrelated records.

The proposed therapy program is Little Learners Program, operated by the clinician's employer. It is separate from Little Learners Daycare. The coordinator explained the similar names so parents could identify the service provider correctly.

The family occasionally attends Meadow Lantern Public Library. Volunteer Basil Hart leads its informal story circle. Parents may use books from that activity for home practice. No information will be shared with the volunteer.

Parents asked about future attendance at Willow Path Preschool. Transition options will be discussed later. This plan does not reserve a place or commit the family to that school.

OUTCOME 1: REQUESTS DURING MEALS

By February 28, 2027, the child will communicate a food, drink, or help request during family meals using a gesture, picture, spoken word, or word combination. The criterion is 4 of 5 natural opportunities across consecutive observed meal routines, with min cues.

Baseline: Requests occurred in 3 of 10 opportunities without an adult model. Adults often anticipated needs or supplied several items before the child selected one.

Strategies: Place familiar choices within view. Offer a small serving, then pause when another serving is appropriate. Model "more", "mas", "water", or "agua" with a gesture. Accept either language. Respond promptly to a clear request. Do not require imitation before giving food or drink.

The clinician will use Enhanced Milieu Teaching and family coaching. Early practice may include mod cues, followed by less adult support. Parents will identify comfortable pauses and signs that the child needs immediate help.

Progress will be reviewed through caregiver examples and brief observation. A request counts when the child directs a clear message toward another person. Repeated adult questions do not count as independent communication.

OUTCOME 2: SHARED PLAY AND TURN TAKING

By February 28, 2027, the child will participate in short play exchanges with an adult, sibling, or classmate. The child will use a gesture or word to request a turn, offer an object, or continue play in 8/10 opportunities with min cues.

Baseline: Exchanges required max cues when another child held a preferred object. Adult-supported exchanges were more successful with duplicate toys.

Strategies: Start with enjoyable games that have clear turns. Adults will model "my turn", "mi turno", "go", and "va". They will keep turns brief and acknowledge reaching, pointing, and appropriate words. Adults may offer duplicate objects when waiting becomes too difficult.

During assessment, Majo said "Nico go" while handing over a block. This phrase showed an emerging effort to direct another person's action. The clinician will build on that function through play.

The clinician may introduce selected Hanen interaction strategies, including following the child's interest and balancing turns. The family is not enrolled in a complete parent course. Staff will practice the same strategies during classroom play.

OUTCOME 3: PARTICIPATION IN TRANSITIONS

By February 28, 2027, the child will communicate a choice, protest, or request for help during arrival, cleanup, and departure in 3 of 4 opportunities with min cues.

Baseline: Adults reported crying or dropping to the floor during some departures. A familiar object and advance notice often helped. The team did not observe enough transitions to estimate a reliable frequency.

Strategies: Show a simple picture before changing activities. Use a short statement and allow processing time. Offer a meaningful choice when possible. Model "help", "ayuda", "all done", and "ya". Honor an appropriate protest when the activity can wait.

Parents will practice during leaving the house. Classroom staff will practice during cleanup and pickup. The clinician will coach adults to reduce rapid questions and use predictable language. Adults will record useful examples rather than count every difficult moment.

Progress will include the child's participation and the family's report of easier routines. The team will adjust the strategies if the child needs more support, becomes distressed, or stops using a previously helpful message.

SERVICES AND DATES

Speech-language intervention will begin on September 1, 2026 and continue through February 28, 2027. Visits will occur once weekly for forty-five minutes. The usual home appointment is Tuesday at 9:00 a.m.. Selected visits may occur at daycare at 10:15 a.m. with parental agreement.

The service uses individual intervention and caregiver coaching through Little Learners Program. Home visits will address meals and family play. Daycare visits will address peer interaction and transitions. The clinician will coordinate strategies across settings.

Billing information, when applicable: CPT 92507, modifier GN, and ICD-10 F80.2. These codes do not determine whether the family has achieved an outcome.

Service coordination will continue throughout the plan period. The coordinator will contact the family monthly and when needs change. A progress discussion is scheduled for November 20, 2026. The formal review is planned for February 19, 2027.

Missed visits will be discussed promptly. The team will arrange another appointment when schedules permit. Parents may request changes in setting, frequency, strategies, or participants through the coordinator.

REVIEW AND FAMILY AGREEMENT

The team will review outcomes 1, 2, and 3 using direct observation, caregiver report, and classroom examples. New standardized testing is not required at every review. The team will consider whether communication becomes more useful across both languages.

Parents agreed that gestures, pictures, and spoken language are acceptable communication methods. They requested that adults avoid repeated demands to say a word. The clinician will provide a brief written summary after visits.

The coordinator will confirm consent before sharing this plan with classroom staff or another agency. The family received a copy and identified no additional referral request during the meeting.

Parent acknowledgement: Tomas Vega Leon, August 28, 2026

The coordinator will check scheduling to prevent duplicate visits. The family may review local resources at https://pinehaven-family.example.com. No referral requires the family to stop using Spanish.

### 8. IFSP Outcomes and Strategies

#### 8.1 Outcome 1: Communicate During Meals

During meals and snacks, Elena will request an item, assistance, or continuation through a word, gesture, or picture in 4 of 5 opportunities across two routines.

Adults will offer meaningful choices, pause, and acknowledge all communication. The clinician will use focused stimulation and Hanen strategies. Practice targets include "help", "more", "open", and "más".

Initial support may include mod cues, followed by reduced assistance. Caregivers will record successful requests on a brief routine checklist. Progress will be reviewed by January 7, 2027.

#### 8.2 Outcome 2: Participate in Transitions

During departure, cleanup, and bedtime, the child will use a communication response and complete the next routine step in 80% of opportunities with min cues.

Adults will present a picture sequence and model "all done" or "one more". They will allow processing time before repeating directions. The clinician will demonstrate routines-based coaching during an actual transition.

Caregivers and classroom staff will compare observations weekly. The team will review progress by February 7, 2027.

#### 8.3 Outcome 3: Join Shared Play

During familiar play, the child will initiate or answer a peer using a gesture, word, or short combination in 3 of 5 opportunities.

Adults will arrange paired activities, model "my turn" and "your turn", and reduce support from mod cues to min cues. Staff will support interaction with Mila Hart and Owen Reed without requiring speech before access to toys.

### 9. Services, Dates, and Review Responsibilities

Speech-language services will occur weekly in home or childcare routines, beginning October 14, 2026 and continuing through April 6, 2027. Each visit will include direct interaction, caregiver practice, and planning.

Service coordination will continue monthly. Classroom consultation will occur twice monthly with family consent. The fictional authorization is SL-260914-782.

The service entry lists CPT 92507, modifier GN, and ICD-10 F80.2. These entries identify the planned clinical service. Billing eligibility remains subject to the fictional payer record.

### 10. Family Participation and Agreement

The parents helped select all outcomes and accepted the proposed schedule. They requested advance notice when a substitute provider attends. The coordinator will address transportation and scheduling concerns.

The clinician explained assessment limits, caregiver choice, and review procedures in both languages. The family may request changes when routines or priorities change.

The next team review is scheduled for April 7, 2027 at 10:00 a.m.. Prepared by Isabel Serrano, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, on October 7, 2026.

FAMILY INFORMATION / CONTACTS

Pt lives w/ mother, Elena Cordero Salvatierra, father, Tomás Valdés Arriaga, and brother, Nicolás Valdés Cordero, age 7 years. Maternal grandmother, Rosa Salvatierra Beltrán, provides afternoon care. Pt walks independently, carries preferred toys, and uses gestures effectively. Attention varies w/ activity interest and environmental noise. Bilingual exposure includes Spanish at home and mixed Spanish-English input at daycare. Team interprets communication across both languages and does not count language difference alone as impairment.

FAMILY CONCERNS / PRIORITIES IN FAMILY’S OWN WORDS

Mother: “I know María José understands our routines. I worry when she pulls my hand and cries because I cannot tell what she needs. I want her to ask for water, help, or another turn.”

Father: “When Majo says something in Spanish, I want daycare to know that it counts. We do not want to stop Spanish at home. We want everyone to wait and let her try.”

Grandmother: “I can practice while we wash hands and feed Canela. I need short ideas, because I also prepare lunch. Show me what to say when she points.”

Parents prioritize requests during meals, participation w/ other children, and simpler bedtime transitions. They also want pt to communicate discomfort before crying. Family does not prioritize naming colors or completing worksheets. CG asks for strategies that fit existing routines and use familiar household items.

Strengths include shared enjoyment, strong attachment to CG, interest in music, and persistence when adults respond. Parents report that brief pauses help more than repeated questions. Team will build from these observations.

DAILY ROUTINES / NATURAL ENVIRONMENTS

Wake-up occurs approx 6:45 a.m.. Pt seeks father, brings shoes, and watches breakfast preparation. CG can offer two visible choices and pause. Breakfast begins approx 7:10 a.m.; pt accepts familiar textures and indicates more by reaching. Adult models "más", "agua", and "help" w/ gesture support. Family prefers modeling before asking questions.

At Little Acorn Crossing Childcare, arrival is approx 8:15 a.m.. Pt separates more easily when teacher shows the picture schedule. Peer Amaya Torres often brings a book. Peer Jonah Reed joins block play. Pt watches peers, hands over materials, and occasionally protests when a toy moves away. Staff will acknowledge the message and model a brief replacement phrase.

Lunch w/ grandmother occurs approx 12:20 p.m. on home-care days. Handwashing, opening containers, and choosing a cup offer useful practice. Grandmother will keep preferred items visible and accessible after a brief communication opportunity; prolonged withholding is not part of the plan.

Afternoon play begins approx 3:30 p.m.. Brother Nicolás Valdés Cordero likes rolling cars w/ pt. CG will support turn-taking without requiring exact repetition. At bath, pt follows familiar actions but needs visual support for transitions. Bedtime routine starts approx 7:40 p.m. and includes pajamas, a book, and a song. Parents will use the same short transition language across nights.

ASSESSMENT / CURRENT COMMUNICATION

Initial bilingual assessment occurred on 03/03/2025, when pt was approx 26 months, or 2;2. PLS-5 results were considered alongside parent interview, observation, and language sampling. Expressive Communication standard score: 74; percentile: 4th; confidence interval: 69–81 at 95%; age equivalent: 1;6. Total Language standard score: 75; percentile: 5th.

Age equivalents summarize test performance and do not describe every daily skill. Observed communication clustered across approximately 1;6–2;0. Familiar pretend-play behaviors included scattered skills within 2;6–3;0, without consistent performance across that range. Scores require cautious interpretation given bilingual exposure and variable participation.

Current sample included "más agua", "no mío", "all done", and "mamá ven". Pt also said “Canela come” while pointing toward the doorway. Speech inventory included /m/, /p/, /b/, /t/, and [w]. Productions containing /k/ were inconsistent. Spanish /ɾ/ was not selected as a current target.

SLP used SALT conventions to document spontaneous language; [EW] marked an extraneous word. Today’s sample served as a functional progress measure. No standardized retest was completed.

OUTCOME 1 — REQUESTS DURING FAMILY ROUTINES

Family outcome: Pt will tell a familiar adult what she needs during meals, play, and handwashing using words, gestures, or pictures. Success criterion: independent or supported requests in 4 of 5 opportunities across three routines for two consecutive weeks. Baseline: requests in 2/10 opportunities w/ max cues.

Strategies: Use routines-based coaching, focused stimulation, and total communication. CG offers a meaningful choice, models a brief message, then waits. Accept pointing, a picture, or a word as a valid request. Expand pt’s message by one useful word without requiring repetition. Targets include "open", "abre", "more", and "ayuda".

Review data: pt requested in 8/10 structured opportunities, or 80%, w/ mod cues. Requests generalized to 3 of 5 unplanned home opportunities w/ min cues. Outcome remains active b/c adult prompting is still frequent. Parents will record successful opportunities using a simple tally, with no requirement to record every interaction.

OUTCOME 2 — SHARED PLAY AT DAYCARE

Family outcome: Pt will join a brief play exchange w/ a peer and communicate a turn, protest, or invitation. Success criterion: participation in 3 of 4 exchanges during familiar play across two observation days. Baseline: 1/4 exchanges w/ max cues and adult proximity.

Strategies: Use milieu teaching during blocks, cars, and books. Adult joins the activity, models "my turn", "mi turno", "go", or "ven", and allows processing time. Teacher may offer a picture cue and describe the peer’s action. Staff will support safe boundaries while honoring an appropriate protest.

Review data: pt completed 3/4 exchanges, or 75%, w/ mod cues. During book play, pt said “Amaya Torres look” and pointed to a picture. Staff reports similar exchanges occur inconsistently outside clinician visits. Continue this outcome, reduce adult language during turns, and collect brief observations during ordinary classroom play.

OUTCOME 3 — UNDERSTANDING TRANSITIONS

Family outcome: Pt will follow familiar transition directions and communicate a need for help or another turn. Success criterion: completion of 4/5 transitions w/ visual support and no more than min cues. Baseline: 2/5 transitions w/ max cues.

Strategies: Pair a short direction w/ an object or picture. Use "shoes on", "wash hands", and "one more". Offer a predictable closing action before moving activities. Parents may acknowledge distress, pause, and repeat the same concise direction.

Review data: pt completed 4/5 familiar transitions, or 80%, w/ mod cues. Novel transitions remained harder. Continue the outcome and practice first in familiar routines. CG demonstrated the sequence in 3 of 3 opportunities. Team will review whether visual support alone becomes sufficient before changing the success criterion.

SERVICES / SESSION SCHEDULE

Authorized service interval: 03/10/2025 through 09/02/2025. Schedule below begins 06/09/2025. Each listed SLP visit lasts 30 minutes. Alternate locations require CG agreement.

OTHER AGENCIES / COORDINATION

Transportation dispatcher, Dorian Vale, at Fernwheel Family Transit can arrange approved rides. Preschool transition contact is Nadia Quintero at Cedarbend Early Learning School. No placement decision has been made.

CONSENT / NEXT REVIEW

Next review target: 09/02/2025. Coordinator will arrange transition discussion before the current authorization ends. CG will report scheduling barriers promptly. SLP will share short practice notes after visits and review progress w/ family monthly.

FAMILY INFORMATION AND PARTICIPATION

The family reviewed this plan in English with Spanish interpretation available throughout the meeting. Mother preferred to discuss concerns in Spanish and review the written summary in English. Father participated by telephone during his work break. Both parents approved the wording below after the interpreter read it back.

Luna lives with both parents and her sister, Inés Solano, age 6 years. Grandmother Celia Armenta provides care on weekdays. Neighbor and babysitter Alma Neri helps when work schedules overlap. The household dog, Chispa, often joins floor play.

Mom works nights at Lantern Bend Packaging Cooperative as a packing line inspector. Father works at Cedar Kite Bicycle Works as a repair technician. Mother requested appointments after her daytime sleep. The family wants strategies that all caregivers can use without buying special materials.

FAMILY CONCERNS AND PRIORITIES

Mother stated, through interpretation, “I know what she wants when she takes my hand. Other people do not understand. I want her to ask before she gets upset.”

Father stated, “At dinner she points, and we guess. I want to give her time, but I need to know what to do.”

Grandmother Celia Armenta stated, “She understands our familiar routines. When something changes, she cries and follows me.”

The family identified communication during meals, dressing, and transitions as its priorities. Mother also wants more comfortable participation in community play. The family values Spanish for relationships at home and English for childcare participation. Neither parent wants to stop using Spanish.

Parents reported no loss of previously used skills. Their main concern is that unfamiliar adults miss gestures and then offer repeated questions. The family asked the team to teach adults how to notice communication before frustration increases.

DAILY ROUTINES AND NATURAL ENVIRONMENTS

Breakfast usually begins at 7:30 a.m.. Grandmother offers familiar foods and places two choices within view. Luli points, reaches, or brings a cup. Adults sometimes provide the item before she has time to add a sound or word.

Childcare attendance at Little Lantern Grove Childcare occurs on three mornings each week. Ms. Mara Quiles reported that Luna watches peers Nico Beltrán and Asha Marin during songs. She joins when an adult models the action nearby.

Dressing happens beside a low basket. Bath play includes cups, floating animals, and predictable turn taking. Evening meals begin around 6:15 p.m.. Parents described bedtime books as a calm routine. During shared reading, Luna turns pages and points to pictures. Adults can pause at familiar pages without making the routine feel like a test.

DEVELOPMENTAL AND COMMUNICATION REVIEW

The evaluation dated 2025-02-24 included caregiver interviews, play observation, and an English administration of PLS-5. Reported results were Auditory Comprehension standard score 79, percentile 8, confidence interval 74-87, and age equivalent 1;10. Expressive Communication standard score was 74, percentile 4, confidence interval 69-83, and age equivalent 1;7. Total Language standard score was 75, percentile 5, with confidence interval 70-83.

These scores describe performance in English during that assessment. They do not fully represent skills across both languages. The bilingual clinician used Spanish language samples and caregiver examples to guide this review. Language exposure alone does not explain the functional concerns.

During familiar play, Luna used gestures, "más", "up", and "agua". She said “Chispa go” while pointing toward the door. Observed sounds included /m/, /b/, and [w]. She followed familiar directions in 4 of 5 opportunities with gestures.

Birth history included gestational age 38 weeks, birth weight 3,120 grams, and Apgar scores 8 and 9. Parents reported no current hearing concerns. Formal hearing follow-up remains planned.

OTHER PROVIDERS AND COMMUNITY SUPPORTS

Dr. Priya Caldera at Lantern Fern Children's Hospital provides primary care. Occupational therapist Tessa Bellamy supports utensil use and dressing participation. Physical therapist Owen Serrat monitors balance during outdoor play.

The family receives nutrition support through Laurel Lantern Family Nutrition Office. It attends story time at Arroyo Claro Lantern Library and a family play group at Open Meadow Community Center. Pastor Silas Orell coordinates rides through Cedar Lantern Fellowship when requested.

The coordinator will confirm contact details before sharing this plan. The family approved coordination with childcare, the pediatrician, and the current therapists. Approval does not extend to community volunteers.

OUTCOME 1: COMMUNICATION DURING MEALS

The family wants Luna to request an item, help, or another turn during meals so adults can respond before frustration grows. By 09/15/2025, she will use a gesture paired with a sound, word, or picture in 8/10 naturally occurring opportunities across home and childcare routines, with min cues.

Adults will offer two visible choices, pause, and accept communication in either language. They will model targets such as "more", "más", "help", and "ayuda". Access to food will not depend on speech.

The clinician will use Hanen responsive interaction strategies and demonstrate how to expand a message without repeated testing. Caregivers will record brief examples twice weekly. Current performance is 3 of 10 opportunities with mod cues. Review will consider comfort, independence, and participation as well as the count.

OUTCOME 2: PARTICIPATION IN DRESSING

The family wants dressing to include shared attention and useful communication. By 15/09/2025, Luli will complete a familiar dressing sequence and communicate a choice or request in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues, across two caregivers.

Grandmother will place clothing within reach and use the same short sequence each day. Adults will model "sock", "calcetín", "on", and "help", then pause. A gesture, picture selection, sound, or word will count when its meaning is clear.

The occupational therapist will advise on positioning and clothing access. The speech-language pathologist will coach communication within the routine. Current participation is 2 of 5 opportunities with max cues. Adults will shorten the sequence when fatigue affects participation. They will avoid physical prompting that causes distress.

OUTCOME 3: SHARED PLAY AND TRANSITIONS

The family wants Luna to join familiar people in play and move between activities with less distress. By September 15, 2025, she will participate in a shared play exchange and use an agreed transition support in 80% of observed opportunities with mod cues.

Adults will start with preferred toys and imitate her actions. They will model targets including "my turn", "otra vez", and "all done". A simple picture sequence will show play, cleanup, and the next activity.

Ms. Quiles will offer paired play with Nico when both children show interest. Current success is 40% with max cues. The physical therapist will advise on safe movement between play areas. Adults will offer a quiet pause when noise or crowding limits participation.

SERVICE PLAN AND DATES

Speech-language services will occur weekly in the home or childcare setting from 06/23/2025 through 12/15/2025. Each visit will include caregiver coaching, direct observation, practice, and a brief review of what worked. Billing information lists CPT 92507, modifier GO, and ICD-10 F80.2.

Occupational therapy will continue every other week from 23 de junio de 2025 through 15 de diciembre de 2025. Physical therapy will continue monthly during the same service period. The coordinator will arrange the hearing appointment and review transportation needs.

The interpreter will attend requested meetings. Language support will not reduce the planned service time. Providers will notify the family before schedule changes.

REVIEW, FOLLOW-UP, AND FAMILY AGREEMENT

Noelia Voss will contact the family on 07-07-2025 to check service access. A prior outreach entry dated el martes 4 de junio de 2024 remains in the fictional record history; it does not indicate a current service.

The team will review progress on September 16, 2025. Caregiver examples will guide changes if the strategies do not fit daily routines. Parents can request an earlier review.

North Carolina Infant-Toddler Program
Individualized Family Service Plan Review and Communication Evaluation

Review date: October 8, 2026
Previous IFSP date: April 8, 2026
Child record: FICT-ITP-604817
Medicaid member number: 000642817Z
Evaluation authorization: FICT-AUTH-728406

FAMILY INFORMATION AND PARTICIPATION

Nico Maravilla was born on August 8, 2024 and is 26 months old. His parents, Elena Maravilla and Tomás Maravilla, share decision-making responsibility. His sister, Sol Maravilla, is 4;2. His grandmother, Inés Varela, provides care on weekdays. The family’s dog is named Pipo.

The family lives at 4186 Lantern Finch Lane, Bellmere, North Carolina 00027, in Larkwell County. The preferred telephone number is (919) 555-0146. The alternate number is (984) 555-0182. The parent’s email is elena.maravilla@example.invalid. Spanish and English are used at home. The parents requested an English report and verbal explanations in both languages.

The father works for Lantern Orchard Packaging. His changing shifts affect visit availability. The family prefers home visits after breakfast and asks that grandmother participate whenever possible. Both parents attended this review and consented to share the service summary with the early learning classroom.

COORDINATION AND COMMUNITY CONNECTIONS

Service coordinator Ms. Mara Fenwick represents the Larkwell County Children’s Developmental Services Agency. Her telephone number is (919) 555-0128, and her email is mara.fenwick@example.invalid. The office is at 72 Meadowglass Court, Bellmere, North Carolina 00027. Its family resource page is https://larkwell-cdsa.example.invalid/families.

Current supports include Larkwell County WIC, Larkwell County Partnership for Children, and Larkwell County Early Head Start. The family requested information about transportation assistance through Larkwell County DSS. That referral remains pending; no eligibility decision was reported.

The child attends Little Lantern Learning House. Classroom teacher Ms. Beatriz Lorne supplied a routine checklist. Pediatrician Dr. Sofia Calder practices at Meadowglass Children’s Hospital. The parents authorized the coordinator to request the most recent hearing documentation.

FAMILY CONCERNS AND PRIORITIES

Mother Elena Maravilla said, “He knows what he wants, but we guess too much. I want him to tell us before he cries.”

Father Tomás Maravilla said, “At dinner, I want to understand whether he wants more food or wants to leave. I also want him to keep learning Spanish.”

Grandmother Inés Varela said, “When we get dressed, I want him to help and tell me which shoes. I need ideas I can remember without a worksheet.”

The parents identified communication during meals, dressing, and sibling play as their first priorities. They value gestures, spoken words, and pictures equally when these help the child participate. They do not want practice to interrupt meals or turn family play into testing.

The family described strengths in affection, curiosity, music, and helping with simple household tasks. They want adults to recognize communication attempts sooner. They also want consistent responses across home and the classroom.

HEALTH, DEVELOPMENT, AND EVALUATION METHODS

The parent reported delivery at 38 weeks gestation, birth weight 3.12 kg, and Apgar scores of 8 and 9. No prolonged neonatal admission was reported. Current age is 2;2. The parent reported no loss of previously acquired skills.

The evaluation occurred on October 6, 2026, from 9:05 a.m. to 10:00 a.m., in the home. Bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist Lydia Serrano, M.S., CCC-SLP, of Willow Lantern Pediatric Therapy, completed caregiver interviews, play observation, an oral mechanism screening, and the PLS-5 Spanish.

Spanish was the primary assessment language. English responses were accepted according to the test’s bilingual procedures. Results describe performance during this visit and require interpretation with language exposure, parent report, and participation in familiar routines. Attention varied when unfamiliar materials replaced preferred toys.

| Test or subtest | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish — Auditory Comprehension | 82 | 12th | 76–89 | 1;9–2;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Expressive Communication | 76 | 5th | 70–84 | 1;6–1;9 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Total Language | 78 | 7th | 72–85 | 1;8–1;11 |

Confidence intervals reflect a 90% confidence level. Age-equivalent ranges are descriptive and do not establish placement or eligibility alone.

COMMUNICATION FINDINGS

Nico followed familiar one-step directions in 8/10 opportunities with gestures and 5/10 without gestures. He identified familiar objects in 4 of 5 opportunities. He used a gesture, vocalization, or word to request in 7/10 opportunities with min cues.

Spontaneous productions included "agua", "más", "go", and "mama". During dog play, he said, “Pipo go.” During sibling play, he said, “Sol come.” These utterances referred to household members.

The lexical target "sol", meaning sun, was selected for a picture routine because it shares its form with his sister’s name. Adults will clarify whether he means the picture or the person through context and pointing.

Observed consonants included /m/, /p/, /b/, and /t/. An occasional [w] occurred during vehicle play. Productions of /k/ and /ɾ/ were inconsistent. A language sample contained an extraneous word coded [EW]. Speech sound observations were insufficient to establish a separate motor speech diagnosis.

Clinical impression: mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, F80.2. Evaluation billing: CPT 92523 with modifier GN.

DAILY ROUTINES AND PARTICIPATION

Breakfast begins near 7:30 a.m.. The child chooses between cereal and fruit by reaching. Adults often anticipate his choice before he communicates. Dressing follows at 8:00 a.m., when he enjoys carrying shoes but protests unfamiliar clothing.

Classroom arrival is approximately 8:45 a.m.. Staff report that visual choices help with separation. During play, peers Milo Quill and Ada Fern frequently offer toy vehicles. He joins briefly but needs adult help to request a turn.

Lunch occurs at 11:30 a.m.. Rest begins around 12:30 p.m.. After pickup at 3:15 p.m., grandmother uses songs during handwashing and snack. The family eats dinner at 6:15 p.m. and reads together at 7:40 p.m..

Transitions are easier when adults show the next activity and allow a pause. Communication becomes less clear when several people speak at once. The family will practice within existing routines, using available objects and pictures.

OUTCOMES AND STRATEGIES

Outcome 1: During meals and dressing, the child will communicate a choice, request, or refusal using a word, gesture, or picture in 8/10 opportunities across two familiar routines.

Baseline is 4/10 independent opportunities. Adults will offer two meaningful choices, wait, and respond to the attempt. Coaching will use Hanen principles and It Takes Two to Talk. Pictures may supplement speech. Success will be reviewed through caregiver examples and brief observation.

Outcome 2: During family play, the child will combine two communication elements in 3 of 5 opportunities with min cues.

Baseline is 1 of 5 opportunities with mod cues. Adults will model short combinations such as "más agua" and "go car", then pause. The clinician will support sibling turn-taking and accept mixed-language combinations. Models will follow the child’s interests without requiring repeated imitation.

Outcome 3: During transitions, the child will follow a familiar direction with a visual support in 80% of opportunities across home and classroom.

Baseline is 50% without a consistent visual support. Adults will use the same pictures, reduce competing speech, and acknowledge refusals. Staff will record examples without interrupting participation. The family and teacher will compare which supports help most.

The clinician discussed PECS, PROMPT, Cycles, and Kaufman as distinct approaches that require individual consideration. None will be added automatically. Current intervention emphasizes functional communication and caregiver coaching. No speech motor protocol is indicated from this visit alone.

SERVICES, DATES, AND REVIEW PLAN

Speech-language intervention will begin on October 15, 2026 and continue through April 8, 2027. Planned home visits occur weekly, from 9:15 a.m. to 10:00 a.m.. Treatment billing is CPT 92507, modifier GN. Classroom consultation will occur monthly, from 10:30 a.m. to 11:00 a.m., with family consent.

The coordinator will check referral progress by October 22, 2026. The team will review participation on January 14, 2027. The next IFSP review is scheduled for April 8, 2027. Adults will bring examples of successful communication and difficult routines.

Prepared by Lydia Serrano, M.S., CCC-SLP, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, Willow Lantern Pediatric Therapy. Signed electronically on October 8, 2026, at 4:20 p.m..

Family concerns and priorities

Mother Elena Cardenas Vega said, “I understand her pointing, but other people do not. I want her to tell us when something hurts or when she needs help. I want Spanish to stay part of our home. I do not want every meal to feel like a lesson.”

They want strategies that fit these activities without adding separate homework periods.

Daily routines and participation

The child usually wakes at 6:45 a.m.. Breakfast begins around 7:15 a.m.. Mother offers two familiar foods and places a picture choice beside the plate. The child attends Little Lantern Learning House on weekdays. She arrives near 8:00 a.m. and leaves around 3:30 p.m.. She is assigned to Ms. Lopez's room, named Sunflower Room. At home, sibling Sol enjoys blocks and pretend cooking. The family dog, Rocky, often stays beside the play area. During a recent visit, the child said, “Rocky run.” Later, she called, “Sol come.” These productions occurred during meaningful play and were recorded without requiring repetition.

Bath begins near 6:30 p.m., followed by books and bedtime around 7:30 p.m.. Grandmother uses familiar Spanish songs. The child chooses a book by bringing it to an adult. The family will add one predictable pause during reading and respond to any communication attempt.

Other agencies and community supports

Cedar Lantern Family Services Department maintains a separate childcare assistance record, CC-604219. The service coordinator will confirm which documents each agency needs before sharing information.

Father works at Willow Cart Packaging Cooperative. His schedule changes weekly, so visits will use a consistent afternoon window when possible. The sibling attends Pine Thread Primary School. School pickup sometimes limits the mother's availability. Babysitter Hope Bennett may attend a coaching visit with parental consent. Community transportation driver Will Mercer is listed only as a pickup contact.

Health and communication review

The birth summary from Mallow Creek Children's Hospital lists gestational age 39 weeks, 2 days, birth weight 7 pounds, 4 ounces, and Apgar scores 8 and 9. The pediatrician reported no new medical restrictions. Hearing follow-up remains scheduled for November 3, 2026. The team will review the result before interpreting persistent listening concerns.

The communication evaluation dated September 24, 2026 included PLS-5. Recorded results were Auditory Comprehension standard score 78, percentile 7, and confidence interval 73-83; Expressive Communication standard score 74, percentile 4, and confidence interval 69-81; and Total Language standard score 75, percentile 5. Recorded age-equivalent ranges were 1;11-2;1 for comprehension and 1;8-1;10 for expression.

These English assessment results provide limited descriptive information because the child uses two languages. Spanish observations, caregiver reports, play samples, and participation across routines informed the plan. The team did not use English scores alone to describe overall language ability.

A play sample included spontaneous requests in 6/10 opportunities and successful shared attention in 8/10 opportunities. Familiar adults understood approximately 60% of spoken attempts in context. An unfamiliar listener understood approximately 35%. The child used “[ [EW] ]” in the draft transcription key; the corrected sample code is [EW].

Observed productions included “mas,” “agua,” “more,” and “help.” The child sometimes used [w] where an adult model contained /r/. Production of /k/ varied across play samples. These observations guide further assessment and do not establish a motor speech diagnosis.

Outcomes and strategies

Outcome 1: Communicate choices and requests during meals.

By January 14, 2027, the child will communicate a food, drink, or finished message in 8/10 natural opportunities across three meals, with min cues. Baseline performance is 4/10 opportunities with mod cues. Adults will offer two visible choices, pause, and accept a gesture, picture, sign, or spoken attempt. Target words include “agua,” “mas,” “milk,” and “all done.” The clinician will coach responsive interaction using Hanen principles and selected It Takes Two to Talk strategies. The family will record brief examples rather than drill repetitions.

Outcome 2: Request help or a break during difficult routines.

By January 14, 2027, the child will communicate help or a break in 3 of 5 opportunities during dressing, cleanup, or transitions, with min cues. The current baseline is 1 of 5 opportunities with max cues. Adults will model “help,” “ayuda,” or “break” while showing the matching picture. They will provide help immediately after a clear request. If the child becomes distressed, the adult will reduce demands and support regulation. The team will count successful communication separately from compliance with the routine.

Outcome 3: Participate in short exchanges with another child.

By April 8, 2027, the child will complete three reciprocal play turns in 4 of 5 observed play opportunities, with mod cues or less. Baseline is one reciprocal turn in 2 of 5 opportunities with max cues. Daycare staff will arrange familiar materials, model giving and receiving, and allow sufficient wait time. Targets include “my turn,” “your turn,” and “take it.” Peers may decline participation. Adults will support comfortable play and will not require eye contact or spoken language to count a turn.

Outcome 4: Expand useful communication during shared play.

By April 8, 2027, the child will use a two-part message in 6/10 meaningful opportunities across home and daycare, with min cues. Baseline is 2/10 opportunities with mod cues. Adults will expand the child's message once, then continue the activity. Examples include “more bubbles,” “mas agua,” and “baby sleep.” Two-part messages may combine speech, signs, and pictures. The clinician will help adults identify messages that serve the child's current purpose. Success will not depend on exact imitation of an adult sentence.

Outcome 5: Improve clarity of selected functional words.

By April 8, 2027, familiar listeners will recognize selected functional words in 7/10 context-supported opportunities, with mod cues or less. The initial baseline is 3/10. The clinician will select a small set of useful words after additional bilingual speech sampling. Cycles and Kaufman methods may inform later treatment if assessment supports their use. PROMPT was discussed as a possible approach requiring further assessment and specific caregiver consent for touch. It was not administered during this review. Adults will preserve the child's message while offering a clear model.

Outcome 6: Use an accessible communication system across routines.

By January 14, 2027, caregivers will make the child's communication pictures available during 4 of 5 selected routines and respond consistently to exchanges. Baseline availability is 2 of 5 routines. The clinician will review picture placement, access, and partner responses. PECS was discussed as a formal program option; the current plan uses informal picture choices and does not claim formal program implementation. The team will compare participation with different supports and retain those that help the child communicate. Spoken attempts remain welcome without becoming a condition for access.

Services, dates, and review arrangements

Speech-language services through Carolina Little Voices Pediatric Therapy, PLLC begin October 12, 2026 and continue through April 8, 2027. The planned frequency is one 45-minute individual visit each week, primarily at home. One visit each month may occur at daycare to support agreed routines. The clinician will use caregiver coaching, direct observation, and brief supported play.

The proposed billing entry is CPT 92507 with modifier GO. The recorded diagnosis code is ICD-10 F80.2. Authorization number AUTH-CLV-261012 covers the listed period. Service coordinator Nora Ellis will verify administrative approval before the first billed visit. The authorization entry itself does not confirm payment.

Occupational therapy will continue twice monthly for 45 minutes through Cedar Lantern CDSA, beginning October 15, 2026. Service coordination will occur monthly and as needed. The parents selected natural routine settings. Travel, missed visits, and schedule changes will be discussed directly with the family.

The team will review caregiver examples, daycare observations, and brief opportunity counts. A successful response must serve a clear communication purpose. Adults will note the support provided and the child's comfort. The clinician will compare performance across languages and settings before changing targets.

Both parents approved these outcomes during the meeting. The clinician explained how to request a review sooner if priorities change. The family received the plan by secure delivery at elena.cardenas@example.com. The next review remains scheduled for January 14, 2027, at 4:45 p.m..

Prepared and electronically signed by Marisol Vega Benton, bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist, CLV, on October 8, 2026.

La logopeda bilingüe Elena Mar Varela, de Puentes de Voz Infantil, atendió a Nicolás Prado Luján, de 4;2, en su domicilio: 184 Calle del Sauce, Villa Brisal, Carolina del Norte, 27500. Expediente SLP-582640; Medicaid 847206391Q. Su mamá Alma Luján autorizó la participación de la tía Rosa Luján. Su hermano Gabriel Prado observó el inicio. La familia informó descanso adecuado y ausencia de cambios médicos desde la visita anterior.

La mamá trabaja dos empleos: uno en la tienda BMS y otro en el servicio de limpieza Cleaning Service Moon Clear. Su papá Esteban Prado trabaja actualmente en la empresa de construcción Construction Company Bridge Green. Antes trabajó en la fábrica Factory Paper Golden, el restaurante Restaurant Garden Quiet y la granja Farm Meadow Long. Los turnos dificultan practicar diariamente. La niñera Celia Montalvo puede apoyar durante las tardes. Acordamos incorporar oportunidades breves al preparar meriendas, vestirse y guardar juguetes.

Los antecedentes incluyen nacimiento el 08/09/2021, edad gestacional de 38 semanas, peso de 3,180 g y Apgar de 8 y 9, según documentación del hospital Hospital Infantil del Arroyo Claro. La evaluación del 3 de marzo de 2025, registrada también como 2025-03-03, incluyó Rossetti, Goldman-Fristoe, Bayley y Peabody. El niño mostró avances en comprensión durante tareas conocidas. Las peticiones fueron más completas cuando el adulto esperó y ofreció un modelo breve. La producción del sonido posterior todavía requiere apoyo directo. El desempeño cambió con la longitud del mensaje; las frases largas redujeron su claridad. La mezcla de idiomas se documentó como parte de su experiencia bilingüe. La diferencia entre las puntuaciones apoya mantener objetivos separados para comprensión y expresión. Estos resultados describen esta sesión y deben interpretarse junto con muestras de ambos idiomas.

Plan

Continuar las sesiones semanales. Practicar “quiero más”, “abre caja” y “mi turno” durante rutinas breves. La mamá recibió una demostración y practicó la espera antes de ayudar. Se acordó registrar peticiones espontáneas sin corregir cada producción. La próxima sesión será el 10/16/2026 a las 09:10. Revisar la generalización en el aula con autorización familiar. El conductor J. Orbel acompañó la salida; no participó en la intervención.

11 de octubre de 2026

Estimada señora Guadalupe Serrano Vidal:

Le comparto la nota de la sesión de hoy de su hijo Mateo Serrano Vidal, a quien ustedes llaman Teo. Soy Elena Marín Solano, patóloga bilingüe del habla y del lenguaje de Palabras del Colibrí. Trabajamos en español durante la visita en El Paraguas de las Luciérnagas, en Cedraluna, Carolina del Norte.

La sesión comenzó a las 9:15 a. m. y terminó a las 9:55 a. m.. El expediente es SL-604218; el número de Medicaid registrado es 731604928Q. La edad actual es 4;2. Registré el servicio con CPT 92507, modificador GN, y diagnóstico ICD-10 F80.2.

Usted, señora Lupita, comentó que trabaja en RVC por las mañanas y en Panadería Brisa de Canela por las tardes. Su pareja, Jesús Vidal Robles, conocido como Chuy, acompaña la rutina nocturna. La abuela Rosa Serrano Ávila recoge al niño algunos días. Su hermano José Vidal Serrano, llamado Pepe, disfruta mirar cuentos con él. Estas rutinas ofrecen oportunidades para practicar sin añadir tareas largas.

La maestra Nora Beltrán Ponce informó que hoy pidió materiales con más claridad. Al entrar, Mateo saludó a su compañero Juan Ortega Ledesma, conocido como Juanito, y aceptó compartir bloques. Mostró interés por los animales de juguete. Necesitó una pausa breve cuando el salón tuvo mucho ruido, pero regresó tranquilo después de elegir un asiento junto a la ventana.

Revisé los resultados previos de PLS-5, obtenidos el 24 de septiembre de 2026. En Comprensión auditiva, la puntuación estándar fue 78, con percentil 7 e intervalo de confianza 73-83. La edad equivalente fue 2;6–3;0. Estos resultados orientan el tratamiento; también consideramos lo que logra en sus actividades diarias y en ambos idiomas.

Hoy seguimos el objetivo 2 del plan familiar de servicios: pedir ayuda o materiales mediante palabras combinadas. Con estrategias de Hanen, esperé antes de entregar objetos, ofrecí opciones y amplié sus mensajes. Produjo "quiero agua" y "dame carro" con apoyo mínimo. Combinó palabras en 8/10 oportunidades, equivalente al 80%. Al principio necesitó apoyo moderado; al final inició varias peticiones por sí mismo.

También practicamos el sonido /k/ con la palabra "casa". Dijo "tasa" en algunos intentos y logró el sonido esperado en 3 de 5 oportunidades con apoyo máximo. Aceptó mirar mi boca y repetir durante el juego. En la muestra de lenguaje registré [EW] para una palabra adicional. Al hablar de su mascota, dijo: “Mochi corre”. Esa frase surgió espontáneamente.

Para casa, recomiendo elegir un momento corto durante la merienda. Ofrezcan dos opciones, esperen y respondan a cualquier intento de comunicación. Si dice una palabra, añadan otra. Eviten pedir repeticiones cuando esté cansado. La participación fue buena y no observé señales de dolor ni malestar.

En la próxima sesión practicaremos pedir turnos y seguir instrucciones sencillas durante juegos compartidos. La coordinadora M. R. recibirá esta nota en el expediente interno. La próxima visita está prevista para el 18 de octubre de 2026 a las 9:15 a. m.. Puede llamarme al (919) 555-0146 o escribir a elena@palabrascolibri.example. Gracias por compartir los avances de casa.

Con cariño,

Elena Marín Solano

**Nota diaria de terapia del habla y lenguaje con reevaluación focal**

Fecha: 8 de octubre de 2026. Horario: 09:10–10:00.
Paciente: Samuel Iván Ledesma, edad 4;2.
Expediente: SL-2601847. Medicaid: 684219753Q.
Lugar: Senderos del Lenguaje Pediátrico, 418 Calle del Robledal, Pinar Claro, Carolina del Norte, 27500.
Servicio: CPT 92507, modificador GO; diagnóstico ICD-10 F80.2.

**S — Información familiar**

Su mamá Daniela Ledesma acompañó a Samuel. Su papá Óscar Pineda participó por teléfono desde su trabajo, Talleres Horizonte de Madera. La familia reportó más peticiones espontáneas durante la merienda, pero dificultad para explicar lo ocurrido en el salón. Su hermana Inés Pineda suele anticipar sus necesidades. Su abuela Celia Montes pidió estrategias para esperar una respuesta antes de ayudar.

Según la mamá, nació con edad gestacional de 35 semanas, peso de 2,340 gramos y puntuaciones Apgar de 8 y 9, en el Hospital Infantil Los Cedros. Estos antecedentes fueron reportados; hoy no se revisaron documentos hospitalarios.

La maestra Mariela Soto, de la Escuela Primaria Arroyo de Luna, informó dificultad para iniciar conversaciones con su compañero Bruno Salcedo. También asiste a la Guardería Pequeños Faroles.

**O — Evaluación y desempeño**

La sesión se realizó en español, con apoyo de la intérprete Elisa Navarro para aclarar información previa registrada en inglés. Se combinaron observación, juego compartido y una muestra breve de lenguaje. Se revisaron resultados anteriores de PLS-5; las puntuaciones corresponden a aquella administración y no constituyen una nueva evaluación normativa.

| Prueba o subprueba | Fecha de evaluación | Puntuación estándar | Percentil | Intervalo de confianza | Edad equivalente |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5: Comprensión auditiva | 17/09/2026 | 78 | 7 | 73–85 | 2;10–3;2 |
| PLS-5: Comunicación expresiva | 17/09/2026 | 75 | 5 | 70–82 | 2;8–3;0 |
| PLS-5: Lenguaje total | 17/09/2026 | 74 | 4 | 69–81 | 2;9–3;1 |

Los intervalos corresponden al nivel de confianza del 90%. Las edades equivalentes se presentan como referencia descriptiva; no determinan por sí solas la selección de objetivos.

Durante el juego, Samuel siguió instrucciones con objetos en 8/10 oportunidades con claves mínimas. Produjo combinaciones de palabras en 3 de 5 oportunidades con claves moderadas. La precisión inicial de /k/ fue 60%; se observó sustitución por /t/. Para "casa", produjo "tasa". Durante una conversación sobre su perro, dijo “Chispa ven”; después añadió "quiero jugar".

Se aplicaron estrategias de Hanen: seguir su iniciativa, esperar y ampliar sus mensajes. La transcripción incluyó el código [EW]. El visitante administrativo Julián Varela permaneció fuera del espacio terapéutico.

**A — Impresión clínica**

Se observaron avances en intención comunicativa y participación. Persisten necesidades en comprensión de instrucciones, expansión de frases y claridad del habla. La atención mejoró con pausas y materiales elegidos por el niño. La comparación entre lenguas requiere información adicional; los errores observados hoy no permiten atribuir las dificultades al bilingüismo.

**P — Plan y coordinación**

Continuar intervención semanal y práctica familiar durante rutinas. Mantener el objetivo 2 del IFSP: pedir ayuda con frases funcionales. La coordinadora Patricia Solís pertenece a la Red Comunitaria de Coordinación de Servicios Infantiles de Pinar Claro (RCCSI Pinar Claro). Se preparó un resumen para la Oficina de la Agencia de Servicios de Desarrollo Infantil de Valle Brumoso (CDSA Valle Brumoso).

Coordinar recomendaciones con la terapeuta ocupacional Lorena Vidal, el fisioterapeuta Andrés Beltrán y la pediatra Natalia Cordero. Revisión prevista: 22 de octubre de 2026.

Firma: Camila Duarte, MS, CCC-SLP, patóloga bilingüe del habla y lenguaje, Senderos del Lenguaje Pediátrico.
Contacto: 919-555-0146; camila.duarte@senderoslenguaje.example; https://senderoslenguaje.example.
