> Diagnostic impressions: ICD-10 F80.2 and F80.0
>
> MOTIVO DE CONSULTA / BACKGROUND
>
> The family requested an assessment because María José often understands routine directions but struggles to explain events or repair misunderstandings. Her parents described longer messages in Spanish during familiar activities. At school, she sometimes watches other children before joining a task. The referral asked whether these differences reflect bilingual development, a communication disorder, or both.
>
> Her mother reported, “En casa habla más, pero cuando no la entienden, se queda calladita.” Her father added, “She knows what she wants; le cuesta ponerlo en palabras.” Their priorities are clearer requests, safer communication about discomfort, and more comfortable participation with classmates. Neither parent identified English-only performance as the main goal.
>
> Ms. Tessa Hollis, the classroom teacher, reported that the child enjoys pretend cooking and picture books. Classroom assistant Maribel Solano described successful participation when an adult previews the activity in Spanish. Classmates Amaya Reed and Nicolás Vega often invite her into play. The child follows their actions but rarely explains a new play idea.
>
> The assessment included parent interview, record review, structured testing, bilingual play, speech sampling, and observation during transitions. Parents attended the interview together. The clinician conducted Spanish activities directly. Interpreter Inés Duarte assisted with a brief scheduling discussion; she did not administer tests or interpret test items.
>
> HISTORIA DEL NACIMIENTO Y SALUD
>
> María José Morales Castañeda was born at Willow Lantern Community Hospital in Willow Lantern. Records supplied by the family document delivery at 38 weeks, 4 days and birth weight of 3.12 kg. Apgar scores were 8 and 9. The birth record describes brief feeding support without prolonged respiratory assistance.
>
> Her mother recalled difficulty maintaining an effective latch during the first 6 weeks. The family later used bottle feeding and gradually introduced textured foods. Current meals include rice, beans, fruit, tortillas, and soft meat. Parents deny frequent coughing during meals. They report selective eating when foods have mixed textures, especially when the child is tired.
>
> Dr. Samuel Ibarra documented recurrent ear infections and referred the child for hearing assessment. Audiologist Priya Mendel at Willow Lantern Community Hospital completed testing on September 22, 2026. The supplied report indicates hearing adequate for the tested speech frequencies. Parents should report new hearing concerns because today’s language findings do not replace ongoing hearing care.
>
> Occupational therapist Camila Ríos previously addressed transitions and participation in dressing routines. The family reports no current prescription medication. Sleep varies when parents change work shifts. No loss of previously acquired language was reported. Oral structures appeared adequate for speech during this assessment; a full feeding evaluation was outside the referral.
>
> FAMILIA, TRABAJO Y LENGUAS
>
> The child lives with her mother, Lucía Belén Castañeda, her father, Rafael Antonio Morales, and her brother, Diego Morales Castañeda, age 7 years. Her sister, Ana Lucía Morales Castañeda, age 18 months, also lives in the home. The family resides at 73 Copper Wren Lane, Cedar Lantern, North Carolina 27998.
>
> Her mother currently works at Copper Finch Market, a store she calls la tienda Mercado del Pinzón Cobrizo. She also accepts shifts through Clear Window Cleaning Service, identified in Spanish as servicio de limpieza Ventana Clara. Her previous job was at Lantern Creek Restaurant, or restaurante Arroyo del Farol. These are alternate workplace names reported by the family.
>
> Her father currently works at Pine Loom Manufacturing Plant, described as planta Tejidos del Pino. Seasonal work includes Blue Heron Farm, or granja Garza Azul. He previously worked for Stone Sparrow Construction Company, identified as compañía de construcción Gorrión de Piedra. Their changing schedules affect transportation and which caregiver joins practice.
>
> Maternal grandmother Teresa Belén Castañeda provides afternoon care. Aunt Adriana Castañeda Ruiz helps on weekends. Babysitter Rosa Varela uses Spanish during meals and outdoor play. Neighbor Owen Mercer occasionally drives the family to appointments but does not provide therapy. The family dog, Chispa, frequently appears in the child’s spontaneous stories.
>
> Spanish is the main home language. English exposure increased after preschool enrollment. Parents estimate current exposure at 65% Spanish and 35% English, with considerable variation by day. These estimates describe opportunity, not proficiency. The child hears regional Spanish forms from relatives in Mexico and different English models at school.
>
> Her brother often starts play in English, then changes to Spanish when she appears confused. Grandmother reported, “Conmigo pide todo en español, pero mete palabras de la escuela.” Such code-switching is expected in a bilingual household. Language mixing alone was not treated as an error or evidence of disorder.
>
> OBSERVACIÓN CLÍNICA / PARTICIPATION
>
> Marijo entered holding her mother’s hand and explored the toy kitchen after a short warm-up. She shared attention, showed objects, and used facial expression effectively. Participation improved with a visual sequence and predictable turns. She needed min cues for familiar play routines and mod cues for transitions between unfamiliar tasks.
>
> When the clinician increased the number of verbal directions, the child paused and watched the adult’s face. Repetition alone helped less than demonstration. After movement breaks, she returned readily. Fatigue appeared near the end of structured testing, so the clinician used shorter activity blocks and completed the speech sample during play.
>
> Social interest was clear. She offered pretend food, noticed missing materials, and laughed during playful mistakes. Communication breakdowns sometimes led to withdrawal. When the clinician acknowledged her intended message and offered choices, she resumed interaction. This response suggests that supportive repair routines may improve participation while language skills develop.
>
> PRUEBAS Y RESULTADOS
>
> The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) provided structured information about receptive and expressive language. Administration followed the bilingual procedures described for the instrument. Family examples and spontaneous Spanish responses contributed to the clinical interpretation. No single score determined the diagnosis.
>
> The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) supplied English speech targets. Its norm-referenced result is presented with caution because English exposure differs from that of the normative sample. The clinician also collected Spanish words and connected speech. Cross-language patterns, consistency, and functional intelligibility carried greater weight than the English score alone.
>
> Selected items from the Rossetti Infant-Toddler Language Scale supported a descriptive review of earlier skills. The Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, Fifth Edition (PPVT-5) was used only for qualitative English vocabulary probing. Neither activity produced a valid standardized composite in this session. A prior report used the Bayley Scales of Infant and Toddler Development, Fourth Edition (Bayley-4).
>
> | Instrument or subtest | Score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | PLS-5 Spanish — Auditory Comprehension | Standard score 78 | 7th percentile | 73-83 | 2;6–3;0 |
> | PLS-5 Spanish — Expressive Communication | Standard score 74 | 4th percentile | 70–80 | 2;3–2;8 |
> | PLS-5 Spanish — Total Language | Standard score 75 | 5th percentile | 71-81 | 2;5–2;10 |
> | GFTA-3 — Sounds-in-Words | Standard score 72 | 3rd percentile | 68–79 | Not interpreted |
> | Prior Bayley-4 — Receptive Communication | Scaled score 6 | Not supplied | Not supplied | 18–21 months |
> | Prior Bayley-4 — Expressive Communication | Scaled score 5 | Not supplied | Not supplied | 16-19 months |
>
> Current confidence intervals use the 90% level. The prior developmental evaluation occurred on October 14, 2024, at age 26 months. Its values are transcribed from the supplied report, not recalculated. Age equivalents summarize performance on particular items. They do not describe the child’s overall developmental age or establish expected classroom placement.
>
> COMPRENSIÓN / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE
>
> The child identified familiar objects in 8/10 opportunities without added support. She followed familiar single-step directions in 9/10 trials. Performance decreased to 3 of 5 for related two-step directions with min cues. Demonstration and contextual Spanish increased successful responses, but unfamiliar grammatical relationships remained difficult across languages.
>
> She understood routine location words more consistently than directions involving sequence or exclusion. During play, target words “inside”, “under”, “adentro”, and “debajo” were easier when objects were visible. Questions about absent events required mod cues. Parents described similar difficulty when asking about something that happened earlier in the day.
>
> EXPRESIÓN / EXPRESSIVE LANGUAGE
>
> Spontaneous messages ranged from gestures with single words to short combinations. Examples included “quiero más jugo”, “baby no sleep”, and “se cayó down”. These examples show useful meaning and flexible access to both languages. Limited sentence expansion and inconsistent grammatical marking appeared in Spanish as well as English.
>
> During pretend play, she said “Chispa come aquí” and “Diego help me.” Those utterances contained names and were recorded separately from other production examples. She used “yo tiene” for target “yo tengo”. With mod cues, she expanded a request in 6/10 opportunities.
>
> A bilingual sample used Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) conventions. Word-level errors received [EW], and utterance-level errors received [EU]. Code-switching did not automatically receive an error code. The sample showed better message length during familiar play than during picture description, which supports using everyday routines for treatment.
>
> HABLA / SPEECH
>
> Speech patterns included fronting of /k/ and /g/, cluster reduction, and variable production of Spanish /ɾ/. The child sometimes substituted [w] for English /ɹ/. The clinician considered language-specific development when interpreting these patterns. Errors affecting shared sounds and syllable structures contributed most clearly to reduced intelligibility.
>
> For target “casa”, she produced “tasa”. For target “spoon”, she produced “poon”. Familiar listeners understood approximately 70% of connected speech in context; the clinician understood approximately 50% without contextual support. These are session estimates. Stimulability for /k/ improved to 4/5 trials with max cues.
>
> IMPRESIONES
>
> Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder. Difficulties appeared across languages and settings. They exceeded the differences expected from English learning alone. Bilingual exposure remains a strength and a necessary part of assessment and treatment. The child’s social interest, persistence with support, and family participation are positive treatment factors.
>
> Interpretation has limits. English articulation norms require caution, attention varied, and the language sample covered a narrow set of activities. The evaluation does not diagnose intellectual disability, autism, or a feeding disorder. Continued classroom observation and progress monitoring will help refine the treatment plan without reducing access to either language.
>
> RECOMENDACIONES / PLAN
>
> 1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy weekly. Alternate individual practice with caregiver coaching. Use Spanish for familiar routines and include English targets that support classroom participation.
> 2. Use Hanen strategies for responsive interaction. Model one manageable expansion, wait, and accept gestures or mixed-language responses.
> 3. Use the Cycles approach for selected speech patterns. Consider PROMPT supports only when the treating clinician determines that tactile cueing is appropriate.
> 4. Provide pictures for choices and repair. Consider PECS only after assessing the child’s communication needs and caregiver preferences.
> 5. Coordinate with Ms. Hollis and Ms. Solano to preview vocabulary and allow additional response time.
>
> The previous IFSP outcome 2 addressed requesting help. Current proposed goal 1 targets functional requests in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Goal 2 targets related two-step directions in 4/5 opportunities with min cues. Goal 3 targets selected shared consonants at 80% accuracy with mod cues.
>
> Review progress on January 18, 2027. Service coordinator Nora Benítez will help the family compare school and outpatient supports through Willow Lantern Children’s Developmental Services Agency. Existing contacts with Willow Lantern WIC Office and Willow Lantern Smart Start may help with transportation and family activities.
>
> Elena Marisol Valdés, MS, CCC-SLP
> Cedar Lantern Pediatric Speech

Educational history: Attends La Nube de Papel Academy in Mossbridge on weekdays. Lead teacher Ms. Paloma Duarte and classroom assistant Mr. Evan Pike supplied a written questionnaire dated September 30, 2026. Teacher described strong interest in blocks, toy vehicles, movement songs, and helping jobs. Difficulty noted with multistep directions, answering classroom questions, and negotiating turns. Visual demonstrations improve participation.

Classmates Amaya Brooks, Leo Núñez, and Zuri Hale are frequent play partners. Staff reported that Leo sometimes interprets requests for other children. When misunderstood, Mateo may repeat louder, point, or leave the activity. No aggression reported. Teacher quote: “He joins us, pero necesita más tiempo para decirlo.” Staff requested short, consistent language models that fit classroom routines.

Earlier services: Bellfern Foothills CDSA completed an intake on February 9, 2025. Service coordinator Tessa Moreno supported the family under case CDSA-BF-250209-18. Prior IFSP outcome 2.1 addressed requesting assistance during daily routines. Prior IFSP outcome 2.2 addressed participation in shared play. Services ended at transition; current preschool referral remains pending with Bellfern Early Learning Connections. No current outside speech therapy reported.

Parents identified strengths: affectionate, persistent, enjoys books, notices routines, and seeks other children. Mother stated, “Quiero entenderlo sin quitarle el español.” Primary family priorities are clearer requests, longer messages, and easier communication with unfamiliar adults. Father also wants strategies that grandmother and babysitter can use consistently. These priorities guided task selection and proposed goals.

O: OBJETIVO / PROCEDIMIENTOS Y RESULTADOS

Evaluation completed in a quiet room at Brisa Lantern Therapy. Parents remained available throughout. Procedures included caregiver interview, record review, play observation, oral mechanism screening, standardized Spanish language testing, English articulation sampling, informal bilingual probes, and dynamic assessment. Breaks provided between structured tasks. Examiner used Spanish for initial rapport and shifted languages according to task instructions and child response.

Behavior / participación: Teo separated from parents for table activities with reassurance. Attention improved with a visual sequence and alternating play tasks. He explored materials, initiated requests, and accepted turn-taking. Movement breaks helped sustain participation. Performance varied with linguistic load and familiarity. No refusal pattern prevented completion. Results represent this session and should be integrated with classroom observations and caregiver reports.

The Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) was administered using its bilingual procedures. The Auditory Comprehension and Expressive Communication subtests contributed to Total Language. Standardized tasks were completed before teaching activities. Dynamic probes occurred separately. The Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3) supplied English elicitation pictures; its Sounds-in-Words subtest was interpreted descriptively because English experience and bilingual sound patterns limit normative comparison.

Score table / tabla de resultados:

| Measure | Raw score | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | 37 | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-86, 90% CI | 3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | 34 | 76 | 5th percentile | 71-84, 90% CI | 2;10 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | — | 75 | 5th percentile | 70-83, 90% CI | 2;11 |
| GFTA-3: Sounds-in-Words | 42 errors | Not interpreted | Not interpreted | Not calculated | Not interpreted |

Age equivalents describe performance on this instrument; they do not establish developmental age or treatment placement. The PLS-5 Spanish findings suggest reduced language performance relative to its reference sample. English articulation scoring was retained only as a descriptive error count. No English standardized language composite was calculated. Clinical interpretation relied on converging evidence across languages and settings.

Lenguaje receptivo: Followed familiar single-step directions in 8/10 opportunities without added support. Followed related two-step directions in 3/8 opportunities independently and 6/8 with mod cues, gesture, and repetition. Identified common actions in pictures in 7/10 trials. Understood basic location concepts more consistently than quantity, exclusion, or temporal concepts. Performance decreased when directions contained unfamiliar vocabulary.

On informal Spanish probes, identified arriba and abajo in 4/4 opportunities. Demonstrated detrás in 1/4 opportunities, improving to 3/4 after modeled play. English probes showed a similar need for demonstration, aunque el vocabulario familiar helped. Responded to concrete what questions in 6/10 trials; inferential questions remained difficult. Repeating the full question alone did not consistently improve accuracy.

Lenguaje expresivo: Used gestures, single words, and short combinations. Spontaneous productions included "yo quiero agua", "más car", "se cayó", and "my turn ahora". These switches were communicatively appropriate and were not scored as errors. Vocabulary included nouns, common actions, familiar social words, and a limited range of descriptive terms. Verb endings and grammatical markers varied across utterances and contexts.

The bilingual play sample contained 50 utterances. Descriptive mean utterance length was 2.4 words per utterance; no bilingual normative comparison was applied. Different words counted across both languages totaled 41. Examiner excluded immediate imitations from spontaneous-language summaries. The Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) conventions were used for annotation; [EW] marked an extraneous word and [EU] marked an omitted obligatory word.

During picture description, Mateo named a person and action together in 4/10 trials. Expanded to an agent-action-object message in 2/10 trials independently and 7/10 with mod cues. Answered personal-routine questions more readily than unfamiliar picture questions. A name-containing production was “Rocky run.” Another was “Sol ven.” These messages were interpreted within family context.

Narrative / cuento: Sequenced familiar routine pictures with physical arrangement support. Independently supplied an opening event but omitted the problem and outcome. With max cues, added "baby cayó" and "mamá ayuda". No stable causal connector appeared spontaneously. During retell, repeated salient labels without preserving all event relationships. Difficulty occurred in both language versions, though Spanish descriptions were somewhat longer.

Speech / habla: Oral structures appeared symmetrical at rest. Lip closure, tongue movement, and jaw excursion were adequate for sampled speech tasks. No obvious structural concern observed. Voice and resonance were unremarkable during conversational sampling. No persistent stuttering-like behavior observed. This screening did not establish detailed motor speech function; connected speech and response to cueing informed the provisional interpretation.

Frequent patterns included final consonant omission, cluster reduction, and inconsistent substitution of velars. Examples: "tat" for "cat", "pane" for "plane", and "do" for "dog". Spanish examples included "tasa" for "casa" and "pato" for "plato". Errors involving English-only contrasts were separated from patterns affecting both languages.

For Spanish /ɾ/, substitutions were variable; this sound was not selected as an immediate priority. English /ɹ/ frequently became [w]. Production of /k/ improved in syllables with visual placement support and max cues. Production of /g/ remained inconsistent. Consonant sequencing was more accurate in practiced words than unfamiliar combinations. No diagnosis of childhood apraxia was established from this evaluation.

The picture target "sol" was included because it was familiar and motivating; sister Sol shares the same spoken form. Initial production was "so". After a slowed model, produced "sol" in 3/5 opportunities with mod cues. When shown a family photograph, he instead said “Sol conmigo.” Lexical elicitation and naming a family member were documented separately.

Intelligibility was estimated from connected speech: approximately 65% to the familiar parent and 45% to the examiner without contextual support. These are session estimates, not standardized scores. Pictures and gestures improved message recovery. During a pretend pickup routine, neighbor Dalia Finch was discussed as a familiar listener; parents reported that unfamiliar adults usually need repetition.

Dynamic assessment / aprender con apoyo: Following brief teaching, action vocabulary increased from 4/8 to 7/8 pictured responses. Related two-step direction accuracy increased from 3/8 to 6/8. Gains required demonstration, repeated exposure, and mod cues. Independent transfer to new materials was limited. He accepted correction and attempted revised productions, indicating useful learning responsiveness despite ongoing support needs.

Pragmatics / uso social: Shared attention, showing, pointing, and reciprocal enjoyment observed. Requested help, protested, commented, and invited participation. Repair strategies consisted mainly of repetition and gesture. With min cues, used "help me" instead of abandoning a difficult activity. In pretend peer play, he offered a toy to Amaya in a photograph-based scenario and added "tu turn".

Parents reviewed findings before departure. Examiner emphasized that bilingual exposure and code-switching are expected features of this child's language environment. Parent report, preschool report, direct observation, and bilingual probes showed overlapping concerns. Hearing information was available by written summary; classroom functioning was assessed by questionnaire rather than direct observation. These limits remain relevant when setting treatment priorities and reviewing progress.

A: ANÁLISIS / IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder, ICD-10 F80.2, with a co-occurring speech sound disorder, ICD-10 F80.0. Difficulties affect comprehension of longer directions, grammatical organization, message expansion, and intelligibility. Functional effects occur during home routines and classroom participation. This impression reflects the combined evidence, not an isolated test cutoff. Severity judged moderate for functional language needs; speech clarity also requires intervention.

Language differences alone do not explain the profile. Weaknesses appeared during familiar Spanish tasks and during supported English tasks. Parents and staff described comparable communication breakdowns. Code-switching, Spanish influence on English production, and uneven vocabulary distribution across languages were treated as language variation. Los dos idiomas count toward communication ability. Treatment should support the family's preferred bilingual environment.

Strengths include social interest, shared attention, symbolic play, persistence, and improvement with models. These strengths support participation in direct therapy and caregiver coaching. Learning response was positive but depended on substantial scaffolding. Limited independent generalization suggests that repeated practice within meaningful routines will be necessary. Family involvement and preschool collaboration can help maintain consistent language models across settings.

Speech patterns affecting shared sounds warrant treatment consideration. English-specific patterns require continued monitoring against bilingual exposure and developmental expectations. Stimulability suggests an initial focus on final consonants and velar placement in meaningful words. No single error pattern establishes a motor planning disorder. Reassess if inconsistency, disrupted transitions, or unusual prosody become prominent in future samples.

Current communication needs exceed what classroom exposure alone is likely to address. Skilled SLP services are indicated to select appropriate bilingual targets, adjust cueing, monitor generalization, and coach communication partners. No feeding treatment indicated from today's referral information. Medical follow-up remains with established providers. Hearing changes, recurrent ear symptoms, or loss of skills should prompt reassessment through the appropriate clinical team.

Prognosis for improved functional communication is favorable with consistent attendance, accessible practice, and coordinated supports. Exact rate of progress cannot be predicted from one visit. Barriers include rotating caregiver schedules and reduced intelligibility outside familiar routines. Plan should use brief activities that several adults can implement. Parents agreed that practical gains matter more than memorizing isolated picture labels.

P: PLAN / RECOMENDACIONES Y METAS

Recommend individual bilingual speech-language therapy twice weekly for twelve weeks, with caregiver participation during each visit. Use Spanish and English according to functional targets and family routines. Initial treatment at BLPCS will emphasize comprehension, message expansion, and speech clarity. Proposed start date: October 19, 2026. Preferred appointment: 4:15 p.m.. Frequency may change after attendance, response, and classroom access are reviewed.

Proposed goals / metas:

1. During familiar play and daily routines, follow related two-step directions in 8/10 opportunities with min cues, across successive treatment samples. Include spatial and action vocabulary in both languages. Record the language, support, and materials used so improvement reflects comprehension rather than memorized routines.

2. Produce agent-action-object messages in 8/10 opportunities with min cues during functional play. Accept appropriate code-switching. Expand existing messages through models and recasts; do not require word-for-word repetition before honoring a meaningful request.

3. Use a communication repair strategy in 4/5 opportunities with min cues. Strategies may include adding a key word, pointing, showing, or using a picture. Practice when the listener truly needs clarification, con calma and without repeated pressure.

4. Produce selected final consonants and initial /k/ in functional words with 80% accuracy given mod cues. Advance to short phrases after stable word-level performance. Select language-appropriate targets and document independent productions separately from imitations.

5. Caregivers will demonstrate responsive language modeling in 4/5 observed opportunities with min cues. Focus on following the child's interest, adding one meaningful element, and allowing processing time. Review feasibility with each caregiver and adapt routines as needed.

Use Enhanced Milieu Teaching for functional language targets and consider Hanen-based caregiver strategies when appropriate to clinician training and family needs. A modified Cycles approach may organize phonological targets after additional speech sampling. Do not initiate PROMPT solely from today's findings. Picture supports may supplement speech; a formal PECS program is not currently prescribed.

Home practice / en casa: Use brief, enjoyable practice during snack, dressing, and toy cleanup. Model "quiero más agua" or "I want more" after a shorter request. Pause, then respond to the message. For directions, pair words with a gesture first and gradually reduce help. Avoid repeated demands to speak perfectly. Continue Spanish conversations, songs, and shared books.

Provide grandmother Rosa Beltrán and babysitter J. Ortiz with the same small set of routines. Parents may share a picture-supported request board after receiving instruction. Involve sister Sol in natural turn-taking without assigning responsibility for correcting speech. Pet Rocky may provide motivating vocabulary during supervised play; maintain ordinary family safety routines.

With signed consent, send the report to Ms. Duarte at La Nube de Papel Academy. Recommend visual directions, extra response time, adult recasts, and supported peer turns. Encourage staff to confirm meaning before correcting a word. Classmates Zuri and Leo may participate in ordinary shared play; adults should remain responsible for communication support.

Coordinate preschool service review with Tessa Moreno and Bellfern Early Learning Connections. Carry forward the functional intent of prior IFSP outcome 2.1 and IFSP outcome 2.2 while developing current preschool goals. Clinic treatment does not determine educational eligibility. Obtain direct classroom observation if consent and scheduling permit. Track whether gains transfer beyond the therapy room.

Continue scheduled hearing follow-up with Avery Chen. Return medical questions to Dr. Elena Prado. Review progress on January 11, 2027 using functional probes, caregiver report, and an updated speech sample. Repeat standardized testing only when clinically appropriate. Parents received findings in English and Spanish, demonstrated understanding, and agreed with the initial priorities.

Signed electronically: Marisol Vega, MS, CCC-SLP
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist
Brisa Lantern Pediatric Communication Services, PLLC

BILINGUAL PEDIATRIC SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION / EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y LENGUAJE

Document status: Fictional testing record  Record number: SL-260918-0472  Evaluation date: September 18, 2026
Child: Emilio Javier Salceda  Preferred name: Milo  Date of birth: July 18, 2022  Age: 4;2
Parent: Mariela Salceda  Parent: Tomás Salceda  Medicaid member: 583710264Q
Address: 418 Willow Lantern Lane  City: Bellhaven  State: North Carolina  ZIP: 27964
Telephone: 252-555-0148  Parent email: mariela.salceda@example.com  Preferred contact language: Spanish
Clinician: Daniela Marín Vélez, MS, CCC-SLP  Role: Bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist  License: NC-SLP-087431
Employer: Willow Lantern Pediatric Communication Services, PLLC  Office: 62 Orchard Glass Court, Bellhaven, North Carolina
Company telephone: 252-555-0163  Company email: intake@willowlantern.example.com  Website: https://willowlantern.example.com
Visit start: 9:15 a.m.  Visit end: 11:05 a.m.  Setting: Outpatient office  Participants: Child and mother
Referral source: Dr. Nadia Varela  Referral date: August 26, 2026  Authorization: AUTH-884206-SL
Billing procedure: CPT 92523  Proposed treatment procedure: CPT 92507  Modifier: GN
Diagnostic impression: ICD-10 F80.2  Additional impression: ICD-10 F80.0  Report completed: September 22, 2026

All people, organizations, locations, contacts, events, identifiers, and clinical findings in this report are invented. This document is a synthetic record for offline testing.

Motivo de consulta / Reason for referral

The family requested an evaluation because Emilio uses short messages and becomes upset when listeners misunderstand him. His mother wants him to explain what happened at daycare and ask for help without depending on gestures. She stated, “Él sabe lo que quiere, pero las palabras se le quedan cortitas.” His father reported that familiar routines go smoothly, although unexpected questions often lead to silence.

The referral described concerns about following directions, sentence length, and speech clarity. The family also asked whether using Spanish at home could slow English learning. I explained that both languages belong in the assessment and treatment plan. A bilingual child’s abilities must be understood across people, settings, and opportunities to use each language.

The evaluation included caregiver interview, record review, structured testing, play observation, speech sampling, and supported learning tasks. The family provided consent for the assessment and approved discussion of practical classroom supports. Information below identifies whether a finding came from caregiver report, a supplied record, or direct observation.

Antecedentes / Background and daily participation

Milo attends Little Lantern Early Learning House in Bellhaven, Alder Sound County. He participates in Ms. Lopez’s room, called the Garden Room. Ms. Elena Lopez completed a classroom questionnaire. Assistant teacher J. Ortiz added examples from snack and outdoor play.

The teachers described a friendly child who watches other children before joining an activity. He follows predictable cleanup routines and enjoys vehicles, animal figures, and water play. During circle time, he sometimes copies another child’s movement without responding to the spoken direction. Transitions become harder when staff provide several instructions together.

Classmates Nora Bell and Isaac Moreno often invite him into pretend play. His mother reported that he names his friend Isaac at home but rarely explains their games. Another classmate, Tavi Chen, sometimes interprets his gestures. Staff want to help him speak directly while preserving these positive peer relationships.

The family previously contacted Alder Sound Children’s Developmental Services Agency. Service coordinator Rosa Niebla documented an earlier plan under case CDSA-AS-220731. The supplied plan listed IFSP Outcome 2 for requesting help during family routines. That historical outcome informs this report but does not establish current eligibility.

Historia de nacimiento y salud / Birth and medical history

The mother reported delivery at Pine Harbor Health System, Mariner Campus Hospital following an uncomplicated pregnancy until premature contractions began. Gestational age was 35 weeks, 6 days. Birth weight was 2,480 g. Recorded Apgar scores were 7 at one minute and 9 at five minutes.

The supplied discharge summary described a stay in Pine Harbor Health System, Mariner Campus NICU for feeding support and temperature monitoring. The family reported discharge on July 29, 2022. There was no reported surgery, prolonged ventilation, or diagnosed neurologic condition. The child currently eats ordinary family foods, with preferences for familiar textures.

Primary care occurs at Pine Harbor Health System, Willow Campus Pediatric Clinic. Dr. Nadia Varela documented recurrent middle-ear fluid and referred the family for hearing assessment. The mother reported ear discomfort during colds but no current pain. Medication history included occasional prescribed treatment for ear infections; no daily medication was reported.

Audiologist Celia Robles evaluated hearing at Pine Harbor Health System, Reed Campus Audiology and ENT on August 12, 2026. The supplied summary described hearing adequate for speech access under the conditions tested. ENT physician Dr. Owen Lira recommended follow-up if fluid or symptoms returned. Today’s language findings should not replace that monitoring.

The family reported independent walking at 15 months, first meaningful words near 20 months, and consistent word combinations around 32 months. There was no reported loss of previously acquired communication skills. Sleep varies after busy days. No swallowing difficulty was observed during the snack sample.

Historia familiar y de idiomas / Family and language history

The household includes the child, his mother Mariela Salceda, his father Tomás Salceda, and sister Sol Salceda, age 7 years. His grandmother Inés Cordero provides care after daycare. His aunt Paloma Cordero visits regularly, and babysitter M.R. helps during occasional evening shifts.

Spanish is the main language during meals, family visits, and bedtime. English is common at daycare and during some play with his sister. The mother estimated Spanish exposure at 65% and English exposure at 35%. These estimates describe opportunity, not measured proficiency, and may change with weekly schedules.

The father works at Harbor Loom Packaging Cooperative. The mother works at Bellhaven Garden Supply Collective. Their shifts sometimes change who handles pickup. The family’s dog is named Chispa. The child often tries to tell relatives what the dog did, which creates useful opportunities for connected speech.

The mother said, “Con la abuela habla más; con personas nuevas espera.” Grandmother Inés reportedly understands familiar phrases and gestures quickly. Sister Sol sometimes answers for her brother. We discussed giving him time to respond while keeping sibling help warm and supportive.

During this visit, Emilio code-switched naturally. He used Spanish for several requests and English during vehicle play. Mixing languages did not, by itself, indicate confusion. The clinician considered vocabulary and sentence information across both languages, including concepts expressed in only one language.

Observación clínica / Participation and communication sample

The child entered with his mother and explored the toy shelf after a brief pause. He shared enjoyment, looked toward the clinician during surprises, and brought objects to show. Engagement improved when activities had a clear purpose. He needed breaks between structured tasks but returned readily with a visual choice.

He communicated through pointing, facial expression, single words, and short combinations. Observed productions included "más carro", "my turn", "no cabe", and "quiero el blue one". He also said, “Chispa corre,” while looking at a dog picture. The name-containing production remains recorded exactly as heard.

During pretend cooking, he said "baby eat", then added a gesture for drinking. With a model, he produced "el bebé toma agua". He independently repaired one misunderstood request by pointing and repeating "ese grande". Other breakdowns led to louder repetition or moving the adult’s hand toward the object.

A sample contained 50 utterances. The clinician used SALT conventions descriptively, including [EW] for an extraneous word and [EU] for an unintelligible utterance. Coding supported review of the sample; it did not provide a separate diagnostic score. Longer messages were less clear than familiar short requests.

Procedimientos y resultados / Assessment procedures and results

The clinician administered Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish) using the manual’s bilingual procedures. English responses were considered where permitted. Parent information supported interpretation but did not substitute for responses required by the instrument. Scores represent this synthetic assessment and should be read alongside functional observations.

Speech elicitation used selected items from Goldman-Fristoe Test of Articulation, Third Edition (GFTA-3). Administration was descriptive because the child’s bilingual background and the selected-item format limited normative interpretation. No standardized articulation score was calculated. Supported learning tasks examined response to models, choices, repetition, and reduced language demands.

| Measure | Score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | Standard score 76 | 5th percentile | 71-83, 90% confidence | 3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | Standard score 81 | 10th percentile | 75-89, 90% confidence | 3;3 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | Standard score 77 | 6th percentile | 72-85, 90% confidence | 3;1 |
| GFTA-3: Sounds-in-Words | Descriptive administration | Not calculated | Not applicable | Not reported |
| Supported direction task | 8/10 with mod cues | Not applicable | Not applicable | Not applicable |

Age equivalents describe performance on a particular measure. They do not define the child’s overall developmental age or establish a treatment level. Across informal activities, skills varied within an approximate task range of 2;6–3;6. This range is descriptive and does not replace the standardized results.

Comprensión / Receptive language

On Auditory Comprehension, strengths included identifying familiar objects, recognizing common actions, and following routine directions with contextual support. The child identified named pictures in 8/10 opportunities when the field was small. He followed familiar single-step directions in 9/10 opportunities without an added model.

Difficulty increased with spatial concepts, negatives, unfamiliar vocabulary, and directions containing several relationships. He completed related two-step directions in 3 of 5 opportunities independently and 5/5 with mod cues. Cuando bajamos la carga verbal, he showed better understanding and less guessing.

He sometimes chose the most visually interesting picture before the instruction ended. Repeating the whole sentence did not consistently help. A brief pause, an emphasized key word, and a gesture improved participation. These responses suggest that classroom adults should check understanding through action rather than asking whether he understood.

Expresión / Expressive language

On Expressive Communication, the child named common objects and used words for requests, protests, and comments. He combined words more often during play than during direct questioning. He described an action in 4/8 opportunities independently and 7/8 following a model with min cues.

His messages frequently omitted information about who acted, where an event happened, or what occurred next. Examples included "se cayó", "truck broken", and "allá está". These phrases were useful within the immediate activity but required listener support when the event or object was absent.

Spanish articles, verb forms, and English sentence patterns varied across contexts. The clinician did not treat every difference from a monolingual pattern as an error. Concern arose from limited message detail and difficulty learning or using structures across both languages. The family’s examples supported similar functional concerns at home.

Habla / Speech production and intelligibility

The oral mechanism screening showed functional lip movement, tongue movement, and jaw stability for the sampled activities. Voice and resonance sounded appropriate during this visit. Fluency did not limit participation. This screening does not establish performance in contexts that were not observed.

Speech patterns included omissions in longer words and reduced contrasts for some consonants. The child sometimes produced [t] for /k/ and [w] for English /ɹ/. Spanish /ɾ/ was inconsistent. The clinician considered language-specific development and exposure when interpreting these patterns.

During picture naming, target "casa" was produced as "tasa". Target "plato" was produced as "pato". Target "sol" referred to the sun picture; sister Sol was not present. When discussing his sister, he said, “Sol juega,” which was recorded separately from the target-word trial.

An unfamiliar listener understood approximately 60% of the connected sample with visual context. The mother reported approximately 85% understanding during familiar routines. These estimates reflect different listening conditions. They should not be compared as if they were equivalent standardized measures.

Aprendizaje apoyado / Response to support

The child learned a new action word during play and used it again after a short delay. He improved from 2/6 to 5/6 successful responses with mod cues. After supports decreased, he retained the word in 3/4 opportunities. This pattern supports intervention that provides models and repeated meaningful use.

He responded well to focused stimulation, recasting, and naturalistic language intervention. A visual choice board helped him stay engaged when speech was difficult. The board supplemented spoken language. Formal use of PECS was not evaluated. The family showed interest in caregiver strategies consistent with Hanen.

Impresiones / Clinical impressions

The combined findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder within this fictional profile. Challenges affect daily directions, message detail, and understanding by unfamiliar listeners. Bilingual exposure does not adequately explain the concerns because functional difficulty appeared across both languages and several communication settings.

Strengths include social interest, shared enjoyment, persistence, and a positive response to support. The child uses available language flexibly and accepts models when the activity remains meaningful. These strengths provide a practical starting point for treatment. His family already offers responsive interactions that can support carryover.

Results reflect one visit, supplied records, and caregiver and teacher reports. Attention, familiarity, language opportunity, and hearing history may influence performance. Ongoing observation should refine treatment targets. No conclusion about broader developmental conditions is made from this speech-language evaluation alone.

Recomendaciones / Recommendations

1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy through Willow Lantern Pediatric Communication, abbreviated WLPCS. Initial visits should address understanding, message expansion, and speech clarity within play and daily routines. Review progress after 12 weeks and adjust frequency according to participation and functional change.

2. Use Spanish and English in ways that fit the family’s routines. Encourage each caregiver to speak comfortably and respond to the child’s meaning. Give a short model, then pause. For example, expand "más carro" to "quiero más carros", without requiring repetition every time.

3. Target related two-step directions with concrete materials. A proposed goal is completion in 8/10 opportunities with min cues across different activities. Teach spatial words through action and contrast. Coordinate classroom examples with Ms. Lopez so practice connects with familiar routines.

4. Expand messages to include an actor, action, and useful detail. A proposed goal is an informative phrase in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. Accept either language and meaningful code-switching. Use focused stimulation and recasting while preserving the child’s intended message.

5. Select speech targets after further sampling across both languages. Consider Cycles if broader pattern assessment supports that approach. Practice selected contrasts in meaningful words before increasing sentence demands. Do not begin PROMPT solely from this screening; additional assessment and appropriate clinician preparation would be needed.

6. Provide classroom supports at Little Lantern Early Learning House. Use brief directions, visual context, and a pause before repeating. Invite the child to answer directly during peer play. Record successful strategies and difficult routines for discussion with the treating clinician.

7. Continue hearing follow-up through the existing medical team when recommended or when new symptoms occur. Share this report with Dr. Nadia Varela only with family authorization. The family may also request an educational evaluation through the local school system.

MOTIVO DE REFERENCIA / BACKGROUND

Mateo Andrés Velasco was referred for concerns re: reduced phrase length, difficulty following classroom directions, and low intelligibility w/ unfamiliar listeners. CG requested evaluation in Spanish and English b/c pt communicates differently across settings. Primary concerns involve communicating needs before frustration escalates, answering simple questions, and joining peer play.

Su mamá Lucía Velasco stated, “En casa entiende más cuando hablamos despacio. Tiene muchas ideas, pero se le quedan adentro.” Father Daniel Velasco reported that pt becomes upset when adults guess incorrectly. Family hopes pt can explain what happened, request help, and communicate discomfort w/o pulling an adult toward the desired item.

Pt attends Little Learners Daycare on weekdays. Classroom teacher Ms. Nora Bell described strong interest in vehicles, pretend cooking, and outdoor play. Pt frequently watches classmates before entering an activity. He sometimes copies a peer’s action successfully but misses a spoken change in the game. Staff requested practical supports that fit existing routines.

The family also enrolled pt in Little Learners Program, a fictional community therapy program offering coached play and CG education. Although the daycare and therapy program share head words, they maintain separate records and staff. CG authorized this evaluation to consider reports from both settings. No direct observation at either setting occurred during this visit.

Records reviewed included the pediatric referral, CG questionnaire, daycare communication log, and archived early intervention summary. Service coordinator Renee Salcedo supplied the prior summary from Pine Hollow Children’s Developmental Services Agency. Archived NC ITP enrollment is historical; pt currently receives services through preschool and community settings. CG confirmed that the identifying numbers above refer to different records.

Success for this evaluation was defined as describing pt’s skills across both languages, separating language difference from impairment indicators, and identifying usable supports. CG priorities guided testing, especially requests for help, routine directions, and communication during play. Pt’s strengths and response to teaching received equal attention.

ANTECEDENTES DE NACIMIENTO Y SALUD

CG reported pregnancy complicated by maternal nausea and late pregnancy blood pressure monitoring. Delivery occurred at Brooklight Children’s Hospital at gestational age 38 weeks 2 days. Birth weight was 6 lb 11 oz. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. Pt remained w/ CG after delivery; no NICU admission was reported.

Newborn feeding involved breast and bottle feeding. CG recalled a sleepy latch but no persistent choking, cyanosis, or tube feeding. Pt transitioned to textured foods at approx 9 months. Current diet includes mixed textures and familiar family foods. CG denied coughing during meals, recurrent chest infections, or unexplained weight loss. Feeding was discussed briefly; no formal feeding assessment occurred.

Medical history includes recurrent ear infections between ages 14 months and 28 months. Dr. Priya Mendez referred pt to an ENT provider after repeated episodes. Bilateral tympanostomy tubes were placed on 11/18/2024 at Brooklight Children’s Hospital. CG reported fewer infections afterward. Current tube status was not verified during this assessment.

Audiologist Owen Castañeda documented hearing adequate for speech access on 08/21/2026 in the referral packet. Today’s assessment did not include audiometry or tympanometry. CG denied a recent ear infection but noted occasional requests for repetition in noisy rooms. Continued hearing follow-up remains relevant to interpretation of language and speech performance.

Developmental history, per CG: independent sitting at 7 months, walking at 15 months, first consistent words at 19 months, and emerging word combinations at 31 months. CG described gradual progress rather than loss of established skills. She recalled that early words occurred in both languages and often named desired foods or familiar people.

Pt has no reported seizure history, major head injury, or daily prescription medication. CG reported seasonal congestion and occasional mouth breathing during illness. Sleep is generally stable, although transitions after daycare can be difficult. Pediatric follow-up will address sleep or breathing concerns if symptoms persist outside illness.

FAMILIA, IDIOMAS Y RUTINAS

Pt lives w/ mother Lucía Velasco, father Daniel Velasco, older sister Elena Velasco, age 7;2, and younger brother Nicolás Velasco, age 2;0. Maternal grandmother Rosa Calderón provides aftercare. Babysitter Maribel Soto assists during occasional evening shifts. The family dog, Rocky, frequently appears in pt’s play and conversation.

Home address is 72 Lantern Moss Court, Alder Cove, North Carolina 27986, in Willowbend County. Mother works at Fern Harbor Packaging. Father works at Cedar Finch Repair Cooperative. Work schedules sometimes change who completes pickup. CG requested that communication supports remain consistent across adults.

Spanish is the primary home language. CG estimated exposure at 65% Spanish and 35% English across a typical week. These estimates describe exposure, not proficiency scores. Grandmother uses Spanish almost exclusively. Father uses both languages during play. Siblings often switch languages depending on the activity, especially when discussing school or television.

Older sister Elena Velasco attends Willowbend Creek Elementary School. She sometimes translates pt’s requests for adults, but CG wants pt to communicate independently. Family discussed giving pt adequate time before a sibling answers for him. The clinician supported sibling involvement while preserving pt’s own communication opportunities.

At daycare, peer Amara Chen often invites pt into pretend cooking. Classmate Luis Peña shares an interest in trucks. Assistant teacher Mr. Evan Price reported that pt participates more readily in small groups. CG stated, “Con otros niños quiere jugar, pero si van muy rápido, se queda mirando.”

Transportation helper Harold Keene sometimes accompanies the family to community appointments. He does not provide language instruction or therapy. CG identified grandmother and babysitter as additional adults who could practice agreed routines. Home practice must remain brief b/c family schedules vary. CG prefers examples that use ordinary household materials.

CONDUCTA Y OBSERVACIONES / PARTICIPACIÓN

Pt entered holding a toy truck and initially stayed near CG. Following a brief play routine, he approached the clinician and shared materials. Eye gaze, pointing, showing, and facial expression supported communication. Pt coordinated gaze and gesture during requests, although verbal information often remained incomplete.

Attention improved when tasks alternated between movement and table activities. Pt completed short adult-directed activities w/ min cues after a demonstration. Longer tasks required mod cues, visual choices, and a planned break. Fatigue appeared near 9:45 AM, when pt leaned on CG and gave fewer verbal responses.

During pretend cooking, pt offered food, waited for a response, and repaired one misunderstood request by pointing. He said "más sopa" and later "I want spoon". When the clinician selected the wrong utensil, pt used "no, ese" plus a clear gesture. These exchanges showed communicative intent despite limited sentence detail.

Pt also said “Rocky run” while moving a toy dog. Later he called “Elena mira” toward CG’s phone photograph. Names inside these productions identify the intended referents. The remaining utterances were recorded as heard. No inference about grammatical ability was based on these name-containing phrases alone.

Pt tolerated oral inspection after modeling w/ a puppet. He declined one task, then returned after a choice of materials. No restraint or physical prompting was used. CG interpreted several unfamiliar approximations, which helped establish intended words but also showed the family’s familiarity w/ pt’s speech.

The clinician used both languages flexibly during play. Pt did not show distress when language changed, though responses were shorter during unfamiliar English tasks. Rapport remained adequate for assessment. Results reflect a structured clinic sample w/ one familiar adult present; performance in a larger classroom may differ.

PROCEDIMIENTOS Y LIMITACIONES

Assessment included PLS-5 Spanish, selected items from GFTA-3, bilingual language sampling, speech probes, CG interview, and a brief dynamic teaching task. Formal testing followed the selected instrument’s bilingual procedures where applicable. Extra teaching occurred separately from scored items. Scores below are fictional results for this synthetic record.

The Auditory Comprehension and Expressive Communication components of PLS-5 Spanish examined receptive and expressive language. The Total Language composite summarized those results. Pt received credit according to the assessment procedures, including accepted responses across languages. CG clarification supported interpretation but did not replace an independent response when the item required one.

The Sounds-in-Words task from GFTA-3 provided an English speech sample. Its score requires caution b/c pt’s language history differs from the comparison group used for that task. Spanish probes and connected speech were therefore essential. The English score alone did not determine the speech impression.

Dynamic assessment used test–teach–retest procedures during a novel play sequence. The clinician taught an action, modeled a phrase, and reduced support when possible. This task examined learning response rather than producing a standardized score. Pt’s improvement was documented by accuracy and cueing level.

No separate standardized pragmatic, literacy, fluency, or voice measure was administered. Those areas received clinical observation only. A classroom observation remains needed to verify how noise, group size, and routine familiarity affect pt’s participation. Interpretation incorporates family report, available records, direct observation, and performance across tasks.

RESULTADOS / SCORE SUMMARY

| Measure | Score type | Result | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | Standard score | 78 | 7th percentile | 73-83 | 3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | Standard score | 74 | 4th percentile | 69–81 | 2;8 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | Standard score | 75 | 5th percentile | 70–82 | 2;10 |
| GFTA-3: Sounds-in-Words | Standard score; interpret cautiously | 67 | 1st percentile | 63–74 | 2;6–3;0 |

Confidence intervals above use the 90% level. Age equivalents describe performance on particular test items. They do not mean that pt functions globally at those ages. No scaled scores were generated by these measures. Informal accuracy values below describe specific probes and cannot be compared directly w/ standard scores.

COMPRENSIÓN / RECEPTIVE LANGUAGE

Pt identified familiar objects and common actions in pictures. He understood routine directions when the materials supported the message. For familiar one-step directions, accuracy was 8/10 independently. For novel one-step directions containing a location concept, accuracy was 4/10 independently and 8/10 w/ mod cues.

Pt understood the target words "in", "on", "adentro", and "arriba" more consistently during play than in isolated picture selection. Difficulty increased when the direction required both an action and an unfamiliar object. Repetition helped, but repetition alone was less effective than showing the relevant materials.

Two-step related directions were completed in 3 of 5 trials w/ mod cues. Unrelated directions were less successful. Pt often completed the last action only. In Spanish, he sometimes requested repetition using "¿qué?". In English, he more often watched the clinician’s hands before responding.

Responses to simple questions depended on question type. Pt answered familiar identification questions in 7/10 opportunities. Location questions were correct in 4/10 opportunities. Questions about reasons required max cues and frequently produced an unrelated object label. Similar difficulty occurred across languages, although vocabulary knowledge affected individual responses.

During a brief story task, pt identified the main character and pointed to a pictured action. He did not independently explain the event sequence. After visual support, he selected the first event in 3 of 4 trials. These findings suggest that shorter messages, visual context, and explicit sequencing support comprehension.

EXPRESIÓN Y MUESTRA DE LENGUAJE

Pt used gestures, single words, and short combinations to request, protest, comment, and direct another person. Spontaneous examples included "quiero agua", "truck go fast", "se cayó", and "help me open". Code-switching appeared purposeful and consistent w/ the family’s communication pattern. It was not counted as an error by itself.

The bilingual play sample contained fifty intelligible utterances. Mean length was approx 2.4 words per utterance, calculated descriptively across the sample. Because the languages differ structurally, this combined value served only as a broad summary. It did not substitute for analysis of forms within each language.

Pt named familiar foods and vehicles more readily than actions or descriptive concepts. He used the target "big", then switched to "grande" when CG joined the activity. In a supported description task, pt supplied two relevant details in 3/8 opportunities independently and 6/8 w/ mod cues.

English samples showed variable articles, auxiliaries, and verb endings. Spanish samples showed short clauses, variable agreement, and limited use of connectors. Examples included "la perro come" and "he running". Interpretation considered language exposure and utterance context. Concern arose from limited formulation and detail across both languages.

For sample coding, [EW] marked an extraneous word and [EU] marked an utterance-level error. These codes remained separate from name labels. Unintelligible portions were excluded from grammatical conclusions. Pt occasionally abandoned an utterance after an adult misunderstood him, then used a gesture instead.

During the teaching task, pt described a novel action in 2/6 trials before teaching and 5/6 afterward w/ min cues. He retained the phrase after a brief play break. This response supports use of modeling and repeated meaningful practice. Independent carryover into a new activity remained inconsistent.

HABLA / SPEECH SOUND FINDINGS

Connected speech was easier to understand when the topic and materials were visible. Estimated intelligibility was 58% for the unfamiliar clinician during sampled play and 82% for CG. These estimates came from the same recorded sample. They describe this session and may change w/ listener familiarity or task demands.

Pt showed omissions in longer words, cluster reduction, and variable substitutions involving velars. The target "cat" was produced as "tat"; target "casa" was produced as "tasa". Productions suggested fronting of /k/ in both languages. Accuracy for /g/ varied by word and vowel context.

Pt substituted [w] for /r/ in several English words. Spanish tap /ɾ/ and trill /r/ were variable. These findings require developmental and language-specific interpretation. They were not weighted equally with errors that affected earlier sounds or occurred consistently across both languages.

For isolated /k/, pt achieved 6/10 attempts w/ mod cues. Accuracy decreased in words. For target "key", pt achieved 3/8 attempts after modeling. For target "coco", pt achieved 5/8 attempts w/ mod cues. Pt benefited from slower pacing and visual attention to the model.

Oral structures appeared adequate for the sampled tasks. Lip closure, tongue movement, and jaw opening were observed during play and imitation. No consistent groping or disrupted transitions emerged in this brief sample. Voice sounded functional, and no persistent stuttering-like behaviors were observed. These observations do not replace focused assessment if new concerns arise.

IMPRESIONES CLÍNICAS

Findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder in this fictional case. Communication difficulty appeared across Spanish and English, including familiar contexts. Pt’s bilingual exposure explains some vocabulary differences and code-switching. It does not fully explain the reduced comprehension, limited sentence detail, and frequent breakdowns observed across languages.

Language strengths include communicative intent, gesture use, familiar vocabulary, interest in shared play, and a positive response to teaching. Pt can learn new phrases when adults connect language to a meaningful action. He also notices misunderstandings and attempts repair. These strengths provide clear entry points for intervention.

Primary language needs involve understanding directions beyond familiar routines, expanding action vocabulary, answering simple questions, and combining information into clearer messages. Speech needs involve increasing intelligibility through selected sound contrasts and word shapes. Targets should support useful communication rather than increase drill demands without a clear functional purpose.

Functional effects include missed classroom directions, reduced independence during peer play, and reliance on familiar adults to interpret speech. CG reported frustration during pickup and sibling play. The current findings support direct intervention plus CG and classroom coaching. Treatment should preserve Spanish and provide meaningful access to English.

Prognosis for measurable functional improvement is favorable given participation, CG involvement, and learning response. Progress rate remains uncertain. Attendance, hearing status, opportunities for practice, and classroom support can affect outcomes. The clinician will review progress using repeated functional probes, language samples, and reports from the adults who support pt.

RECOMENDACIONES / PLAN

1. Begin bilingual speech-language therapy twice weekly for thirty-minute sessions, with an initial twelve-week review period. Use Spanish and English according to the activity, family priorities, and pt’s response. Combine direct treatment with brief CG coaching. Coordinate scheduling around daycare transitions when possible.

2. Use Enhanced Milieu Teaching and focused stimulation to build requests, comments, and action phrases during play. Consider Hanen strategies for CG coaching. Start w/ meaningful phrases such as "ayúdame", "help me", "quiero otro", and "my turn". Accept clear gestures while expanding spoken language.

3. Address speech using selected minimal pairs activities and, if repeated probes support it, a Cycles approach. Choose targets that improve frequent words across languages. Begin w/ stimulable velars and useful word shapes. Do not target Spanish tap or trill solely because the English speech score was low.

4. Support comprehension by giving a short direction, pausing, and checking the action. Add a picture or gesture when needed. Gradually reduce support from mod cues to min cues. Avoid repeated rapid questions. During routines, emphasize the same location and action words before introducing additional concepts.

5. Practice communication repair. Model "otra vez", "show me", and "no, this one". Adults should state what they understood and give pt another way to clarify. Praise the successful message. Keep practice brief and embedded in meals, dressing, pretend play, or cleanup.

6. Coordinate goals with Little Learners Program and Little Learners Daycare after signed release procedures are complete. Classroom staff can provide visual choices, extra response time, and small-group opportunities. The clinician recommends observing a routine with Ms. Nora Bell before adding classroom-specific targets.

OBJETIVOS Y SEGUIMIENTO

Goal 1: Pt will follow novel one-step directions containing an action and location concept in 8/10 opportunities w/ min cues across two activities. Baseline was 4/10 independently. Measure performance in both languages where vocabulary is familiar.

Goal 2: Pt will use a phrase containing an action and relevant detail in 4 of 5 opportunities w/ min cues. Accept appropriate code-switching. Baseline supported description was 3/8 independently. Track spontaneous use separately from direct imitation.

Goal 3: Pt will produce selected velars in functional words with 80% accuracy w/ mod cues, then reduce support. Baseline varied by word. Select targets after confirming stimulability and family relevance. Monitor connected speech rather than relying only on drill accuracy.

Archived IFSP Outcome 2 addressed requesting help during family routines. The prior IFSP date was 05/16/2025. That record informs current planning but does not establish an active IFSP. Current goals will be reviewed on 01/08/2027 using treatment probes and CG feedback.

CG received verbal feedback in Spanish and English. Su mamá Lucía Velasco summarized, “Seguimos hablando español, le damos tiempo, y practicamos poquito en las rutinas.” CG demonstrated the waiting strategy w/ min cues. Written practice examples were provided. No outside message was sent during this visit.

Recommended appointment window: 3:30 PM after daycare, subject to family scheduling. Hearing follow-up remains with the medical team. A classroom observation and treatment baseline are pending. Final report prepared and electronically signed by Juliana Ortiz, MS, CCC-SLP, on 10/11/2026 at 4:20 PM.
