Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Evaluation  
Evaluación del habla y del lenguaje  
Fictional training record

Child: Mateo Andrés Solvera  
Preferred name: Teo  
Date of birth: August 9, 2022  
Age at evaluation: 4;2  
Evaluation date: October 9, 2026  
Report date: October 11, 2026  
Session start: 9:10 a.m.  
Session stop: 10:25 a.m.  
Parents: Lucía Solvera and Daniel Solvera  
Home address: 418 Willow Finch Lane, Briarvale, North Carolina 27863  
Telephone: (919) 555-0146  
Email: lucia.solvera@example.com  
Record number: SLP-26-10482  
Medicaid number: 583021746Q  
Authorization number: AUTH-7041938  
Clinician: Elena Maribel Varela, MS, CCC-SLP  
Practice: Willow Bridge Pediatric Communication  
Practice website: https://willowbridge.example.org  
Referral source: Dr. Rafael Montivero  
School district: Briarvale Meadow School District  
School: Juniper Nest Elementary School  
Classroom teacher: Ms. Iris Bellara

Dear Lucía Solvera and Daniel Solvera,

Thank you for sharing your family’s story and joining this visit. Mateo brought curiosity, humor, and a strong wish to connect. This letter explains what we observed, what the results mean, and how adults can help. I used Spanish and English throughout the visit because both languages belong in his assessment.

Your main question was whether his difficulty expressing ideas reflects learning two languages or a need for extra support. You also wanted practical ways to help when he gets frustrated. The findings suggest that he needs support for language development and speech clarity across both languages. Using Spanish at home remains a valuable part of that support.

**Motivo de consulta — Why we met**

Lucía reported that Mateo often knows what he wants but cannot explain it clearly. She said, “En casa nos busca, nos lleva de la mano, pero cuando tiene mucho que decir, se queda atorado.” She described more frustration when adults ask several questions quickly or cannot see the object he wants.

Daniel reported that familiar routines are easier than unexpected changes. During breakfast, Mateo can request food and follow simple directions. When a toy breaks or a game changes, he may repeat a short phrase, raise his voice, or leave. The family wants him to ask for help without having to become upset first.

Ms. Bellara described similar concerns at Juniper Nest Elementary School. He joins songs and building activities but needs extra time to answer questions. Classroom assistant Mr. Tomas Eldren reported that showing an object helps more than repeating a direction louder. Staff also want clearer ways for him to enter play with classmates.

Before preschool, Mateo attended Little Learners Daycare. The family later contacted the Little Learners Program for communication support. These are separate services with similar names. Service coordinator Nora Estival at Briarvale Children’s Developmental Services Agency helped the family organize earlier records and understand the transition to school services.

**Nacimiento y salud — Birth and medical history**

According to the parent interview, Mateo was born at Pinewater Children’s Medical Center after a pregnancy lasting 38 weeks, 2 days. His birth weight was 6 pounds, 11 ounces. Reported Apgar scores were 8 and 9. He stayed with his mother after delivery and went home without feeding equipment or oxygen.

Lucía recalled early breastfeeding difficulty that improved with positioning support. He later accepted bottles, soft foods, and family meals. Current concerns involve expressing preferences, rather than chewing or swallowing. No coughing with meals, repeated choking, or unexplained weight loss was reported. Today, he drank water comfortably and ate a small snack without visible difficulty.

The family reported several ear infections during toddlerhood. Dr. Montivero reviewed his ears on September 18, 2026. Audiologist Camila Renswick completed a hearing visit on September 25, 2026 at Pinewater Children’s Medical Center. The supplied summary described hearing responses adequate for speech access. Changes in hearing should still be discussed with his medical team.

First words reportedly appeared around 19 months, and regular word combinations appeared around 32 months. These ages come from family recall. No loss of previously used words was reported. His mother described steady progress, aunque despacito. He currently sleeps well on most nights and takes no daily medication, according to the interview.

**Familia e idiomas — Family and language history**

Mateo lives with both parents and his sister, Lina Solvera, age 7 years. His grandmother, Rosa Celinda Mavero, provides care after school. A regular babysitter, Alma Quintera, sometimes helps during work shifts. The family dog, Canelo, is a favorite play partner and a frequent topic during conversation.

Mom works nights at Silver Lantern Packaging as a quality inspector. Her usual shift runs from 10:00 p.m. to 6:00 a.m.. Daniel handles bedtime on those nights. The family’s busiest communication time is often around 7:30 p.m., when dinner, homework, and preparations for work happen together.

The family maintains close contact with relatives in Guatemala. His grandmother’s hometown is the fictional village of Las Brisas del Cedral. A family mailing address there is Casa 12, Calle del Níspero, Las Brisas del Cedral, Guatemala. Video calls offer meaningful Spanish practice through family stories, jokes, and familiar routines.

Spanish is the main home language. English is common at school and during some sibling play. Lucía said, “No queremos perder el español; queremos que pueda hablar con todos.” I agree with that goal. Adults can use the language in which they feel most comfortable and responsive. Mixing languages does not, by itself, show a disorder.

During the visit, Mateo moved naturally between languages. He sometimes understood a direction in Spanish and answered in English. At other times, he used a Spanish verb with an English noun. We considered his combined skills, family reports, classroom observations, and learning during supported tasks. No single English-only result determined the impressions below.

**Cómo evaluamos — What we did**

The evaluation included an interview, record review, play observation, a speech sample, and structured language activities. Lucía remained present. I provided the assessment directly in both languages; no interpreter was needed. We used blocks, animals, pictures, and a pretend kitchen to create chances for requesting, explaining, and following directions.

Mateo settled after a brief period of watching. He preferred standing for some activities and accepted movement breaks. His attention improved when he could handle the materials. He responded well to a predictable sequence: first an activity, then a choice. He showed fatigue near the end, so speech findings include both structured responses and earlier play.

I administered PLS-5 Spanish using the instrument’s bilingual procedures. The table presents fictional results for this training record. Scores describe performance under assessment conditions. They do not capture every skill used at home or school. Age equivalents are especially limited and should not be treated as his overall developmental age.

| Test or subtest | Raw score | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| PLS-5 Spanish — Auditory Comprehension | 34 | 76 | 5th percentile | 70–84 | 2;10 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Expressive Communication | 31 | 71 | 3rd percentile | 66–80 | 2;6 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Total Language | 65 | 72 | 3rd percentile | 67–81 | 2;8 |

The intervals above use a 90% confidence level. They show that a score is an estimate, rather than an exact measure. The pattern across activities matters more than a small difference between scores. Understanding familiar language was a relative strength. Explaining ideas and building flexible sentences required more support.

**Lo que observamos — Understanding and expression**

Mateo identified familiar objects, understood routine action words, and followed directions involving objects in view. He completed 8/10 familiar directions with min cues. Directions containing two related actions were harder. He completed 3 of 5 after repetition and a gesture, with mod cues.

Questions about what an object does were easier than questions about why something happened. Picture choices helped him show knowledge that was difficult to express aloud. When I reduced the amount of language and paused, he often responded successfully. This suggests that adults should allow processing time before adding more words or another question.

In play, he requested, protested, commented, and called for attention. Examples included “yo want más,” “no cabe aquí,” and “help me abrir”. These productions show useful communication and flexible use of both languages. He also pointed, looked toward adults, and brought objects over to share a problem.

The language sample contained 42 usable utterances. Mean length of utterance was 2.4 words in this descriptive sample. This measure included both languages and was not compared with a monolingual cutoff. He expanded a message after an adult model in 6/10 opportunities with mod cues, especially when the message concerned something he wanted.

He had more difficulty explaining a short event without pictures. He might name the object but leave out who acted or what changed. Sentence models helped: an adult could describe the action, pause, and accept his response. Repeated demands to say a sentence exactly increased frustration and reduced his willingness to communicate.

**Habla y sonidos — Speech findings**

Familiar listeners understood more than unfamiliar listeners. During connected speech, estimated intelligibility was 62% for an unfamiliar listener in the room. This estimate reflects the sample and listening conditions, rather than a standardized score. Speech became less clear when sentences grew longer or when he spoke quickly during an exciting activity.

Observed patterns included fronting of /k/ and /g/, occasional final consonant omissions in English, and variable production of Spanish /ɾ/. He produced [w] in some English words containing /r/. These findings need interpretation within each language because sound expectations and word structures differ between Spanish and English.

For the target “car,” he said “tar”. For “gato,” he said “dato”. He produced /k/ accurately in 4/8 practice attempts with max cues. Accuracy improved when we slowed the task and used a visual model. There was no consistent visible struggle to begin a sound during this visit.

During animal play, he said, “Canelo run aquí.” Later, he called, “Lina mira esto.” These utterances combined a person or pet name with useful language. Oral structures appeared adequate for the observed speech tasks. A brief observation cannot rule out every motor speech concern, but the current pattern supports further phonological assessment and treatment.

**Juego y participación — Everyday communication**

Mateo shared materials and enjoyed pretend feeding. He waited for short turns with support. His mother reported that classmates Nico Fernal and Ada Mirel often invite him into block play. He sometimes follows their actions without telling them his own plan, which can lead to disagreements over materials.

During a supported repair task, he tried another way to communicate in 3/5 opportunities with mod cues. Pointing, showing, and using a shorter phrase all helped. We should count these strategies as progress. The goal is successful communication, con palabras y también con apoyos, while spoken language continues to develop.

**Impresiones — What the findings mean**

The combined findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and a speech sound disorder in this fictional case. Proposed diagnostic codes are F80.2 and F80.0. Concerns appeared across languages and settings, including familiar Spanish routines. Bilingual exposure alone does not explain the full pattern of difficulty.

Strengths include social interest, meaningful gestures, pretend play, family involvement, and a positive response to models. These strengths provide a good starting point for therapy. The assessment does not establish a reading diagnosis or a broader developmental diagnosis. School and family observations should continue to guide decisions as demands change.

**Recomendaciones — Our next steps**

1. Begin speech-language therapy twice weekly, with each visit lasting about thirty minutes. Use both languages according to the activity and communication partner. Initial work should focus on useful messages, understanding directions, and clearer speech. Reconsider frequency after the first treatment block based on participation and progress.

2. Coordinate with Ms. Bellara and the school team. Helpful classroom supports include short directions, visual choices, demonstration, and time to respond. Adults can check understanding by asking him to show the next action. They should avoid treating silence as proof that he did not understand.

3. Use family coaching informed by Hanen. Follow his interest, describe what he is doing, and expand one step beyond his message. If he says “más jugo,” an adult can model “quiero más jugo” without requiring an exact repetition.

4. Start speech practice with functional words selected by the family. A Cycles approach may help organize work on sound patterns. PROMPT is not proposed at this time. Picture supports can supplement speech; a formal PECS program is not currently planned. Review these choices as new evidence appears.

5. Use brief practice during enjoyable routines. Dinner preparation, bath play, and feeding the dog provide natural opportunities. Ask fewer testing questions and make more comments. When he struggles, offer “ayuda” or “help me” as a model, then respond to his attempt.

6. Carry forward the communication priority from the earlier IFSP, Outcome 2, into current school planning. Proposed Goal 1 is to request or comment using flexible phrases in 8/10 opportunities with min cues. Goal 2 is to follow related directions in 4/5 opportunities with min cues.

Billing references for this evaluation are CPT 92523 with modifier GN. Planned individual treatment uses CPT 92507 with modifier GN, subject to authorization. Scheduler Vera Bellmont will help arrange visits. Proposed review date: January 15, 2027.

Thank you for helping us understand Mateo across the places and languages that matter to him. Please share new examples of successful communication and difficult moments. Those examples will help us adjust the plan. Queremos que pueda participar, pedir ayuda, y compartir sus ideas con confianza.

Warmly,

Elena Maribel Varela, MS, CCC-SLP  
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist  
Willow Bridge Pediatric Communication  
(919) 555-0182  
elena.varela@willowbridge.example.org

**CONFIDENTIAL — FICTIONAL SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION**

**Información de la familia / Family information**

Child: Nicolás Vega Cruz  
Preferred name: Nico  
Date of birth: May 19, 2022  
Evaluation date: July 23, 2026  
Report date: July 30, 2026  
Age at evaluation: 4;2  
Parents: Elena Cruz Vega and Gabriel Vega Soto  
Address: 418 Willow Lantern Lane, Alder Cove, North Carolina 27863  
County: Laurel Bend County  
Family telephone: (252) 555-0146  
Family email: elena.vega@familymail.example  
Child record: LLP-2026-0472  
Medicaid member number: 583104762Q  
Authorization: ST-260723-118  
Daycare: Little Learners Daycare  
Therapy program: Little Learners Program  
Clinician: Marisol Valdés Peña, MS, CCC-SLP  
Clinician’s company: Bright Bridge Pediatric Speech Services  
Office telephone: (919) 555-0178  
Clinician email: marisol.valdes@brightbridge.example  
Family information website: https://brightbridge.example/families  
Evaluation billing: CPT 92523, modifier GN  
Clinical impression: ICD-10-CM F80.2

Dear Elena Cruz Vega and Gabriel Vega Soto,

Thank you for sharing your concerns, your home routines, and your hopes for Nico. This letter explains what I observed and what the results mean. I assessed communication in Spanish and English because both languages belong to your family’s daily life. Please keep using both languages with love and confidence.

**Por qué nos reunimos / Reason for this visit**

You requested this evaluation because Nico sometimes uses short messages when a longer explanation would help. At home, he may point, repeat one word, or bring an adult to an object. At daycare, adults sometimes need to guess whether he wants help, wants a turn, or feels upset.

Your main concern is practical communication. You want Nico to tell someone when something hurts, explain a small problem, and join play without an adult speaking for him. You also want his Spanish to remain strong so he can talk comfortably with relatives. These are useful priorities for treatment.

Su mamá Elena Cruz Vega said, “En español se anima más, pero cuando tiene prisa, las palabras no salen.” His father, Gabriel Vega Soto, described a similar pattern during English play. He said, “I can usually understand the idea, but somebody who does not know him needs more clues.”

The visit began at 9:05 a.m. and ended at 10:20 a.m.. We included play, conversation, caregiver interview, structured language tasks, and a brief speech screening. We paused for a snack and movement. Those pauses helped Nico return to the activities with better attention.

This report describes communication on one evaluation day. It also includes information from home and daycare. A test score gives one view of a child’s skills. Daily communication, learning with support, language exposure, and family priorities give other important views. I considered all of these before making recommendations.

**Antecedentes / Background and daily routines**

Nicolás Vega Cruz attends Little Learners Daycare on weekdays. His main classroom is Ms. Lopez's room. The classroom includes free play, books, music, outdoor time, lunch, and rest. Staff reported that he follows familiar routines more easily than new verbal directions.

Miss Ana helps with arrival and small-group activities. La maestra Carmen often uses Spanish during songs and transitions. Both described Nico as interested in other children. He watches their play, brings materials, and laughs with the group, even when he needs help finding words.

During classroom observation, Julia offered a toy plate. Nico accepted it and added pretend food. When Benji moved a truck, he reached toward the truck and looked at an adult. He did not independently explain that he wanted another turn. An adult model helped him make that request.

Mr. Tom, the daycare van driver, reported that Nico greets him with a wave during afternoon pickup. This was caregiver information, not a directly observed finding. I included it because greetings across familiar settings can show useful social strengths that a structured task may miss.

The family’s busiest communication periods occur at 7:30 a.m. before departure and at 6:15 p.m. during dinner preparation. You reported more frustration when adults hurry. On slower weekend mornings, Nico uses longer messages and stays with shared play for a longer period.

The referral came through Laurel Bend Child Development Services Agency. Service coordinator Rosa Méndez supplied the intake summary with family permission. The current record includes an IFSP dated June 12, 2026. The preschool transition process remains underway; the family has not yet selected a school placement.

**Nacimiento y salud / Birth and medical history**

According to the parent interview and the fictional intake record, Nico was born at Willow Harbor Women’s and Children’s Hospital in Pine Lantern, North Carolina. Pregnancy reached 39 weeks 2 days gestation. Birth weight was 7 lb 2 oz. Delivery was vaginal, without a reported emergency.

Recorded Apgar scores were 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. The family reported no neonatal intensive care stay. Feeding began with breast milk and later included formula. Early feeding did not require a tube or a specialized feeding program.

The family recalled sitting independently around 7 months and walking around 14 months. First meaningful words appeared around 18 months. Consistent word combinations emerged around 30 months. These ages are parent estimates. They help describe the developmental history but do not establish a diagnosis by themselves.

Primary care physician Dr. Daniel Ríos follows routine health needs at Alder Cove Children’s Medical Center. The family reported several middle-ear infections during toddlerhood. No ear tubes were reported. The most recent documented hearing visit occurred on March 18, 2026 with audiologist Aisha Benton.

That hearing report described responses within expected limits for the measures completed. Today’s language visit did not include a full hearing evaluation. If listening changes or ear infections return, the family should contact the medical team. Consistent access to speech sounds supports communication in both languages.

You reported no loss of previously learned skills, current swallowing concerns, or daily prescription medicine. Nico eats a range of familiar textures. He sometimes avoids mixed foods but accepts fruit, tortillas, rice, eggs, and crunchy snacks. Food preferences did not interfere with the evaluation activities.

Sleep usually begins near 8:30 p.m.. You reported occasional waking and better participation after a full night’s sleep. Oral structures appeared adequate for the speech tasks observed. I did not complete a specialized motor speech or feeding assessment, because the referral and findings primarily concerned language.

**Familia e idiomas / Family and language history**

Nico lives with his parents and his sister, Inés Vega Cruz, who is 7 years old. Spanish is common during meals, family calls, and caregiving. English is common during some sibling play, daycare activities, and community outings. Language use changes naturally with the person and activity.

Su mamá Elena Cruz Vega works at Lantern Shore Market Cooperative. His father, Gabriel Vega Soto, works at Cedar Window Repair Collective. Work schedules affect pickup arrangements. These schedules also explain why several trusted adults support homework, meals, and communication practice during the week.

Grandmother doña Lupe provides afternoon care twice weekly. Her full name is Lupe Salcedo. She speaks mainly Spanish with Nico. She reported, “Cuando le doy tiempo, me cuenta más. Si lo corrijo mucho, se queda calladito.” Her observation supports using patient, responsive conversation.

An aunt, Marina Cruz, sometimes provides weekend care. Babysitter Sofía Duarte uses both languages. Each caregiver described gestures as helpful when a message is unclear. The family dog, Rocky, often becomes a topic during play and offers a familiar reason to request, comment, and explain.

The family estimated current exposure at about 60% Spanish and 40% English across a typical week. These estimates describe opportunities to hear and use language. They do not measure proficiency. A child can have stronger skills in one activity or language and different strengths elsewhere.

Nico sometimes combines languages within one message. This occurred most often when a useful word was easier to retrieve in English. Code-switching alone is not evidence of a disorder. We looked instead at whether he understood messages, organized ideas, learned new forms, and communicated across familiar situations.

For example, a parent reported that he said "quiero the big truck" during play. That message communicates a clear request. We can expand it naturally in either language without demanding a translation. The goal is a fuller, clearer message while keeping the conversation comfortable and meaningful.

**Cómo evaluamos / Assessment process**

I am the bilingual pediatric speech-language pathologist who completed this evaluation in North Carolina. I used Spanish and English directly. No interpreter attended. Caregivers supplied context when a word, routine, or gesture had a family-specific meaning. I documented those explanations separately from directly observed responses.

The formal language measure was Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish). I followed the manual’s bilingual administration procedures for the scored tasks. Spanish responses and permitted English responses contributed according to those procedures. I completed supported teaching tasks afterward and kept them outside the standardized scores.

The assessment included the Auditory Comprehension, Expressive Communication, and Total Language results. I also gathered a bilingual play sample, caregiver examples, classroom observations, and informal speech tasks. Those additional activities helped connect the formal findings to everyday needs. They were not treated as separate standardized tests.

Nico entered cautiously and stayed close to his mother. After several minutes with toy animals, he explored more freely. He shared attention, showed objects, and responded to playful surprises. His participation improved when I offered a choice of materials and explained what would happen next.

Directions were easier when they included gestures, familiar vocabulary, and a clear action. During harder tasks, he sometimes repeated the last word or looked toward a caregiver. Repetition could indicate uncertainty rather than agreement. I checked understanding through actions and choices instead of accepting every repeated response.

Results are considered a useful estimate of current performance. Attention varied, but he completed the required scored activities. The bilingual format helped reduce language-access barriers. Even so, no test fully represents a child’s experience. The family interview and learning tasks remained essential to the interpretation.

**Resultados / Score table**

| Measure | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish — Auditory Comprehension | 88 | 21st percentile | 81–96 | 3;3 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Expressive Communication | 82 | 12th percentile | 76–90 | 2;11 |
| PLS-5 Spanish — Total Language | 84 | 14th percentile | 78–92 | 3;1 |

The intervals above are 95% confidence intervals. They describe uncertainty around each score. Age equivalents summarize performance on particular test items. They are not the child’s overall developmental age. Please do not use them to choose younger activities or reduce opportunities for age-appropriate play.

The Auditory Comprehension standard score of 88 showed stronger understanding than expression on this measure. The Expressive Communication standard score of 82 reflected difficulty building messages. The Total Language standard score of 84 supported concern when considered with the functional observations and family reports.

**Lo que vimos / Communication during play**

Understanding was strongest for familiar objects, simple actions, and predictable routines. Nico identified familiar pictured items in 8/10 informal opportunities. He followed related two-step directions in 3 of 5 opportunities with min cues. New location words and longer spoken directions caused more difficulty.

Expression included single words, short combinations, gestures, and some longer familiar phrases. He independently requested in 6/10 play opportunities. With mod cues, successful requests increased to 9/10. These informal counts describe this session only. They do not replace the standardized results.

Examples included "más agua", "truck go ahí", and "no cabe". After a model, he expanded a message to "el carro no cabe". The change showed that supported practice could help him add information. He did not yet use that longer pattern consistently with new materials.

During animal play, Nico said “Rocky run” and later “Inés tiene.” Both messages included meaningful people or pets. He used their names to connect the activity with home. I preserved those examples because they show communication purpose as well as sentence length.

In the language sample, I used SALT conventions where applicable. A repeated extra word received the code [EW]. These codes describe a transcript feature, not a diagnosis. I interpreted Spanish grammar within Spanish and English grammar within English, with attention to normal bilingual variation.

Informal speech observations included occasional replacement of /k/ with [t] in English tasks. The phonemes /k/ and /t/ were clearer with a slowed model. Spanish /ɾ/ varied across words. I did not count every difference between languages as an error or establish a separate speech diagnosis.

**Impresiones / What the findings mean**

The findings support a mixed receptive-expressive language difficulty, with greater difficulty in expression. The clinical impression is ICD-10-CM F80.2. Concern comes from needs across languages and settings, not from speaking Spanish, learning English, or combining languages. Bilingualism does not explain all the observed difficulties.

Nico shows several strengths: social interest, shared enjoyment, functional gestures, familiar vocabulary, and responsiveness to teaching. These strengths give us useful starting points. He needs help understanding less familiar messages and adding enough information for another person to understand his request, comment, or explanation.

This evaluation does not establish an attention, autism, intellectual, or motor speech diagnosis. Those areas require their own assessment when concerns warrant it. His play and interaction today offered useful information, but one speech-language visit cannot answer every developmental question. Continued observation across settings will help guide future decisions.

**Recomendaciones / Our next steps**

I recommend speech-language therapy through Little Learners Program with a bilingual clinician. Begin with two sessions each week, each lasting thirty minutes. Include caregiver coaching and coordination with daycare. Review participation and progress before changing frequency. The proposed service uses CPT 92507 with modifier GN.

Treatment should focus on useful messages during play and routines. Begin with requesting help, describing a problem, and giving another person a short explanation. Support understanding through pictures, actions, and clear language. Increase difficulty gradually after success, rather than giving several new demands at once.

Use responsive interaction informed by Hanen principles. Follow his interest, pause, respond to the message, and add a small amount of language. For example, when he says "carro", model "el carro corre". Accept an attempt without requiring repeated imitation before he can continue playing.

At home, choose one brief routine each day. During snack, offer a choice and wait. During dressing, describe the problem and model a request. During books, comment on pictures instead of asking a question on every page. Keep practice playful: poquito a poquito, within activities the family already enjoys.

At daycare, Ms. Lopez can offer visual choices and a predictable turn-taking phrase. Miss Ana can pause before helping. La maestra Carmen can model Spanish during familiar songs and play. Adults should acknowledge the message first, then provide a fuller version without public correction.

Picture supports may help when frustration rises. This recommendation does not prescribe PECS or PROMPT at this time. The clinician should select a specific approach only after examining the skill it targets. Likewise, Cycles may be considered later only if a fuller speech assessment supports that need.

**Horario propuesto / Proposed session schedule**

These appointments are proposed, not confirmed. The service coordinator will verify room availability and transportation. Please use the listed start and stop times when planning arrival. The schedule allows practice in the daycare setting and time for caregivers to learn strategies.

| Day | Start time | Stop time | Location | Main activity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tuesday | 9:00 a.m. | 9:30 a.m. | Little Learners Daycare, Ms. Lopez's room | Play and classroom communication |
| Thursday | 3:15 p.m. | 3:45 p.m. | Little Learners Program, family therapy room | Direct treatment and caregiver coaching |
| First Friday of each month | 12:10 p.m. | 12:25 p.m. | Little Learners Daycare, staff meeting room | Caregiver and staff consultation |

**Metas y seguimiento / Goals and follow-up**

Proposed IFSP outcome 1 addresses communicating wants, needs, and problems during daily routines. The initial target is a clear message in 8/10 opportunities with min cues, across two familiar routines. A message may use speech with a gesture or picture when that support improves understanding.

Proposed IFSP outcome 2 addresses understanding directions during play and transitions. The initial target is completing related two-step directions in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues. We will record the language, activity, and support used. This will help distinguish learning from simple familiarity with one task.

The proposed review date is October 22, 2026. At review, we will compare communication samples, caregiver reports, and treatment records. We will also ask whether adults guess less often and whether participation feels easier. Family goals can change as new routines or concerns emerge.

Gracias por compartir su historia. Nico already has meaningful ways to connect with people. Therapy will help him build on those skills and make his messages easier to understand. Please bring examples from either language; both belong in our work together.

Warmly,

Marisol Valdés Peña, MS, CCC-SLP  
Bilingual Pediatric Speech-Language Pathologist  
Bright Bridge Pediatric Speech Services  
Signed: July 30, 2026

Motivo de consulta / Background

María José Valdés Cordero was referred for concerns about understanding classroom directions, combining words, and being understood by unfamiliar listeners. Her mother, Elena Cordero Salvatierra, attended the evaluation and supplied the developmental history. Her father, Andrés Valdés Molina, joined by telephone during the interview.

The family described a child who enjoys pretend cooking, songs, and helping with laundry. “Ella sabe lo que quiere, pero se frustra cuando no encontramos la palabra,” her mother reported. The family wants communication that works across home and school, including asking for help and explaining what happened.

Ms. Corina Bell reported that Majo watches classmates before starting unfamiliar routines. She participates more readily when directions include gestures. Classroom assistant Dario Quinn described difficulty understanding longer spoken messages during transitions.

This evaluation addressed both languages. English performance alone would give an incomplete picture of the child’s communication. The clinician considered caregiver report, classroom information, direct assessment, and supported learning tasks. All findings below belong to this fictional record.

Antecedentes de nacimiento y salud

María José was born at Silver Orchard Regional Hospital in Maplehaven, North Carolina, at 35 weeks, 4 days gestation. Birth weight was 2,410 grams. Apgar scores were 7 at the first recorded interval and 9 at the next interval. Delivery followed maternal hypertension and reduced fetal movement.

The child received care in the NICU at Silver Orchard Regional Hospital for feeding coordination and temperature support. Neonatologist Dr. Owen Calder followed her during admission. The discharge summary dated August 18, 2022 documented stable oral feeding without home oxygen.

Pediatrician Dr. Nadia Serrano currently follows growth and development. Otolaryngologist Dr. Mateo Varela evaluated recurrent middle-ear concerns. Audiologist Keisha Rowan completed behavioral hearing assessment on September 17, 2026; the supplied report described hearing adequate for speech access.

The parent reported no current daily medication, seizures, or swallowing concerns. Early feeding was slow, pero ahora come con la familia. Motor milestones were described as mildly delayed. First consistent words appeared at approximately 20 months, and regular word combinations appeared near 32 months. Occupational therapist Amina Cole provides support for transitions and sensory regulation.

Familia e historia de idiomas

Majo lives with both parents and her sister, Luz Valdés Cordero, age 7;1. Her grandmother, Rosa Salvatierra, provides afternoon care. A family friend and occasional babysitter, Paz Ibarra, uses Spanish during play and meals.

Spanish has been present since birth. English exposure increased with enrollment at Little Lantern Meadow Childcare at 2;8. The family estimates current language exposure as 65% Spanish and 35% English. These estimates describe opportunity, not measured language proficiency.

The father works at Bramble Ridge Packaging Cooperative. His schedule changes, so evening language routines vary. The mother reported, “Con su abuela habla más español; con su hermana mezcla todo.” Code-switching is accepted at home.

The household dog, Chispa, often appears in pretend stories. During the interview, the child said, “Chispa wants comida.” That statement was recorded as a mixed-language production.

The family previously received coordination through Centro de Apoyo al Desarrollo Infantil y Orientación Familiar del Valle del Roble (CADIOFVR). Service coordinator Noelia Park supplied the prior IFSP. CADIOFVR remains a source of family resource information.

Procedimientos y observaciones

Isabel Marín Duarte conducted the visit in Spanish and English without an interpreter. The clinician used PLS-5 Spanish, a bilingual language sample, caregiver interview, play observation, and brief supported learning tasks. English probes were descriptive and did not generate separate standardized scores.

Testing conditions were generally suitable. María José initially stayed close to her mother, then joined tabletop and floor activities. She benefited from movement breaks and a clear sequence: primero jugar, después mirar el libro.

During standardized items, the clinician followed permitted administration procedures. Additional teaching occurred after scored items and was documented separately. Responses obtained with mod cues or max cues during supported tasks did not replace standardized responses.

The language sample included pretend food, a picture book, and a missing-toy activity. The clinician counted meaningful attempts in either language. Dialect features and ordinary bilingual transfer were considered before classifying an error. Fatigue increased toward the end, particularly during tasks requiring repeated verbal responses.

Resultados de pruebas / Score table

| Measure | Score type | Result | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish: Auditory Comprehension | Standard score | 78 | 73-83 | 2;6–3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Expressive Communication | Standard score | 76 | 71–82 | 2;5–2;11 |
| PLS-5 Spanish: Total Language | Standard score | 75 | 70-81 | 2;6–3;0 |

Percentiles were 7th percentile for Auditory Comprehension, 5th percentile for Expressive Communication, and 5th percentile for Total Language. Confidence intervals represent 90% intervals.

Age equivalents are descriptive estimates with limited precision. They do not establish a developmental age or replace functional findings. The reported ranges preserve uncertainty around nearby task levels.

Comprensión y expresión

Across languages, Majo identified familiar objects and understood routine action words. She followed related directions in 8/10 opportunities when materials were visible. Performance decreased to 3 of 5 opportunities when the direction included an unfamiliar location word.

Spanish directions sometimes produced faster responses, aunque los conceptos difíciles remained difficult in both languages. The child understood simple possession and basic contrasts. She needed repetition for questions about events outside the immediate activity.

Expressive communication included gestures, single words, and short combinations. Recorded productions included “yo quiere más agua,” “baby está sleeping,” and “no cabe aquí.” The clinician accepted mixed-language vocabulary when the message was clear.

During pretend play, María José said, “Luz make sopa.” Because that production contains a personal name, the name alone carries an identifier label.

Word retrieval improved when the clinician supplied a choice or initial sound. Independent descriptions often omitted an agent, action, or location. With min cues, the child expanded messages in 4/8 opportunities. With mod cues, expansion increased to 7/8 opportunities.

The sample contained occasional SALT codes [EW] and [EU], reflecting word-level and utterance-level errors under the documented coding convention. These codes were considered alongside the bilingual context.

Habla, voz y fluidez

Speech was clearer in familiar routines than during longer spontaneous messages. The clinician observed inconsistent production of /k/ and /g/, along with reduced consonant clusters. The target word “casa” was produced as “tasa” during one picture task.

For the English target “rabbit,” the initial consonant was realized as [w]. Spanish /ɾ/ varied by word position. These findings require continued sampling across languages before selecting treatment targets.

The parent estimated unfamiliar listeners understand approximately 55% of connected speech. That estimate was reported, not independently measured. The clinician understood 18/25 sampled messages when context was available.

Stimulability improved with mod cues and visual placement support. Voice quality was appropriate during observed speech. No consistent stuttering pattern appeared in this sample. Oral structures appeared adequate for observed speech tasks, although the examination was brief.

Comunicación social y participación

Majo shared attention, offered pretend food, and used facial expression to support meaning. She repaired a misunderstood message by pointing and repeating, pero rarely added new information without support.

Classmate Nina Solano is a preferred play partner. Another classmate, Eli Mercer, sometimes answers before the child finishes. Ms. Corina Bell reported that a quieter partner improves participation.

During a recent classroom group, Tessa Reed offered a toy and waited. The child responded with a gesture and a short phrase. School transportation attendant Jonah Vale reported that greetings are usually brief.

These observations suggest that communication demands, partner pacing, and background noise affect participation. Social interest was a clear strength.

Impresiones clínicas

The fictional assessment findings support mixed receptive and expressive language needs across Spanish and English. Difficulties appeared in both languages and across structured tasks, spontaneous communication, and caregiver report. Bilingual exposure alone does not explain the full pattern.

Speech sound differences also reduced clarity. Some observed patterns may reflect development or cross-language influence. Others require further analysis through repeated samples and response to teaching. Treatment should prioritize functional clarity and language access.

Provisional diagnostic entries are ICD-10 F80.2 and F80.0. These entries summarize the documented communication profile and should be reviewed as additional information becomes available.

María José Valdés Cordero showed useful strengths: social engagement, pretend play, gesture use, and improved performance with teaching. The family’s consistent involvement supports intervention. Findings should guide an individualized plan, with progress judged through functional communication in both languages.

Recomendaciones / Plan de apoyo

Begin speech-language therapy twice weekly, with caregiver participation when available. Treatment should support Spanish and English according to communication partners and daily needs. La familia puede seguir usando el idioma que le resulte más natural.

Use focused stimulation, recasts, visual choices, and supported practice in familiar routines. Elements from Hanen may help caregivers follow the child’s lead and expand messages. Consider a Cycles approach if further speech sampling confirms suitable recurring patterns. PROMPT was not administered during this evaluation.

At home, pause after comments and offer time to respond. Expand the child’s message by adding useful information. For example, expand “más agua” to “quiero más agua.” Avoid requiring repeated imitation when frustration rises.

At school, pair spoken directions with pictures and gestures. Check understanding through action, not repeated yes-or-no questions. Ms. Corina Bell and classroom assistant Dario Quinn should allow additional response time during group activities.

Provide accessible picture supports for requesting, commenting, and asking for help. Formal PECS instruction is not currently part of the plan. Review hearing information with Dr. Nadia Serrano if listening behavior changes.

The clinician will coordinate with Amina Cole and Noelia Park after receiving the family’s release. No external communication occurred during this synthetic visit.

Metas funcionales y seguimiento

The prior IFSP listed Outcome 2 for communicating needs during family routines. The current plan carries that intent into preschool activities.

Goal 1: During play or meals, the child will produce a meaningful expanded message in 8/10 opportunities with min cues, using either language.

Goal 2: Given familiar materials, the child will follow related directions in 4 of 5 opportunities with min cues.

Goal 3: After target selection, the child will produce selected consonants in functional words with 80% accuracy and mod cues.

Progress will be reviewed on January 20, 2027. Collect brief samples from home and school before that review. Report the language, task, partner, and cueing level with each sample.

Cierre y autenticación

Elena Cordero Salvatierra summarized the plan as “darle tiempo, hablar natural, y ayudar sin presión.” Andrés Valdés Molina agreed that routines should support both languages. The family received a written summary and practice examples.

Report completed on October 23, 2026 at 2:15 PM by Isabel Marín Duarte, MS, CCC-SLP, of Piedmont Two Bridges Pediatric Therapy. Electronic signature identifier: SLP-ES-604281.

text:
BILINGUAL PEDIATRIC SPEECH-LANGUAGE EVALUATION / EVALUACIÓN DEL HABLA Y LENGUAJE

Client: María José Herrera Salgado; preferred nickname: Mari
DOB: 08/09/2022
Age at evaluation: 4;2
Evaluation date: 10/09/2026
Visit: 9:05 a.m.–10:35 a.m.
Report date: 10/11/2026
Record ID: SLP-2609417
Medicaid member ID: 731604928K
Authorization: AUTH-68245109
Referring physician: Dr. Elena Varela
Clinician: Camila Ríos Bennett, MS, CCC-SLP; bilingual Spanish-English pediatric SLP
Employer: Puente Claro Pediatric Communication, PLLC
Clinic: 284 Luna Orchard Lane, Suite B, Arroyo Pines, North Carolina 27862
Phone: 919-555-0142
Email: intake@puenteclaro.example
Website: https://puenteclaro.example
Service: Initial bilingual communication assessment; CPT 92523; modifier GN
Informants: Mother, father, preschool teacher; available medical and educational records.
Language: Spanish and English. Interview completed directly in both languages; no interpreter required.

S: SUBJETIVO / ANTECEDENTES

Referral concerns: Reduced intelligibility, short utterances, difficulty explaining events, and inconsistent response to classroom directions. Family requests assessment across both languages. Mother stated, “En casa habla más, pero cuando quiere contar algo se desespera.” Father reported that unfamiliar listeners frequently ask for repetition. Parents want practical supports for home and preschool, con ejemplos en español.

Child resides with mother Guadalupe Salgado Rivera, called Lupita, and father Jesús Herrera Molina, called Chuy. Sibling Mateo Herrera Salgado, called Teo, is 7 years old. Home address: 619 Cedar Lantern Court, Arroyo Pines, North Carolina 27862, Maravilla County. Mother's phone: 252-555-0168. Father's phone: 252-555-0183. Preferred family email: familia.herrera.salgado@example.com. Mother prefers Spanish telephone contact; father accepts either language.

Mother works at Silver Basket Grocery, described during interview as “la tienda Silver Basket”; the named store was confirmed as Silver Basket Grocery. Father works at Blue Heron Packing Plant, which he called “la planta Blue Heron”; employer listed on intake as Blue Heron Packing Plant. Parents alternate shifts. Mother previously worked at Casa Laurel Restaurant, “el restaurante Casa Laurel,” and occasionally accepts shifts through Morning Lantern Cleaning Service, “el servicio de limpieza Morning Lantern.” No workplace contact requested.

Maternal aunt Rosa Elena Salgado Rivera provides afternoon care. Babysitter Daniela Cruz Montes covers occasional shift overlap. Maternal grandmother Beatriz Rivera Solís lives nearby and participates in meals and bedtime routines. Family uses consistent caregivers; no recent change reported. Father noted, “Con su abuela conversa tranquila; conmigo quiere hablar rapidísimo.” Parents described warm interactions, shared play, and frequent reading of picture books.

Prenatal/birth history: Mother reported routine prenatal care, pregnancy-related hypertension near delivery, and no reported prenatal substance exposure. Delivery occurred at Luna Creek Women's Hospital in Luna Creek, North Carolina. Gestational age: 36 weeks, 6 days. Birth weight: 6 lb 1 oz. Apgar scores: 8 at one minute and 9 at five minutes. Brief feeding observation; no respiratory support or prolonged neonatal admission reported. Discharge date: 08/12/2022. Birth information came from the discharge summary supplied by parents.

Medical history: Pediatric care through Maple Lantern Children's Clinic. Dr. Varela documented recurrent otitis media and referred for hearing assessment. Parent reports three infections during the previous winter; no current pain, fever, or drainage. No tympanostomy tubes. Audiologist Nora Ellis Vega completed testing on 09/18/2026 at Cedar Hollow Hearing Center. Available summary indicated hearing adequate for speech access bilaterally, with normal tympanometry. No known seizures, head injury, or diagnosed neurologic condition.

No daily prescription medication reported. Seasonal congestion managed per pediatric instructions. Parents denied swallowing difficulty, choking, or persistent cough during meals. Selective food preferences include mixed textures; accepts varied soft and crunchy foods. Sleep generally stable, with occasional waking during illness. Vision screening reportedly passed, but the screening record was unavailable. Medical history otherwise based on caregiver report; no inference of unreported diagnoses.

Developmental history: Sat independently at approximately 7 months, walked at 14 months, and used first meaningful words around 18 months. Two-word combinations emerged around 30 months. Parents recall early pointing, showing objects, social smiling, and imitation. No loss of skills reported. Current toileting and dressing require routine assistance. Fine motor concerns limited to frustration with scissors; occupational therapy has not evaluated this concern.

Previous services: Referral to Maravilla County CDSA occurred on 02/06/2025. Service coordinator Lidia Santos Price supplied a historical IFSP dated 03/21/2025, case CDSA-MV-250318. IFSP outcome 2 addressed requesting during routines; outcome 3 addressed caregiver use of language models. Services ended at transition. Current support includes Maravilla County WIC and enrollment assistance from Maravilla County Partnership for Children. Family also contacted Maravilla County Smart Start for preschool resources.

Language history / Historia lingüística: Spanish predominates during meals, bathing, and extended-family visits. English predominates at preschool and during sibling-led games. Parents estimate Spanish exposure at 65% and English at 35%, varying by weekday. These are caregiver estimates, not measured language input. Family speaks a Mexican Spanish variety with occasional regional vocabulary. Parents report no expectation that either language should replace the other.

Mother reported, “Dice 'quiero más', pero para explicar por qué, se queda en palabras sueltas.” Father hears 'me do it'] and 'yo open'] during play. Code-switching occurs naturally with family. Parents understand most routine requests but need gestures for unfamiliar topics. Child reportedly follows familiar directions mejor cuando ve lo que estamos haciendo. Difficulty increases with new vocabulary, several steps, or competing noise.

Preschool: Little Orchard Learning Preschool, 82 Willow Lantern Road, Arroyo Pines, North Carolina 27862. Lead teacher Ms. Mara López and assistant Mr. Evan Castillo provided a classroom form dated 10/02/2026. Teacher described interest in peers, music, pretend cooking, and outdoor play. Concerns include limited explanations, reduced speech clarity, and needing demonstrations during group activities. No disciplinary removals reported.

Classmates Ana Lucía Torres Méndez and Juan Esteban Pardo Ruiz, called Juanito, often invite participation. Child plays beside classmate Mila Chen Ortiz but sometimes abandons a message after repetition requests. Cousins José Antonio Rivera Campos, called Pepe, and Isabel Rivera Campos visit weekly. Family pet Canela, a small dog, provides a frequent conversation topic. These names identify social partners only; no concerns about their development were assessed.

Functional priorities: Explain basic needs, tell what happened at school, answer simple questions, and participate without adults guessing. Mother stated, “Queremos que pueda decir lo que necesita en los dos idiomas.” Parents denied concern about bilingualism itself. They requested help distinguishing language-learning differences from communication difficulty. Family accepted assessment breaks, bilingual elicitation, and interpretation that separates standardized scores from descriptive findings.

O: OBJETIVO / RESULTADOS

Evaluation conditions: Quiet clinic room; mother present throughout, father joined final interview. Child entered willingly, explored materials, and returned to shared activities with brief movement breaks. Engagement strongest during pretend kitchen play and animal scenes. Fatigue increased during decontextualized questions. No acute illness observed. Hearing summary reviewed before interpretation. Assessment combined standardized Spanish testing, informal English probes, connected speech, caregiver interview, and classroom report.

Tools: Preschool Language Scales, Fifth Edition Spanish (PLS-5 Spanish), including Auditory Comprehension, Expressive Communication, and Total Language. Also used Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts (SALT) conventions for a descriptive bilingual sample. Informal probes were clinician-developed and not standardized. English responses were accepted only where permitted by the test procedure. Additional teaching trials occurred after scored items and were excluded from standardized scoring.

Score table:

| Measure | Raw score | Standard score | Percentile | Confidence interval | Age equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| PLS-5 Spanish Auditory Comprehension | 36 | 78 | 7th | 73-85 | 3;0 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Expressive Communication | 31 | 74 | 4th | 69-82 | 2;8 |
| PLS-5 Spanish Total Language | 67 | 75 | 5th | 70-82 | Not reported |

Intervals above represent 90% confidence intervals. Standard scores use mean 100 and standard deviation 15. Age equivalents describe performance on this instrument; they do not represent overall developmental age. No scaled scores were generated. Scores support the broader clinical picture but do not independently establish diagnosis. Interpretation considers exposure, dialect, bilingual development, participation, and convergence across methods.

Receptive language / Comprensión: Identified familiar objects, actions, basic body parts, and common clothing. Followed contextual one-step directions in 8/10 opportunities independently. Followed novel two-step directions in 3/8 opportunities independently and 6/8 with mod cues. Difficulty increased when directions contained location concepts or required holding information before acting. Repetition alone helped less than demonstration plus a concise verbal model.

Identified pictured actions in 9/10 Spanish trials and 6/10 English trials. Understood object functions in 5/8 Spanish trials and 4/8 English trials. Answered contextual location questions in 4/6 opportunities. Temporal terms and negatives were inconsistent in both languages. Errors persisted when vocabulary was familiar, suggesting that word exposure alone did not explain all difficulty.

Expressive language / Expresión: Communicated through words, gestures, facial expression, and occasional longer combinations. Independently requested, rejected, labeled, and commented. Explanation and narrative functions required support. Spanish utterances included 'la niña come'], 'se cayó aquí'], and 'yo no puede']. English examples included 'baby sleeping'], 'him go outside'], and 'I want rojo']. Mixed-language utterances were analyzed descriptively and were not treated as errors solely because languages changed.

Sample consisted of 42 analyzable utterances from play and picture description. Mean length of utterance in words was 3.1; this value was descriptive, without a bilingual normative comparison. Unintelligible segments limited analysis. SALT codes included [EW] for selected word errors and [EU] for utterance-level errors. Language choice, dialect forms, and typical code-switching were not automatically assigned error codes.

Grammatical observations: Variable Spanish article agreement, verb inflection, and object pronoun use; English auxiliary and tense marking also inconsistent. Produced occasional complete subject-verb-object sentences, especially after familiar routines. Spontaneous expansions rarely supplied a reason, sequence, or repair. Errors occurred across repeated opportunities in each language. The sample remained too small for firm conclusions about every grammatical form.

Vocabulary: Stronger naming for food, animals, household items, and family routines. Weaker verbs describing less familiar actions and relational vocabulary. Benefited from semantic choices and gesture. For target 'debajo'], initially pointed beside the chair, then placed the toy correctly after a demonstration. For target 'behind'], responded accurately after bilingual explanation. These teaching responses were recorded separately from test scores.

Dynamic assessment / Aprendizaje con apoyo: During brief mediated story teaching, independently identified an event in 2/5 opportunities. Following modeling, visual supports, and mod cues, identified an event in 4/5. Produced agent-action combinations in 3 of 5 retell opportunities after teaching. Retention after a short break was partial. Learning response was positive but support remained necessary for independent explanation.

Speech sound production: Oral mechanism screening showed symmetrical facial movement, functional jaw opening, and adequate visible tongue movement for sampled tasks. Dentition appropriate to history; no obvious structural difference observed. This was a screening, not a dental or medical examination. Voice and resonance judged functional during the visit. No persistent hoarseness, hypernasality, or audible nasal emission observed.

Connected speech showed fronting of /k/ and /g/ in some words, cluster reduction, and inconsistent final consonant omission in English. Spanish tap /ɾ/ and trill /r/ were variable. English approximant /ɹ/ was not considered a primary treatment target at this stage. Dialect and age expectations were considered; not every difference represented disorder.

Examples: Target 'casa'] produced as 'tasa']; target 'gato'] produced as 'dato']; target 'spoon'] produced as 'poon']. Target 'zapato'] produced as 'pato'] in rapid speech. In another context, child said “Canela corre” and later “Juanito go.” These named utterances were retained as contextual speech examples.

Stimulability: Produced /k/ in isolation in 4/6 trials with max cues, then in initial syllables in 2/6 with max cues. Produced /g/ in isolation in 3/6 with max cues. Produced English final /t/ in practiced words in 5/8 with mod cues. Occasional [w] substitutions occurred during English liquid attempts.

Intelligibility: Clinician understood approximately 60% of connected speech with context and approximately 45% without context. Mother estimated familiar-listener understanding at 80%. These are informal estimates, not standardized scores. Reduced clarity reflected interacting speech sound patterns, short grammatical forms, rapid rate, and limited message repair. Repetition sometimes increased rate and reduced clarity further.

Pragmatics / Uso social: Shared enjoyment, coordinated gaze with pointing, initiated pretend play, and responded to bids. Turn-taking sustained with visual structure. Requested help independently in 4/6 opportunities. Following a communication breakdown, attempted repair in 2/5 opportunities independently and 4/5 with min cues. No diagnostic conclusion regarding autism was attempted from this communication assessment.

Play and participation: Symbolic play included feeding dolls, preparing food, and arranging animal homes. Flexible use of materials observed. Child tolerated transitions with a brief preview and cleanup song. Distractibility occurred during lengthy verbal instructions but improved with reduced language load. Findings do not establish an attention diagnosis. Motor activity and participation were adequate for the assessment procedures.

A: ANÁLISIS / IMPRESIONES

Findings support mixed receptive-expressive language disorder and speech sound disorder affecting functional communication across Spanish and English. Clinical codes: ICD-10 F80.2 and F80.0. Evidence includes below-expected standardized performance, difficulty with familiar concepts in both languages, limited independent explanation, persistent speech patterns, and caregiver/classroom concerns. Bilingual exposure and code-switching are normal features of this child's communication environment.

Language needs extend beyond limited English experience. Spanish performance also showed difficulty understanding novel directions and forming clear explanations. Teaching improved performance, yet independent transfer remained limited. Strong engagement, social interest, gesture, and caregiver responsiveness support intervention. The assessment did not measure every dialect feature or all language contexts; conclusions apply to the sampled skills and corroborating reports.

Speech findings reduce access to classroom participation and peer conversation. Some liquid differences remain developmentally expected; intervention should prioritize patterns with the greatest intelligibility effect. Cross-language analysis is necessary before selecting each target. Avoid counting a Spanish-influenced English production as disordered without examining the relevant sound system, dialect, age, and production in Spanish.

Functional impact: Adults frequently infer needs. Unfamiliar listeners miss key words. Child sometimes stops speaking after unsuccessful repair. Longer directions require support, and classroom explanations remain brief. These limitations affect participation rather than reflecting unwillingness to communicate. Family reports match observed difficulty, although performance may differ with familiar partners and quieter surroundings.

Prognosis: Favorable for measurable functional gains with consistent, bilingual intervention and caregiver participation. Rate of progress cannot be predicted from this visit. Barriers include variable parent work schedules, limited opportunities for individual classroom support, and reduced intelligibility during unfamiliar tasks. Strengths include interest in interaction, responsiveness to models, familiar routine vocabulary, and supportive caregivers.

No feeding therapy recommendation based on current history and observation. Recurrent ear infections warrant continued pediatric follow-up. Current hearing information supports access to speech during this assessment; hearing status may change with illness. A repeat evaluation should be considered if new hearing concerns arise or progress differs substantially from expectations.

P: PLAN / RECOMENDACIONES

1. Begin skilled bilingual speech-language therapy once weekly for 45 minutes, with an initial 12-week treatment block. Use Spanish and English according to task, family preference, and classroom demands. Reassess functional progress before changing frequency. Coordinate scheduling through the parent contact information above.

2. Language goal 1: Follow unfamiliar two-step directions containing one location concept in 8/10 opportunities with min cues across three treatment sessions. Use objects, demonstrations, then reduced visual support. Practice equivalent concepts in both languages without requiring word-for-word translation.

3. Language goal 2: Produce an agent-action-object message to request, explain, or comment in 4/5 opportunities with min cues. Accept grammatical forms appropriate to either language. Track independent use separately from imitation and from responses given after direct models.

4. Functional goal 3: Repair a misunderstood message through slower repetition, an added word, gesture, or picture support in 4/5 opportunities with min cues. Adults should signal the missing information calmly: 'Tell me which one'] or 'Dime cuál'].

5. Speech goal 4: Produce /k/ and /g/ in selected functional words with 80% accuracy and mod cues, subject to baseline confirmation. Use phonological contrasts and a Cycles framework when indicated. Monitor generalization in spontaneous Spanish and English.

6. Coach caregivers using Hanen-informed responsive interaction: follow the child's interest, pause, acknowledge meaning, and expand one step. During meals, recast 'más agua'] as 'quiero más agua']. Avoid repeated demands to perform. Provide brief written examples in Spanish and English.

7. Ask classroom staff to pair concise directions with gestures, offer response time, and confirm understanding through action. Use pictures for routines and short event sequences. Encourage supported peer play with familiar partners. Share this report with preschool only after caregiver authorization; no external transmission completed.

8. Maintain both home languages. Read familiar picture books, describe actions, and invite comments without testing every page. Practice during dressing, snacks, and cleanup for five to ten minutes. Caregivers may use whichever language supports natural, sustained interaction.

9. Use simple visual choices when speech fails. Formal PECS is not currently prescribed. PROMPT was not administered; no conclusion about its suitability was made. Treatment selection should follow observed response and clinician training, with emphasis on functional communication.

10. Review progress on 01/08/2027. Repeat selected probes and compare independent performance, intelligibility, and participation. Request teacher feedback with authorization. Consider further developmental consultation if broader concerns emerge. Continue pediatric follow-up for ear symptoms and obtain updated hearing testing when clinically indicated.

Family education completed using examples and teach-back. Parents identified one home routine each for practice and understood that bilingualism should continue. Written recommendations supplied in both languages. Family agreed to contact the clinic about scheduling; treatment appointment remains pending.

Signed electronically: Camila Ríos Bennett, MS, CCC-SLP
Puente Claro Pediatric Communication, PLLC
